title: How IELTS Speaking is marked
bn: What the examiner listens for, and what separates band 6 from band 7
goal: In this chapter you will learn how the Speaking test is organised, what each of the four criteria rewards, and how to use this book over four weeks.

blocks.x: The Speaking test is a face-to-face conversation with one examiner. It lasts **11 to 14 minutes** and it is recorded. The test is the same for Academic and General Training candidates. It has three parts, and each part gives you a different kind of chance to show your English.

head: Part
Time
What happens
rows: The examiner checks your identity, then asks short questions on two or three familiar topics, such as your studies, your hometown, your free time or the weather.

You get a task card, a pencil and paper. You have 1 minute to prepare and make notes. You then talk for 1-2 minutes. The examiner stops you at 2 minutes and may ask one or two short rounding-off questions.
The examiner asks more abstract questions linked to the Part 2 topic. You give opinions, compare, explain causes and speculate about the future.

blocks.x: The examiner follows a script, so you cannot steer the conversation to a topic you have prepared. What you can control is how you answer. Part 1 is about short, natural replies. Part 2 tests whether you can organise a longer talk on your own. Part 3 gives you the most room to show complex grammar and precise vocabulary.

x: You do not have to agree with anything the examiner says. Your opinion is not marked, only your English.
The examiner will not tell you how you are doing. A neutral face is normal and means nothing.
In Part 1 the examiner can repeat a question but cannot explain it. In Part 3 the examiner can rephrase a question if you ask.

blocks.x: In Part 1, aim for two to four sentences per answer: a direct answer, a reason, and one detail or example. Then stop. The examiner has several topics to cover and will move on anyway.

Many Bangladeshi candidates treat Part 1 like a viva and give one-word answers such as 'Yes, I do.' Others recite a memorised paragraph. Both cost marks. Answer directly, then extend the answer in your own words.

You receive a band for each of four criteria. They carry **equal weight**, and your Speaking band is worked out from all four. A weak score in one criterion pulls the whole result down, so you cannot rely on a single strength.

head: Criterion
What it covers
The question in the examiner's mind
rows: Speed, pauses, self-correction, linking ideas, logical order
Can you keep going without long pauses, and do your ideas connect?
Range and precision of vocabulary, collocation, idiomatic language, paraphrase
Do you have the words to talk about any topic clearly and precisely?
Variety of structures and how often they are correct
Can you use complex sentences, and are most of them free of errors?
Individual sounds, word stress, sentence stress, intonation, chunking
Is it easy to understand you all the way through?

blocks.x: For Lexical Resource at band 7, you use vocabulary flexibly across a range of topics. You use some less common words and some idiomatic expressions, and you show that you know which words go together and which ones suit the situation. A few wrong choices are still allowed. When you do not know a word, you find another way to say it without stopping.
For Grammatical Range and Accuracy at band 7, you use a range of complex structures with some flexibility. Many of your sentences have no errors at all, although some mistakes still appear.
Band 7 does not mean perfect English. The examiner expects some errors at this level. What matters is that you attempt a range of language and keep control of most of it.
Students often worry about not sounding British or American. Accent is not marked. What is marked is how easy you are to understand, so work on clear sounds and stress rather than copying an accent.

pages.h: Band 6 and band 7 side by side: fluency and vocabulary

blocks.x: In any single sentence, the gap between band 6 and band 7 can look small. Over a whole test it is obvious. In the pairs below, the left column is typical of band 6 and the right column shows the same idea at band 7.

**Fluency and Coherence.** At band 6 you are willing to speak at length, but you sometimes lose the thread, repeat words or hesitate while you search for language. Linking words appear, but they are used mechanically. At band 7 you speak at length without obvious effort, and you use a range of linking words and spoken discourse markers naturally.

x: I like reading. Because reading is good. And also I read many books. And also I read novels.
I'm a big reader, actually. It helps me switch off after classes, and I tend to go for novels more than anything else.
Firstly, traffic is a problem. Secondly, pollution is a problem.
Traffic's the obvious problem, but the thing is, it's tied up with pollution as well, so you can't really fix one without the other.
Umm... umm... I think... umm... it is good.
Let me think... I'd say it's mostly a good thing, on balance.

blocks.x: **Lexical Resource.** At band 6 you have enough vocabulary to discuss topics at length and make your meaning clear, even if some choices are not quite right. Your paraphrasing works some of the time. At band 7 your words are more precise, you use some less common and idiomatic items, and your collocations sound natural.

x: My hometown is very crowded and very noisy.
My hometown is packed most of the day, and the traffic noise never really stops.
I want to get a good job.
I'm hoping to land a well-paid job in software.
The food was very nice.
The food was absolutely delicious, especially the kacchi.
Students have a lot of stress about exams.
Students are under a lot of pressure at exam time.

blocks.x: You do not need a rare word in every sentence. One or two precise words or collocations per answer is enough to change the examiner's impression.

pages.h: Band 6 and band 7 side by side: grammar and pronunciation

blocks.x: **Grammatical Range and Accuracy.** At band 6 you use a mix of simple and complex sentences, but with limited flexibility. Errors in complex structures are frequent, though they rarely make you hard to understand. At band 7 you use complex structures more freely and many sentences are error-free.

x: If I will get a scholarship, I go to Canada.
If I get a scholarship, I'll probably do my master's in Canada.
I am living in Savar since 2022.
I've been living in Savar since 2022.
People use phone too much. They complain they have no time.
The people who spend hours on their phones are often the ones who complain they've got no time.
Maybe the government should do something before.
Something should have been done about it years ago, to be honest.

blocks.x: **Pronunciation.** At band 6 you use a range of pronunciation features, but your control is mixed. You can generally be understood, although some words or sounds are unclear at times. At band 7 you keep the strengths of band 6 and add some features of band 8: you are easy to follow throughout, and your first language has little effect on how clear you are.

head: Feature
Band 6 habit
Band 7 habit
rows: Every syllable has the same weight: e-co-no-my
Stress falls on the right syllable: e-CON-o-my, de-VEL-op-ment
Word... by... word, or one long stream with no breaks
Groups of words that belong together, with short pauses between ideas
Flat, the same tone for every sentence
The voice rises and falls to show interest, contrast and the end of an idea

blocks.x: Many Bangladeshi speakers add a vowel before words that start with s plus a consonant, so 'school' becomes 'ishkul' and 'station' becomes 'isteshon'. Start the word directly with the /s/ sound. Practise 'sport, speak, student, street, study' slowly, then at normal speed.
Record yourself and listen for word stress in long words. If you are unsure, check the stress mark in a learner's dictionary before you use the word in the exam.
The examiner rates you on the whole test, not the first minute. Even so, your first few answers set an impression, and these are the things that show up early.

x: Whether you answer the question that was actually asked.
How long your answers are. One-word replies and two-minute speeches in Part 1 both stand out.
Whether you sound memorised: a flat rhythm, words far more advanced than the rest of your speech, or an answer that does not quite fit the question.
Basic accuracy: verb tenses, the third-person -s, plurals and articles.
How clear your individual sounds are.

blocks.x: Examiners are trained to recognise rehearsed answers. Language that does not fit the conversation naturally will not help your score, however advanced it looks. Learn phrases and structures, not whole answers.

Dropping the third-person -s is one of the most common errors at band 6: 'My father work in a bank.' Say 'My father works in a bank.' Listen for it in your recordings, because examiners notice it in almost every answer.
Missing articles: 'I am student of software engineering.' Say 'I'm a student of software engineering' or, more naturally, 'I study software engineering.'

Your first question is usually about your work, your studies or where you live. Have a few natural things ready to say about each, but do not memorise sentences. Practise saying them in a different way each time.

pages.h: Why vocabulary and grammar are the fastest route to band 7

blocks.x: Fluency and pronunciation grow slowly. They come from many hours of speaking and listening, and it is hard to see progress from one week to the next. Vocabulary and grammar are different. You can learn them in chunks, practise them on purpose and hear the difference within a few weeks.

x: Lexical Resource and Grammatical Range and Accuracy are two of the four criteria, so they make up half of your Speaking band.
Chunks help your fluency too. If you already know 'it's a bit of a double-edged sword', you do not have to build that sentence word by word, so you pause less.
A small set of structures covers most of what you need: conditionals, relative clauses, the present perfect, the passive, modals of speculation and 'used to' or 'would' for the past.
IELTS topics repeat. Work, study, hometown, technology, environment, health and travel come up again and again.

head: Area
Band 6 default
Band 7 habit to build
rows: very good, very bad, very big
excellent, awful, massive, or a precise collocation
do, make and get for everything
specific verbs: run errands, meet a deadline, catch up on
present perfect for experience and change: 'I've noticed...'
which means, whereas, even though, so that
I think, I think, I think
I'd say, as far as I can tell, to be honest, I suppose

blocks.x: Here is the practical effect. If your current criteria are all at 6 and you lift Lexical Resource and Grammar to 7, your Speaking band rises to 6.5. The work on chunks then pulls your fluency up as well, and that is how most students reach a 7.
Each time you learn a new phrase, say three sentences of your own with it, out loud, on the same day. A phrase you have never said aloud is unlikely to come out under pressure.

pages.h: Two answers to the same question

blocks.x: Here is one Part 1 question answered at two levels. Read the band 6 answer first, sentence by sentence, then compare it with the band 7 version. The question is: 'Do you prefer studying in the morning or at night?'

x: I prefer to study at night.
Definitely at night. I've never been a morning person.
Because at night it is very quiet.
Once everyone's settled down, it's quiet enough to really focus.
In the morning there is many noise in my hall.
My hall is pretty chaotic until about ten, with people rushing off to classes.
So I can concentrate more in night time.
That's when I get most of my work done. If I tried studying at seven in the morning, I'd probably fall asleep over my notes.

blocks.q: Do you prefer studying in the morning or at night?
x: Definitely at night. **I've never been a morning person**, and my hall is **pretty chaotic** until about ten, with people **rushing off to classes**. Once everyone's **settled down**, it's quiet enough to really focus, so that's when I **get most of my work done**. If I tried studying at seven in the morning, **I'd probably fall asleep** over my notes.
notes: 'I've never been a morning person' is a natural idiomatic phrase, and the present perfect shows grammatical range.
'pretty chaotic' and 'rushing off to classes' are precise, less common choices instead of 'very noisy'.
'Once everyone's settled down' uses a time clause with the present perfect and a phrasal verb.
'If I tried..., I'd probably fall asleep' is a second conditional for an imagined situation.
The answer is direct, gives a reason and adds a detail, which is the right length for Part 1.

blocks.x: Notice what changed. The band 6 answer is not wrong in its ideas. It is weaker because the vocabulary is general ('very quiet', 'many noise'), the sentences are all simple, and 'Because...' is left hanging as a sentence on its own. The band 7 answer says the same things with precise words, a phrasal verb, a time clause and a conditional.

blocks.q: Find two grammar errors in the band 6 answer and correct them.
blocks.a: 'many noise' should be 'a lot of noise', because 'noise' is uncountable here. 'in night time' should be 'at night'. You could also join 'Because at night it is very quiet' to the sentence before it.

blocks.x: When you practise, write down your own band 6 answer first, then upgrade it line by line like this. It is the quickest way to see your own habits.

pages.h: A four-week plan for using this book

blocks.x: You need about an hour a day. Short, regular practice works far better than one long session at the weekend. Find a study partner in your hall or class if you can, because speaking to a real person is the best practice there is.

head: Week
Focus
Daily tasks
rows: Learn 10-12 phrases from one topic page. Say each one in a sentence of your own. Answer five Part 1 questions aloud using them.
Pick one structure a day (conditionals, relative clauses, present perfect, passive, speculation). Answer three Part 3 questions using it at least twice.
One cue card a day with exactly 1 minute of preparation and a 2-minute talk. Then answer three linked Part 3 questions.
A full 11-14 minute test every second day, recorded. On the other days, fix the problems you heard.

x: Choose one question and set a timer.
Record your answer on your phone without notes.
Listen once and write down every word you repeated and every error you heard.
Use the pairs tables in this book to upgrade two or three phrases.
Record the same answer again and compare the two versions.

blocks.x: Keep a phrase notebook organised by topic, not by date. Before the exam, read through the topics in the order they are most likely to come up: studies, hometown, free time, technology.
Learning long word lists with Bangla meanings and no example sentences rarely helps in Speaking. Learn each item as a chunk in a sentence, for example 'meet a deadline', not 'deadline'.

title: Lexical resource for band 7
bn: Precise words, natural collocations and the right register
goal: In this chapter you will learn what band 7 vocabulary actually means and how to replace general words with precise, natural ones.

blocks.x: The band 7 description talks about less common words, idiomatic language and collocation. These terms worry many students, who think they need to sound like a dictionary. They do not. Each one has a simple, practical meaning.

head: Term
What it really means
Example
rows: A word that is more precise than the first word most learners reach for. It does not have to be rare.
'exhausted' instead of 'very tired'; 'commute' instead of 'go to work'
Fixed expressions and phrasal verbs that native speakers use in everyday conversation.
'it's not my cup of tea', 'catch up on sleep', 'on a tight budget'
Words that naturally go together. Other combinations are understood but sound odd.
'heavy rain', not 'big rain'; 'make a decision', not 'do a decision'
Choosing words that suit a spoken conversation, neither too formal nor too slangy.
Saying the same thing another way, especially when you do not know or cannot remember a word.
'the person who owns our flat' for 'landlord'

blocks.x: The examiner is not counting rare words. They are listening for **precision and naturalness**: words that say exactly what you mean, in combinations a fluent speaker would use.

Using impressive words in the wrong place lowers your score. 'My village is very picturesque and ubiquitous' sounds memorised, and 'ubiquitous' (found everywhere) makes no sense here. Use a word only if you are sure of its meaning and its usual partners.
A simple test for a new word: can you say it in three different sentences about your own life? If not, it is not ready for the exam yet.

Band 6 speakers lean on 'very' with a small set of adjectives. One strong adjective often does the job better. Strong adjectives such as 'exhausted' or 'delicious' already contain the meaning of 'very', so use 'absolutely' or 'really' with them, not 'very'.

x: very tired
exhausted, worn out
very hungry
starving
very big
huge, massive
very small
tiny
very happy
delighted, thrilled
very angry
furious
very interesting
fascinating
very crowded
packed
very hot

very cold
freezing
very busy
flat out, snowed under
very surprised
amazed
After the exam I was very tired.
After the exam I was completely worn out.
The bus was very crowded.
The bus was absolutely packed.
Dhaka is very hot in April.
Dhaka is scorching in April.
I was very happy when I got the result.
I was thrilled when I got the result.

blocks.x: 'Very delicious' and 'very exhausted' are common errors. Strong adjectives take 'absolutely', 'completely' or 'really': 'absolutely delicious', 'completely exhausted'.

blocks.q: Upgrade each phrase with one strong adjective: (a) very cold water (b) a very big problem (c) I was very surprised.
blocks.a: (a) freezing water (b) a huge problem or a massive problem (c) I was amazed.

blocks.x: Learn strong adjectives with 'absolutely' as a pair: 'absolutely freezing', 'absolutely starving'. Then you will not reach for 'very' by mistake.

pages.h: Replacing good, bad, nice and thing

blocks.x: 'Good', 'bad', 'nice' and 'thing' are not wrong, but they say very little. The examiner hears them dozens of times a day. A more precise word tells the examiner exactly what you mean and shows range.

x: a good teacher
an inspiring teacher, a patient teacher
good food
tasty food, delicious food
a good idea
a sensible idea, a clever idea
good weather
lovely weather, clear skies
a good salary
a decent salary, a well-paid job
good at maths
strong in maths, gifted at maths
bad weather
miserable weather, a downpour
a bad habit
an unhealthy habit
a bad experience
a frustrating experience, a nightmare
bad quality
poor quality
a nice person
a friendly, kind or considerate person
a nice place
a pleasant place, a peaceful spot
a nice view
a stunning view
The main thing is the cost.
The main drawback is the cost.
There are many things to do in Cox's Bazar.
There's plenty to do in Cox's Bazar.
I like music, films, things like this.
I like music, films, that sort of thing.
On Fridays I do my things.
On Fridays I run errands and do my laundry.

blocks.q: Replace 'good' or 'nice' in each sentence: (a) She's a really nice neighbour. (b) He gave me good advice. (c) It was a nice day for a picnic.
blocks.a: Possible answers: (a) She's a really considerate neighbour. (b) He gave me sound advice or useful advice. (c) It was a lovely day for a picnic.

blocks.q: Do you like the area where you live now?
x: Yes, I do. The area around my hall is **surprisingly green** for somewhere so close to Dhaka, and there's a **lively little tea stall** right outside the gate where we hang out most evenings. The one **drawback** is the dust in winter, which **gets into everything**, but on the whole it's a **really pleasant** place to live.
notes: 'surprisingly green' is a precise adverb and adjective combination instead of 'very nice'.
'drawback' replaces the vague 'bad thing'.
'which gets into everything' is a relative clause with a natural idiomatic phrase.
'on the whole' gives a balanced, spoken-style conclusion without sounding like an essay.

blocks.x: A collocation is a pair of words that fluent speakers put together without thinking. 'Big rain' is understandable, but nobody says it. Wrong collocations are one of the clearest signs of band 6 vocabulary, and correct ones are among the easiest band 7 features to learn.

head: Avoid
Natural collocation
Example
rows: We had heavy rain all week.
There's always heavy traffic on the highway.
I need a cup of strong tea to wake up.
Students pay a high price for textbooks.
There's fierce competition for government jobs.
He's been a close friend since school.
I'm living on a tight budget.
We grabbed a quick bite before class.
a busy schedule, a hectic schedule
My schedule is hectic this semester.
There's been a sharp rise in rent.
It's a common mistake among new drivers.
There was a strong smell of smoke.

x: Prices are very high now because of big inflation.
Prices have shot up because of high inflation.
There is big competition for jobs.
There's fierce competition for jobs.
He is my deep friend.
He's one of my closest friends.

blocks.q: Correct the collocations: (a) a big smoker (b) strong rain (c) a high mistake.
blocks.a: (a) a heavy smoker (b) heavy rain (c) a serious mistake or a big mistake.

blocks.q: Do you often eat out?
x: Not that often, since I'm **on a tight budget** as a student. When we do go out, it's usually for **a quick bite** at one of the cheap places near campus. Once a month or so, though, a group of us **treat ourselves to** a proper biryani. It's quite **a heavy meal**, so we usually **skip dinner** afterwards.
notes: 'on a tight budget' and 'a quick bite' are natural adjective and noun collocations.
'treat ourselves to' is an idiomatic verb phrase.
'When we do go out' uses the emphatic 'do', a less common grammar feature.
'a heavy meal' and 'skip dinner' are collocations a fluent speaker would use.

blocks.x: Verb choice is where Bangladeshi speakers lose most collocation marks, because English often uses a different verb from Bangla. Learn the verb and the noun together as one unit.

Common nouns
Example
rows: a decision, a mistake, progress, an effort, friends, a living
I've made a lot of progress this year.
research, a course, homework, the housework, a degree
I'm doing a course in data science.
a break, a photo, an exam, medicine, a risk
a chat, a rest, a look, a word with someone
Can I have a look at your notes?
We paid a visit to my uncle in Sylhet.
a lie, the truth, a story, a joke
I just managed to meet the deadline.
The campaign raised awareness of dengue.
I gave a presentation on climate data.
a cold, a bus, someone's attention
I caught a cold in the rain.

blocks.x: These come from direct translation and are very common: 'give an exam' (say 'take an exam' or 'sit an exam'), 'eat medicine' (say 'take medicine'), 'open the light' (say 'turn on the light'), 'say a lie' (say 'tell a lie'), 'do a mistake' (say 'make a mistake').

x: I will give my final exam in December.
I'm sitting my finals in December.
Please open the fan.
Could you turn on the fan?
I did many mistakes in the test.
I made quite a few mistakes in the test.
She took a decision to study abroad.
She made the decision to study abroad.

blocks.q: Why do some young people find it hard to make decisions about their careers?
x: I think it's partly because there are simply so many options now. When my father was my age, you became a doctor, an engineer or a government officer, and that was it. These days young people **face pressure** from their families to **play it safe**, but they also see friends **making a living** from freelancing or content creation. So it's hard to **make a decision** when every path looks risky in a different way.

On top of that, a lot of students **don't get much guidance** at university. They end up **doing a degree** they're not passionate about, and they only really **take stock** of what they want in their final year.
notes: 'face pressure', 'make a decision' and 'doing a degree' are correct verb and noun collocations.
'play it safe' and 'take stock' are idiomatic expressions used naturally.
'When my father was my age' contrasts past and present with a time clause.
'end up doing' is a natural phrasal verb with an -ing form.
The answer gives a reason, a contrast and an example, which suits Part 3.

blocks.x: Most useful words belong to a family: a verb, a noun, an adjective and sometimes an adverb. Knowing the whole family lets you change the shape of a sentence instead of repeating the same word. It also prevents a very common band 6 error: the right word in the wrong form.

Here is how a family helps you vary a sentence: 'The river near my village has become badly polluted. Most of the pollution comes from factories upstream.' The idea repeats, but the word does not, so the answer sounds controlled rather than repetitive.
'Economic' means connected with the economy ('economic growth'). 'Economical' means cheap to run or careful with money ('an economical car'). Students mix them up all the time.

blocks.q: Use the correct form of the word in brackets: (a) Tuition fees are not ___ for most families. (afford) (b) She's very ___ and hates losing. (compete) (c) Exercise is ___ for mental health. (benefit)
blocks.a: (a) affordable (b) competitive (c) beneficial

blocks.x: When you write a new word in your notebook, write its whole family next to it, with stress marked: SUC-cess, suc-CESS-ful. Stress often moves between forms.

pages.h: Formal and informal register in speaking

blocks.x: The Speaking test is a polite conversation with a stranger. The right style sits in the middle: relaxed and natural, but not slangy. Essay language sounds stiff when spoken, and street slang sounds careless. Both suggest weak awareness of style, which is part of the band 7 description.

head: Too formal for speaking
Too informal for the exam
Natural middle
rows: Quite a lot of, plenty of

x: Individuals who reside in urban areas commence work early.
People who live in cities tend to start work early.
It is evident that numerous youngsters purchase products online.
It's pretty clear that a lot of young people buy things online.
Gotta say, it's kinda bad, you know.
I have to say, it's not ideal, to be honest.

blocks.q: Should the government spend more money on public transport?
x: Yes, I'm fairly convinced it should. In Dhaka, **a huge proportion of** people rely on buses, and most of them are old, overcrowded and honestly a bit unsafe. If the government **invested properly in** the metro and in modern buses, fewer people would **feel the need to** buy cars or motorbikes, and that would **ease congestion** quite a lot.

Of course, it's not cheap, and some people would argue the money should go to hospitals instead. But I'd say transport **has a knock-on effect** on everything else. If people can get to work on time, the whole economy **benefits from** it.
notes: 'a huge proportion of' and 'ease congestion' are precise collocations in a neutral spoken style.
'If the government invested..., fewer people would...' is a second conditional used for a hypothetical policy.
'has a knock-on effect' is an idiomatic expression that fits Part 3 discussion.
Phrases like 'I'm fairly convinced', 'honestly' and 'I'd say' keep the register conversational.

blocks.x: If a word appears mostly in newspapers or essays, use it sparingly in speaking. One formal word in a relaxed sentence sounds educated. A whole sentence of them sounds memorised.
Flexibility means you can talk about the same idea in more than one way and adapt your words to the question. It is what separates band 7 from a candidate who simply knows a lot of words.

x: Do not repeat the examiner's question word for word. If the examiner asks 'Do you like reading?', start with 'I'm quite a keen reader' rather than 'Yes, I like reading.'
Change the word form: 'decide' becomes 'decision', 'pollute' becomes 'pollution'.
Change the structure instead of hunting for a synonym: 'A lot of people use mobile banking' becomes 'Mobile banking is used by almost everyone'.
Use a pronoun or 'that' to refer back, so you do not need to repeat the noun at all.
When you are missing a word, describe it and keep going.
Yes, I like reading. I like reading novels. Reading is relaxing.
Yes, I'm quite a keen reader. Novels are my favourite, mainly because they help me switch off.
I like my hometown because my hometown has good food.
What I love about where I grew up is the food. You can't get fuchka like that anywhere else.
Technology is useful. Technology helps students.
Technology has made studying far easier. I can't imagine doing my degree without it.

blocks.x: Swapping in a new synonym every time you mention something ('my hometown... my native city... my birthplace... my place of origin') sounds forced. Use the noun, then a pronoun, then perhaps one alternative.

blocks.q: Begin an answer to this Part 1 question without repeating its words: 'Do you enjoy cooking?'
blocks.a: Possible answers: 'Not really, if I'm honest. I can make a basic dal, but that's about it.' or 'I'm a bit of a disaster in the kitchen, to be honest.'

blocks.x: Before the exam, practise answering the ten most common Part 1 questions with an opening that paraphrases the question. It quickly becomes a habit.

title: Topic vocabulary bank
bn: Ready-to-use phrases for the topics that come up again and again
goal: In this chapter you will learn the collocations and phrases you need for the eight topic areas that appear most often in the Speaking test.

blocks.x: The same topic areas appear in test after test. If you have ten or twelve natural phrases ready for each one, you will rarely be stuck for words. Each page in this chapter gives you a table of phrases, a set of upgrades and a short model answer.

x: Read the table aloud, including the example sentences.
Cover the example column and make your own sentence for each phrase, about your own life.
Read the model answer and notice how the phrases fit into natural speech.
Answer the same question yourself, out loud, using at least four phrases from the page.
Come back to the page two days later and repeat step 4 without looking.

blocks.x: Do not try to fit every phrase into one answer. Two to five per answer is natural. More than that sounds like a list.
Do not memorise the model answers. The examiner may ask a slightly different question, and a memorised answer will not fit. Learn the phrases, then build new answers.

title: Natural spoken language
bn: Phrasal verbs, idioms, hedging and the small words that make speech flow
goal: In this chapter you will learn the phrasal verbs, idioms and spoken markers that make you sound natural rather than memorised.

blocks.x: Phrasal verbs are a verb plus a small word such as 'up', 'out' or 'on'. In conversation, fluent speakers use them far more often than single formal verbs. 'I put it off' sounds natural. 'I postponed it' sounds like a letter. Using a few phrasal verbs correctly is one of the clearest signs of **idiomatic vocabulary**.

blocks.x: Idioms impress the examiner only when they are current, used correctly and suited to the conversation. Many idioms in older IELTS books are dated or too dramatic. Native speakers rarely use them, so they sound memorised.

blocks.x: Fluent speakers rarely state opinions as hard facts. They soften them with short phrases. This is called **hedging**. It makes you sound thoughtful and polite, it helps with complex Part 3 questions, and it gives you a second to plan the rest of your sentence.

Yes.

blocks.q: Do you think online learning will replace traditional classrooms?
x: **I'd say** probably not completely, at least not in the near future. Online courses are great for **picking up** specific skills, and I've done a couple myself. But **it depends** a lot on the subject. Something like coding works quite well online, whereas lab subjects or medicine **more or less** need people in the same room.

**As far as I can tell**, what's more likely is a mix of both, where lectures are recorded and class time is used for discussion. **I could be wrong**, but most students I know **tend to** lose motivation if they never see their classmates.
notes: Hedges such as 'I'd say', 'it depends', 'more or less', 'as far as I can tell' and 'I could be wrong' make the opinion sound balanced.
'whereas' links a clear contrast between two types of subject.
'what's more likely is a mix of both' is a cleft structure, and 'where lectures are recorded' adds a relative clause with a passive.

blocks.a: Possible answers: (a) I'd say rickshaws can be a bit dangerous, especially on main roads. (b) As far as I know, most people in Dhaka find the traffic really frustrating.

blocks.x: Hedging every sentence makes you sound unsure. Use one or two hedges per answer, then state your main point clearly.

Essay linkers such as 'in conclusion', 'consequently' or 'nevertheless' sound strange in conversation. Speech has its own set of markers. They show the examiner how your ideas connect, and they sound natural because fluent speakers use them all the time.

blocks.x: Saying 'actually' at the start of every answer is a common habit among Bangladeshi speakers. 'Actually' signals a correction or a surprise. If nothing surprising follows, leave it out.

blocks.q: Are people in your country reading less than before?
x: **Actually**, I'm not sure they are. **The thing is**, people read all the time now, it's just that most of it is on a phone. My younger cousins hardly ever touch a printed book, **mind you**, but they read long posts and articles every day.

**Having said that**, I do think deep reading has suffered. It's much harder to **concentrate on** a novel for an hour when your phone keeps buzzing. **So basically**, I'd say we read more words than ever, but in shorter pieces, and **that's a bit of a shame**.

'The thing is', 'mind you' and 'having said that' connect the ideas in a spoken, not written, way.
'I do think' uses emphatic 'do' to stress the speaker's view.
'So basically' signals a short summary, and 'that's a bit of a shame' adds a natural personal reaction.

Everyone needs a moment to think, especially in Part 3. Silence or a long 'umm' hurts your fluency score. A short natural phrase does not. The examiner hears that you are thinking in English, which is what fluent speakers do.

pages.h: Paraphrasing when you forget a word

blocks.x: Every speaker forgets words, even in their first language. The band 7 description rewards you for paraphrasing effectively, so a forgotten word is a chance to show skill. The key is not to stop. Describe the thing and keep talking.

x: Do not freeze or switch to Bangla. Keep your voice moving.
Start with a general word: 'It's a kind of...', 'It's a sort of...'
Say what it does: 'the thing you use to...', 'the person who...'
Say what it looks like or where you find it.
If the word comes back to you, add it: 'Oh, a wardrobe.' If not, move on.

Phrase
Example

blocks.q: What kind of furniture do you have in your room?
x: Not much, since it's a hall room. There's a bed, a desk and, um, **what do you call it**, the tall cupboard **where you hang your clothes**. Oh, a wardrobe. I've also got **a small shelf for** my books and a plastic chair, which, **if I'm honest**, isn't very comfortable.
notes: 'what do you call it' buys time naturally instead of stopping.
'the tall cupboard where you hang your clothes' is an effective paraphrase using a relative clause.
The speaker remembers the word and adds it, which sounds completely natural.
'which, if I'm honest, isn't very comfortable' is a relative clause with a hedge inside it.

blocks.q: Paraphrase these words without saying them: (a) landlord (b) umbrella (c) traffic jam

blocks.x: Practise with a friend: one person names an object in the room, the other describes it without saying its name. Ten minutes of this builds the habit quickly.

title: Paraphrasing and avoiding repetition
bn: Say the same thing in new words, and never get stuck on a missing word
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to rephrase the examiner's question, swap repeated words for synonyms and general nouns, talk around a word you do not know, and change word forms to keep your speech flexible.

blocks.x: One of the clearest differences between band 6 and band 7 in Lexical Resource is **the ability to paraphrase**. At band 6 you have enough words to talk about most topics, but you tend to repeat the same ones. At band 7 you use vocabulary flexibly, you include some less common words and idioms, and you can rephrase an idea when the first word that comes to mind is not quite right.

Examiners notice repetition very quickly. If the question is about 'public transport' and you say 'public transport' five times in one answer, it sounds as if you only know one way to say it. If you say 'public transport', then 'buses and trains', then 'getting around the city', you show range without any extra effort.

x: Repeating the exact words of the question in your first sentence.
Using one key noun again and again in the same answer.
Freezing when you do not know a specific word.
Using a word in only one form (for example, always 'decide' and never 'decision' or 'decisive').
Public transport is cheap. I use public transport every day. Public transport is crowded.
Public transport is cheap, and I use buses every day, although they're always packed.
My hometown is nice. I love my hometown.
My hometown is lovely. I'm really attached to the place.
Social media is useful, but social media wastes time.
Social media is useful, but it can eat up a lot of your time.

blocks.x: This chapter deals with each of these four problems in turn. None of them needs a huge vocabulary. They need a few habits that you practise until they become automatic.
Paraphrasing does not mean finding a rare synonym for every word. A simple, accurate rephrase ('Do you like cooking?' to 'I'm quite into it, actually') is worth more than a strange word used wrongly.

Many candidates start every answer by repeating the question: 'Do you like reading? Yes, I like reading.' It is grammatically correct, but it wastes your first sentence and tells the examiner nothing about your vocabulary. A better opening **answers the question in different words**.

x: Do you like your hometown? Yes, I like my hometown.
Yes, I'm really fond of it, actually.
Do you often use public transport? Yes, I often use public transport.
Pretty much every day. I rely on buses to get to campus.
Is it important to save money? Yes, it is important to save money.
Absolutely. Having something put aside gives you real peace of mind.
What kind of music do you listen to? I listen to many kinds of music.
I've got quite broad taste, but I mostly go for acoustic stuff.
Do you enjoy shopping? I don't enjoy shopping.
Not really. I find crowded markets quite draining.
How often do you go to the cinema? I go to the cinema sometimes.
Once every couple of months, I'd say, usually when a big release comes out.

head: Question phrase
Natural paraphrase at the start of your answer
rows: I'm (quite) into ... / I'm a big fan of ... / It's not really my thing.
Fairly regularly. / Every now and then. / Hardly ever, to be honest.
I'd say it's essential. / It matters a lot. / It's not a big priority for me.
I think the main reason is ... / It mostly comes down to ...
Quite a lot, actually. / It's almost unrecognisable now. / Not as much as you'd think.

blocks.x: Some students overcorrect and avoid the topic word completely, which sounds unnatural. You may use the key word once. The problem is using it in every sentence. Rephrase it at the start, then mix it with synonyms later.

blocks.q: Rephrase the start of this answer: 'Do you like spending time outdoors? Yes, I like spending time outdoors.'
blocks.a: Possible answer: 'Yes, I love being out in the fresh air, especially in winter when it isn't too hot.'

blocks.x: Prepare a small set of alternatives for the topics that come up again and again in Part 1 and Part 3. You do not need perfect synonyms. You need words and phrases that are **close enough in meaning** and natural in the context.

head: Topic
Key word
Alternatives you can rotate
rows: career, position, line of work, what I do for a living
do a degree in, major in, take a course in, be at university
place, area, the capital, an urban area, where I grew up
tasty, really good, mouth-watering, full of flavour
journey, getaway, holiday, a few days away
mate, close friend, someone I've known for years

x: Pollution is a big problem. Pollution makes people sick.
Pollution is a serious problem. The dirty air in Dhaka makes a lot of people ill.
I use my phone a lot. My phone is very useful.
I'm on my phone a lot. It's honestly the most useful device I own.
My friend is kind. My friend helps me.
My closest friend is really kind. She's always there when I need help.
The food was delicious. The sweets were also delicious.
The food was delicious, and the sweets were even better.

blocks.x: Do not cycle through synonyms just to avoid repetition, for example 'city ... metropolis ... urban centre ... municipality' in four sentences. It sounds forced. Two or three natural alternatives are enough, and simple pronouns ('it', 'there') often do the job better.
Learn alternatives as phrases, not single words. 'What I do for a living' is easier to drop into an answer than 'occupation', and it sounds more like real speech.

blocks.q: Give two natural alternatives for 'trip' and one for 'delicious'.
blocks.a: For example: 'journey', 'getaway'; 'really tasty' or 'full of flavour'.

blocks.x: A quick way to avoid repeating a long phrase is to refer back to it with **a general noun** or a pronoun. Native speakers do this all the time. Once you have said 'young people spending hours on social media', you can call it 'this habit', 'that kind of thing' or simply 'it'.

head: Instead of repeating ...
Refer back with ...
rows: this arrangement, that way of working
people like that, those students, they
going to the gym every day
these services, that sort of thing

x: Many people work from home now. Working from home saves time. Working from home is also cheaper.
Many people work from home now. It saves time, and the arrangement is cheaper for companies too.
Students copy assignments from the internet. Students who copy assignments do not learn.
Some students copy assignments from the internet. People like that don't really learn anything.
Traffic jams are terrible in Dhaka. Traffic jams waste hours every day.
Traffic in Dhaka is terrible. The problem wastes hours of people's time every day.

blocks.x: Use 'this' when you point back to something you have just said, and 'that' when it feels more distant or when you are slightly critical: 'That kind of attitude really annoys me.'

blocks.q: Replace the repeated phrase with a general noun: 'A lot of teenagers stay up late gaming. Staying up late gaming affects their marks.'
blocks.a: 'A lot of teenagers stay up late gaming. The habit affects their marks.' ('This habit' or 'It' also work.)

pages.h: Describing a word you do not know

blocks.x: Every speaker forgets a word sometimes. The difference at band 7 is that you keep going. Instead of stopping or saying the word in Bangla, you **talk around the word**: you say what kind of thing it is, what it does or what it looks like. Examiners reward this because it is exactly what fluent speakers do.

head: Strategy
Useful phrases
rows: Say what category it belongs to
It's a kind of ... / It's a type of ... / It's a sort of ...
Say what it is used for
It's the thing you use to ... / You use it for ...
It's long and thin, a bit like ... / It looks a bit like ...
It's the person who ... / Someone who ...
I can't think of the exact word, but it's ...

x: I bought a ... um ... I don't know the word.
I bought one of those metal cupboards with a lock, the kind you keep valuables in.
My uncle is a ... he works with ... sorry.
My uncle is the person who checks the accounts of big companies, an auditor, I think.
We ate pitha. Pitha is pitha.
We ate pitha, which are a kind of rice cake people make in winter.
I was stuck in the ... the thing on the road.
I was stuck at one of those level crossings where the road goes over the railway.

blocks.x: Do not apologise at length ('Sorry, sorry, my English is not good'). It breaks your fluency and draws attention to the gap. A short 'I can't think of the word, but ...' is enough.

blocks.q: What kind of things do you keep in your bedroom?
x: Not much, to be honest, because my room in the hall is **pretty cramped**. There's a bed, a desk and a **sort of metal cupboard** with a lock, **the kind you keep valuables in**. I've also got a **folding rack** for my clothes, and **that's about it**, really.
notes: 'a sort of metal cupboard ... the kind you keep valuables in' describes an object without knowing its exact name.
'pretty cramped' paraphrases 'small' and sounds natural.
'that's about it' is an informal phrase that closes the answer smoothly.

blocks.x: Another way to avoid repetition is to **change the form of a word**. If you have already used the noun 'decision', you can switch to the verb 'decide' or the adjective 'decisive'. This shows the examiner that you control word families, which is part of using vocabulary flexibly.

x: Pollution is bad. Pollution is in the rivers.
Pollution is a big issue. A lot of our rivers are badly polluted.
The job market has a lot of competition.
The job market is extremely competitive.
Making a decision is hard for me.
I'm not very decisive, so I take ages to choose.
Exercise has a lot of benefits.
Regular exercise is really beneficial, especially for students who sit all day.

blocks.x: Watch out for 'economic' and 'economical'. 'Economic' is about the economy ('economic growth'), while 'economical' means it saves money ('an economical car'). Many candidates mix them up.

blocks.q: Rewrite with an adjective: 'Bangladesh has a lot of success in cricket these days.'
blocks.a: 'Bangladesh has been quite successful in cricket these days.' (or 'The national side has become a lot more successful.')

blocks.x: When you learn a new word, learn at least one other form with it. 'Compete, competitive' takes no longer to learn than 'compete' alone.

The answers below use all four techniques. Look for the opening rephrase, the synonyms, the general nouns and the word form changes. The bold items are the language that pushes the answers towards band 7.

blocks.q: Do you like cooking?
x: Yes, I'd say I'm **quite into it**, although I only really started when I moved into my university hall. The canteen food **gets a bit repetitive**, so at weekends I **whip up** something simple, like egg curry or khichuri. It's not restaurant quality, but it's **cheap and filling**.
notes: The answer never repeats 'like cooking'; 'quite into it' rephrases it.
'whip up' is an informal phrasal verb for cooking something quickly.
'gets a bit repetitive' and 'cheap and filling' are natural collocations.

blocks.q: Why do some people prefer to live in big cities?
x: I think the main draw is opportunity. In a place like Dhaka, **most of the well-paid jobs** are concentrated in a few areas, so if you want to **build a career**, moving there **makes a lot of sense**. On top of that, city life offers things you simply can't get in a small town, like **decent hospitals** and good universities.
That said, it comes at a price. **The cost of living** is high and the traffic is **notoriously bad**, so a lot of people who move to the capital end up **missing the slower pace** of their hometown.
notes: 'big cities' becomes 'a place like Dhaka', 'city life' and 'the capital', so there is no repetition.
'the main draw' and 'it comes at a price' are idiomatic and appropriate.
'notoriously bad' and 'build a career' are strong collocations.
The relative clause 'who move to the capital' adds grammatical range.

blocks.q: Do you think technology has made people less creative?
x: Not really, no. I'd argue it's actually given **creative people** more tools than ever. Someone who wants to **create** music used to need an expensive studio, whereas now they can do it on a laptop. **Creativity** isn't really about tools anyway, it's about having ideas.
Having said that, I do think **constant scrolling** leaves less time for **original thinking**, because people **consume** so much content that they rarely stop to **produce** anything themselves.
notes: The word family 'creative', 'create', 'creativity' avoids repeating one form.
'consume' and 'produce' are a precise contrasting pair.
'constant scrolling' refers back to technology use with a specific, vivid phrase.
'Having said that' introduces a balanced counterpoint.

blocks.x: When you practise, record one answer, then listen for any word you used three or more times. Replace it the next time with a synonym, a general noun or a different word form.

title: Grammatical range for band 7
bn: The complex structures that lift your speaking score, and how to use them naturally
goal: In this chapter you will learn the complex structures examiners look for at band 7 and practise turning simple spoken sentences into more varied ones.

blocks.x: Grammatical Range and Accuracy is one of the four equally weighted criteria. At band 6 you mix simple and complex sentences, but the complex ones are limited and often contain errors. At band 7 you use **a range of complex structures** with some flexibility, and many of your sentences are completely error-free, even if a few mistakes remain.

In speech, 'complex' does not mean long. It means sentences built with relative clauses, conditionals, the passive, modal verbs and similar structures. A short sentence like 'If I'd known, I would have come' is more complex than a long chain of 'and ... and ... and'.

x: Relative clauses (defining and non-defining)
Conditionals (zero, first, second, third, mixed)
The passive voice
Modals of speculation and deduction
'wish' and 'if only'
Cleft sentences ('What I really like is ...')
Comparative structures ('the more ..., the more ...', 'nowhere near as ...')

blocks.x: Do not force a structure into every answer. Choose the one that fits the question: speculation for 'why do you think', conditionals for 'what would happen if', the passive for processes and changes.

A relative clause adds information about a noun. **Defining clauses** tell you which person or thing you mean, so you cannot remove them. Non-defining clauses add extra information, and in speech you mark them with a small pause where the commas would be.

head: Type
Pattern
Spoken example
rows: He's the teacher who got me interested in coding.
It's the app I use most.
That's the tea stall where we meet every evening.
My cousin, who lives in Sylhet, is visiting next week.
The bus was late, which meant I missed my class.
I have a friend whose father is a pilot.

x: I have a friend. He lives in Khulna. He is a doctor.
I have a friend who lives in Khulna, and he's a doctor.
The library is quiet. I study there.
The library is the only place where I can actually concentrate.
It rained all day. So we stayed inside.
It rained all day, which meant we were stuck inside.
My neighbour has a son. His son plays cricket for the district.
My neighbour has a son whose cricket is good enough for the district team.
I bought a book. My teacher recommended it.
I finally bought the book my teacher recommended.

blocks.x: Do not use 'which' for people ('my uncle which lives abroad') or add an extra pronoun ('the book that I read it'). Say 'my uncle, who lives abroad' and 'the book that I read'.

blocks.q: Who do you usually spend your weekends with?
x: Mostly with my roommate, Arif, **who's from Rajshahi**, and a couple of friends **I met in my first year**. We usually go to a small tea stall **where the owner knows** us all by name, and we just chat for hours. It's the part of the week **that I look forward to most**.
notes: 'who's from Rajshahi' is a non-defining clause adding extra detail.
'friends I met in my first year' is a defining clause with the pronoun left out, which is very natural in speech.
'where the owner knows us all by name' uses 'where' for a place.
'the part of the week that I look forward to most' ends with a preposition, as people do in speech.

blocks.x: Conditionals let you talk about real situations, imagined ones and regrets. Part 3 is full of questions that invite them: 'What would happen if ...?', 'Should the government ...?'. The key is matching the tense to how real the situation is.

head: Type
Form
Use
Spoken example
rows: If I drink coffee after six, I can't sleep.
If it rains tomorrow, we'll cancel the trip.
If I had more time, I'd learn to swim.
If + had + past participle, would have + past participle
If I'd left earlier, I wouldn't have missed the bus.
If + had + past participle, would + verb
A past event that changes the present
If I hadn't chosen software engineering, I'd probably be a teacher now.
If + past, would have + past participle
A general fact that affected the past
If I were more organised, I would have finished it on time.

x: Maybe I will get a scholarship. Then I will study abroad.
If I get a scholarship, I'll do my master's abroad.
I don't have a car. So I take the bus.
If I had a car, I'd probably drive, but for now I'm stuck with the bus.
I didn't study hard. I failed the test.
If I'd studied a bit harder, I wouldn't have failed that test.
I didn't learn English as a child. My English is not perfect now.
If I'd started English earlier, I'd be far more confident now.
Prices go up. People buy less.
When prices go up, people simply buy less.

blocks.x: Never put 'would' in the if-clause: 'If I would have money, I would travel' is wrong. Say 'If I had money, I'd travel.' In the third conditional, 'If I would have known' is also wrong: say 'If I'd known'.

blocks.q: Should the government make public transport free?
x: I'm not sure it should be completely free, but **if tickets were cheaper**, far more people **would leave their cars at home**. Look at the metro in Dhaka. **If it hadn't been built**, traffic on that route **would be even worse now**.

Still, the money has to come from somewhere. **If you make something free**, people **tend to take it for granted**, and the service **can go downhill**. So **if I were in charge**, I'd keep a small fare and spend the income on more routes.
notes: 'if tickets were cheaper ... would leave' is a second conditional for an imagined situation.
'If it hadn't been built ... would be even worse now' is a mixed conditional combined with the passive.
'If you make something free, people tend to' is a zero conditional for a general truth.
'take it for granted' and 'go downhill' are natural idioms.

blocks.x: The passive is useful when **the action matters more than the person** who did it, or when you do not know who did it. In Part 3 it helps you talk about changes in society, processes and rules: 'New roads are being built', 'Plastic bags have been banned'.

head: Tense
Passive form
Spoken example
rows: Most of our clothes are made in factories near Dhaka.
A new flyover is being built near my area.
Plastic bags have been banned, at least officially.
should / must / will be + past participle
My phone got stolen on the bus last year.

x: People build many new apartments in Dhaka.
Loads of new apartments are being built in Dhaka.
Someone stole my bike.
My bike got stolen outside the hall.
The government should make new laws.
I think new laws should be introduced.
They changed the exam system last year.
The exam system was changed last year.

blocks.x: Do not overuse the passive. A whole answer in the passive sounds like a report. Use one or two passives in an answer, mainly when talking about changes or processes.

blocks.q: How has shopping changed in your country?
x: Quite dramatically, I'd say. Ten years ago almost everything **was bought in local markets**, but now a huge amount **is ordered online** and **delivered within a day or two**. Lots of small businesses **have been set up** on Facebook, so they **don't even need a physical shop** at all.

The downside is that customers **are sometimes misled** by photos that look nothing like the real product. Personally, I think stricter rules **will need to be introduced** before people fully trust it.
notes: 'was bought', 'is ordered' and 'have been set up' use the passive in three different tenses.
'will need to be introduced' combines a modal structure with the passive.
'are sometimes misled' is a precise passive with an adverb placed correctly.
'look nothing like' is an idiomatic way to say 'look very different from'.

blocks.x: When you are not sure about something, modal verbs let you show **how certain you are**. This is common in Part 2 (when you describe an old memory) and Part 3 (when you guess at reasons).

head: Certainty
Present
Past
Example
rows: He must have been exhausted after that journey.
might / may / could have + past participle
They might have moved to Chattogram.
The parcel should have arrived by now.

x: I think he was tired.
He must have been really tired.
Maybe she forgot.
She might have forgotten about it.
I'm sure it was not expensive.
It can't have been that expensive.
Perhaps people were happier in the past.
People might have been happier in some ways, but it's hard to say.

blocks.x: A common error is 'must had' or 'might went'. After any modal you need 'have' plus the past participle: 'must have gone', 'might have left'. In fast speech it sounds like 'must've' and 'might've', but never write or say 'must of'.

blocks.q: Do you remember the first mobile phone you had?
x: Yes, it was a basic Nokia, and I **must have been about twelve** when I got it. It **can't have cost much**, because my dad bought it second-hand, and I think it **might have belonged** to one of his colleagues before. I **must have dropped it** a hundred times, but it never broke.
notes: 'must have been' shows strong certainty about the past.
'can't have cost much' is a negative deduction.
'might have belonged' shows that the speaker is only guessing.
Three different modal structures in one short answer show real range.

blocks.q: Make it a deduction: 'I'm sure the shop was closed, because the lights were off.'
blocks.a: 'The shop must have been closed, because the lights were off.'

blocks.x: Use 'wish' and 'if only' to talk about things you would like to be different. They are useful in Part 1 questions about your home, studies or daily routine, and in Part 2 when you describe a regret. The tense after 'wish' moves **one step back**.

head: What you want to change
Form
Example
rows: I wish I lived closer to campus.
I wish the hall were quieter.
I wish I'd studied harder in my first year.
I wish people wouldn't honk all the time.
I wish I could speak Japanese.

x: I live far from my university. It is a problem.
I wish I lived a bit closer to the university.
I didn't learn to drive. Now I regret it.
I wish I'd learnt to drive when I had the chance.
People throw rubbish on the street. I don't like it.
I wish people wouldn't throw rubbish in the street.
I can't play an instrument.
If only I could play the guitar properly.

blocks.x: Do not use 'will' after 'wish' ('I wish it will rain'). If you mean a hope about the future, use 'hope': 'I hope it rains tomorrow.'

blocks.q: Is there anything you'd like to change about where you live?
x: Honestly, **I wish the hall were** a bit quieter. There are four of us in one room, and someone's always on a call at midnight. **If only we had** a proper study room on each floor. I also **wish I'd picked** a room **facing away from the main road**, because the horns start at six.
notes: 'I wish the hall were' uses 'were' for an unreal present.
'If only we had' is a stronger form of 'wish' for the present.
'wish I'd picked' expresses a past regret with the past perfect.
'facing away from the main road' is a precise participle phrase.

blocks.x: A cleft sentence splits one idea into two parts so that you can **put emphasis** on the important bit. It is very common in natural speech, and it also gives you a moment to think while you start the sentence.

head: Pattern
Simple sentence
Cleft sentence
rows: What I really like is the practical work.
My mother taught me to cook.
It was my mother who taught me to cook.
The thing that annoys me most is the traffic.
All I want right now is some sleep.
I chose it because of the teachers.
The reason I chose it is that the teachers are excellent.

x: I love the food in Old Dhaka.
What I love about Old Dhaka is the food.
My uncle encouraged me to study IT.
It was my uncle who encouraged me to study IT.
The noise is the biggest problem.
The thing that bothers me most is the noise.
I just need a quiet place.
All I need is a quiet place to work.

blocks.x: Keep the verb agreement right: 'What I like most is the people', not 'are the people'. The 'What' part counts as singular, even if the noun after the verb is plural.

blocks.q: What do you enjoy most about your studies?
x: **What I really like is** the practical side. In software engineering, **it's the projects that** teach you the most, not the lectures. **The thing I find hardest**, though, is keeping up with deadlines when three courses **fall in the same week**. **What helps** is planning a bit every Sunday.
notes: 'What I really like is' and 'What helps is' are cleft sentences with 'what'.
'it's the projects that teach you' is an 'It ... that' cleft for emphasis.
'The thing I find hardest' adds a third cleft pattern without sounding repetitive.
'fall in the same week' is a natural collocation for deadlines.

blocks.x: Simple comparatives ('bigger', 'more expensive') are band 5 and 6 language. To sound like band 7, use **more flexible comparative structures** that show degree and relationship between ideas.

head: Structure
Meaning
Example
rows: The more I practise, the more confident I feel.
The bigger the city, the worse the traffic.
My village is nowhere near as crowded as Dhaka.
It's not quite as hot as last year.
Trains are far more reliable than buses.
Rent is getting higher and higher.

x: Dhaka is crowded. My village is not crowded.
My village is nowhere near as crowded as Dhaka.
When I study more, I get more tired.
The more I study, the more tired I get.
Prices are going up a lot.
Prices are getting higher and higher.
Online shopping is more cheap.
Online shopping is usually a bit cheaper.

blocks.x: Do not say 'more cheaper' or 'more better'. One-syllable adjectives take '-er' only. Use 'much better' or 'far cheaper' when you want to make the difference bigger.

blocks.q: Do you think life is better now than it was for your grandparents?
x: In some ways, yes, definitely. **The more technology develops**, **the easier** everyday tasks become. My grandmother had to fetch water from a pond, so her life was **nowhere near as comfortable** as mine.

But I'm not really sure we're **any happier than** they were. People back then had **far fewer choices**, but they were **much less stressed** about money and status. These days, **the more we earn**, **the more we seem to want**, so life isn't **necessarily better**, it's just different.
notes: 'The more technology develops, the easier ...' is a double comparative.
'nowhere near as comfortable as' shows a large difference in a natural way.
'far fewer choices' and 'much less stressed' modify comparatives with 'far' and 'much'.
'any happier than' is a comparative used in a negative statement.

blocks.q: Upgrade with a double comparative: 'If you sleep less, you feel worse.'
blocks.a: 'The less you sleep, the worse you feel.'

title: Tenses in speaking
bn: Choose the right tense for habits, changes, stories and the future
goal: In this chapter you will learn which tenses to use for habits, recent changes, past stories and future plans, so that your answers in all three parts sound accurate and varied.

pages.h: Why tenses matter in the Speaking test

blocks.x: Each part of the test pushes you towards different tenses. Part 1 is mostly about the present ('Do you work or study?'). Part 2 often asks you to describe **a past experience**, so you need past tenses. Part 3 asks about change and the future ('How will ...?', 'How has ... changed?').

Band 6 speakers often stay in the present simple and past simple. Band 7 speakers move between tenses easily: they use the present perfect for change, the past perfect for background in a story and a range of future forms for predictions. Using the right tense is also an accuracy issue, because wrong tenses are among the most frequent errors examiners hear.

head: Part
Typical question
Tenses you will need
rows: What do you usually do at weekends?
present simple, present continuous, present perfect
Describe a time when you helped someone.
past simple, past continuous, past perfect, used to / would
How has education changed? How will it change?
present perfect, passive, will, going to, future perfect

blocks.x: Listen to the tense in the question. 'What did you do ...?' needs the past. 'Have you ever ...?' needs the present perfect at the start, then usually the past simple for the details.

Use the **present simple** for habits, routines and permanent facts. Use the present continuous for things happening around now, temporary situations and current trends. Mixing the two in one answer is an easy way to show range.

head: Tense
Use
Time signal
Example
rows: I usually take a rickshaw to class.
at the moment, this term, these days
I'm staying with my aunt this month.
More people are working from home these days.
My roommate is always borrowing my charger.

x: I study for my exams now.
I'm studying for my exams at the moment.
Many young people start online businesses these days.
A lot of young people are starting their own online businesses these days.
I am living in Dhaka since 2020.
I've lived in Dhaka since 2020.
I am usually going to the gym on Fridays.
I usually go to the gym on Fridays.

blocks.x: State verbs such as 'know', 'like', 'want', 'believe' and 'own' are rarely used in the continuous. 'I am knowing him' is wrong. Say 'I've known him for years.'

blocks.q: Choose the correct form: 'These days, more people (buy / are buying) groceries online.'
blocks.a: 'are buying' (a current trend).

blocks.q: What do you usually do in the evenings?
x: On weekdays I **usually study** in the library until about nine, then I **grab dinner** with friends. At the moment, though, **I'm preparing for** my final exams, so **I'm spending** most evenings at my desk. It's not much fun, but **it's only for a few weeks**.
notes: 'usually study' (present simple) describes a routine.
'I'm preparing for' and 'I'm spending' (present continuous) describe a temporary situation.
'At the moment, though' signals the switch between the two tenses clearly.
'grab dinner' is a natural informal collocation.

pages.h: Present perfect and present perfect continuous

blocks.x: The **present perfect** connects the past to now. Use it for life experience ('I've been to Cox's Bazar twice'), for changes ('Dhaka has grown a lot') and for unfinished time ('I haven't seen him this week'). The present perfect continuous focuses on an activity that started in the past and is still going on: 'I've been learning French for six months'.

head: Form
Use
Example
rows: The roads have got much busier.
have / has + past participle + for / since
I've known my best friend since school.
I've been learning the guitar for two years.
Recent activity with a visible result
I've been running, so I'm a bit out of breath.

x: I learn English for ten years.
I've been learning English for about ten years.
I went to Sylhet two times in my life.
I've been to Sylhet twice.
Dhaka changed a lot.
Dhaka has changed a lot, even in the last five years.
I know him since 2018.
I've known him since 2018.

blocks.x: Do not use the present perfect with a finished time: 'I have visited Sylhet last year' is wrong. Use the past simple: 'I visited Sylhet last year.' Use the present perfect only when no specific past time is given.

blocks.q: Correct this: 'I am working here since January.'
blocks.a: 'I've been working here since January.'

blocks.q: Have you ever learned a musical instrument?
x: Yes, actually. **I've been learning** the guitar **for about two years** now, mostly from YouTube videos. **I haven't had** any proper lessons, so my technique isn't great, but **I've managed to learn** a few Bangla songs my friends like to sing along to. **I've never performed** in public, though.
notes: 'I've been learning ... for about two years' (present perfect continuous) shows an ongoing activity.
'I haven't had' and 'I've never performed' use the present perfect for experience.
'managed to learn' is a useful structure for something achieved with effort.
The answer mixes the present perfect with the present simple ('isn't great') correctly.

blocks.x: Part 2 often asks you to describe a time, an event or a day you remember. To tell a good story you need three past tenses working together. The **past simple** moves the story forward. The past continuous sets the scene. The past perfect goes back to something that happened even earlier.

head: Tense
Job in the story
Example
rows: It was pouring with rain and we were waiting for a bus.
Suddenly a car stopped and a man got out.
Earlier event, before the main story
I'd never met him before, but he'd seen us from the shop.
Earlier activity that had lasted some time
We'd been standing there for nearly an hour.

x: I walk to the market and I see my old teacher.
I was walking to the market when I saw my old teacher.
When I arrived, the film started already.
When I arrived, the film had already started.
I was very tired because I study all night.
I was exhausted because I'd been studying all night.
We go to the beach and we eat and we come back.
We drove down to the beach, had lunch at a small stall and got back just before dark.
Start with the background in the past continuous: 'It was a Friday, and we were having lunch ...'
Move the story on with the past simple: 'Then my phone rang ...'
Add earlier events with the past perfect when you need them: '... because I'd forgotten to tell my mother.'
End with a reflection in the present: 'Looking back, I think it taught me ...'

blocks.x: Many speakers start a story in the past and then slip into the present halfway through. Pick the past and stay there. If you notice the slip, correct it quickly and carry on: 'and he says, sorry, he said ...'.

blocks.q: Put the verbs in the right tense: 'When I (get) to the station, the train (already / leave).'
blocks.a: 'When I got to the station, the train had already left.'

pages.h: Used to and would for past habits

blocks.x: To talk about things that happened regularly in the past but do not happen now, use **used to or would**. Both are excellent in Part 2 stories about childhood and in Part 3 comparisons between the past and the present.

head: Form
Use
Example
rows: I used to live near the river.
Every evening we'd play cricket in the field.
I didn't use to like vegetables.
Did you use to walk to school?
Be familiar with (not a past habit)
I'm used to waking up early now.

x: When I was a child, I play in the rain.
When I was a kid, I used to play outside in the rain.
My grandmother told me stories every night.
My grandmother would tell me stories every night before bed.
In the past people did not have phones.
People didn't use to carry phones everywhere.
I am use to the traffic now.
I'm used to the traffic by now.

blocks.x: 'Would' works only for repeated actions, not states. 'I would live in Mymensingh' is wrong for a past state. Say 'I used to live in Mymensingh.' Also, do not confuse 'I used to' (past habit) with 'I'm used to' (I am familiar with).

blocks.q: Did you play a lot of games as a child?
x: All the time. **I used to live** near a big open field in Mymensingh, and every afternoon **we'd play** cricket until it got dark. If it rained, **we'd just carry on** in the mud. **I didn't use to** care about getting dirty, but my mother certainly did.
notes: 'I used to live' is correct for a past state; 'would' would be wrong here.
'we'd play' and 'we'd just carry on' use 'would' for repeated past actions.
'I didn't use to care' is the correct negative form.
The short contrast at the end ('but my mother certainly did') adds humour naturally.

pages.h: Future forms for plans and predictions

blocks.x: English has several ways to talk about the future, and each has a slightly different meaning. In Part 1 you may talk about your plans. In Part 3 you will often be asked to **predict** how things will change. Using more than just 'will' is a clear sign of range.

head: Form
Use
Example
rows: Prediction based on opinion, sudden decisions
I think more people will work remotely.
Plans already decided, predictions from evidence
I'm going to apply for a master's next year.
I'm meeting my supervisor on Thursday.
Completed before a future time (future perfect)
By 2035, most cars will have gone electric.
In progress at a future time (future continuous)
This time next year, I'll be studying abroad.
Prices are likely to keep rising.

x: I will meet my friend tomorrow at five.
I'm meeting a friend tomorrow at five.
Next year I will apply for a master's, I decided.
I'm going to apply for a master's next year.
In the future, robots will do many jobs.
Within twenty years, robots will have taken over a lot of routine jobs.
Maybe prices will go up.
Prices are likely to go up, especially for food.

blocks.q: Which form fits best? 'Look at those clouds. It (will / is going to) rain.'
blocks.a: 'is going to', because the prediction comes from evidence you can see.

blocks.q: How do you think people will travel in the future?
x: I think cities **will rely much more** on electric transport. The metro in Dhaka **is going to expand**, and I'd say a lot of commuters **will have switched** to trains by the mid 2030s. In fact, my cousin **is selling** his motorbike next month for exactly that reason.

Long-distance travel is harder to predict. Flying **is likely to become** more expensive if fuel taxes go up, so people **might start taking** trains again for shorter trips. And by the time I'm forty, **we'll probably be using** one app for every journey.
notes: 'will rely', 'is going to expand' and 'will have switched' show three different future forms.
'is selling ... next month' uses the present continuous for a fixed arrangement.
'is likely to become' expresses probability without overusing 'will'.
'we'll probably be using' is the future continuous.

blocks.x: Strong Part 3 answers often **move through time**: what used to happen, what has changed and what will happen next. You do not need to plan this. If the question asks about change, simply think 'then, now, next', and the tenses follow naturally.

head: Stage
Typical tenses
Example
rows: Now everyone expects a reply within minutes.
I think we'll see even faster communication.

blocks.q: How has your hometown changed in recent years?
x: It's changed **almost beyond recognition**. When I was a child, the area **was mostly farmland**, but over the last fifteen years **dozens of factories have been built**, and the population **has grown** enormously. **The roads have been widened**, which helps, but the town **is losing** a lot of its green space. My parents still live there, and even they get lost sometimes.
Right now, a new housing project **is going up** near my old school. Honestly, if this carries on, I think it **will have turned** into a suburb of Dhaka within ten years.
notes: 'have been built' and 'have been widened' use the present perfect passive for changes.
'is losing' and 'is going up' use the present continuous for changes in progress.
'will have turned into' is the future perfect for a prediction.
'almost beyond recognition' is a strong idiomatic phrase.

blocks.q: Do you think people today are less patient than in the past?
x: Yes, I think so. **When my parents were young**, they **would wait** weeks for a letter from a relative abroad. By the time it **arrived**, the news **had often become** old, but nobody **seemed to mind**.

Now, if someone **hasn't replied** within an hour, we start to worry. **I've noticed** it in myself too. Last month my internet **went down** for a day, and I **was checking** the router every ten minutes. Even a slow website feels like a small disaster these days.
notes: 'would wait' describes a repeated past action.
'had often become' (past perfect) shows an earlier event in the past.
'hasn't replied' and 'I've noticed' link the past to now with the present perfect.
'went down' and 'was checking' contrast a single event with a background activity.

blocks.x: If you are not sure which future form to use in Part 3, 'I think ... will' and 'is likely to' are safe. Add one 'will have' or 'will be -ing' when it fits, and you have shown range.

title: Accuracy: the errors that keep Bangladeshi speakers at band 6
bn: Find and fix the small, frequent mistakes that cost you a band
goal: In this chapter you will learn to spot the grammar errors that Bangladeshi candidates make most often, fix them and correct yourself naturally when one slips out.

pages.h: Why small errors cost a whole band

blocks.x: At band 7 the descriptor for grammar says that many of your sentences are **completely error-free**, although some mistakes still appear. That means a few errors are fine. The problem is the same few errors happening in nearly every answer. If you say 'informations', 'I am agree' and 'discuss about' in the first five minutes, the examiner hears a band 6 pattern.

The good news is that these errors are predictable. Most of them come from Bangla, which has no articles, does not change verbs for 'he' and 'she' in the same way and uses different prepositions. Once you know your personal list, you can fix it.

x: Articles (a, an, the, no article)
Subject-verb agreement
Plural and uncountable nouns
Wrong prepositions
Tense consistency in stories
Confusing 'he' and 'she'
Question forms
'I am agree'
Double comparatives ('more better')
'too' and 'very'
Double subjects ('My father, he ...')

blocks.x: Record yourself answering three Part 1 questions. Listen once only for these errors, and write down every one you hear. That list is your personal study plan.

**Articles.** Use 'a' or 'an' the first time you mention one countable thing. Use 'the' when the listener knows which one you mean, or when there is only one ('the government', 'the internet'). Use no article for general plural and uncountable nouns ('People love music').

x: I am student of software engineering.
I'm a student of software engineering.
I live in a Savar.
I live in Savar.
The people in my country love the cricket.
People in my country love cricket.
I use internet every day.
I use the internet every day.
He is honest man.
He's an honest man.

blocks.q: Correct this: 'My father is engineer and he works for government.'
blocks.a: 'My father is an engineer and he works for the government.'

blocks.x: **Subject-verb agreement.** With 'he', 'she', 'it' and singular nouns, the present simple verb takes '-s'. Watch out for long subjects ('One of my friends ...') and words like 'everyone' and 'nobody', which are singular.

x: My mother cook very well.
My mother cooks really well.
One of my friends live in Canada.
One of my friends lives in Canada.
