Everybody have a smartphone now.
Everybody has a smartphone now.
The news are always bad.
The news is always bad.
There is many reasons.
There are a lot of reasons.

blocks.q: Correct this: 'My brother don't like spicy food.'
blocks.a: 'My brother doesn't like spicy food.'

blocks.x: **Uncountable nouns.** Some nouns cannot be plural in English, even if they feel plural in meaning. They take no '-s' and no 'a'. To count them, use 'a piece of' or 'some'.

x: I need some informations.
I need some information.
My teacher gave me many advices.
My teacher gave me a lot of advice.
We bought new furnitures.
We bought some new furniture.
I have a lot of homeworks.
I have a lot of homework.
The equipments are expensive.
The equipment is expensive.
I got a good news.
I got some good news.

blocks.q: Correct this: 'He gave me an useful advice about my researches.'
blocks.a: 'He gave me some useful advice about my research.' (or 'a useful piece of advice')

blocks.x: **Prepositions.** Some verbs take no preposition at all, and some take a different one from Bangla. These need to be learnt as fixed chunks.

x: We discussed about the problem.
We discussed the problem.
She is married with a doctor.
She's married to a doctor.
I am good in maths.
I'm good at maths.
It depends of the weather.
It depends on the weather.
I'm interested about AI.
I'm interested in AI.
He entered into the room.
He went into the room. (or: He entered the room.)

blocks.q: Correct this: 'I am waiting the bus and I will reach to campus soon.'
blocks.a: 'I'm waiting for the bus and I'll reach campus soon.' (or 'I'll get to campus soon')

blocks.x: **Tense consistency.** In a Part 2 story, choose the past and stay in it. Slipping into the present ('and then he says ...') is one of the most common errors at band 6. Use the present only for things that are still true now.

x: Last year I go to Cox's Bazar and we stay in a hotel.
Last year I went to Cox's Bazar and we stayed in a hotel.
When I reached home, my mother is waiting for me.
When I got home, my mother was waiting for me.
He told me he is busy, so we meet the next day.
He told me he was busy, so we met the next day.
I have seen him yesterday.
I saw him yesterday.

blocks.q: Correct this: 'Then the teacher comes in and she asked me a question.'
blocks.a: 'Then the teacher came in and asked me a question.'

blocks.x: **He and she.** Bangla uses one word ('se' or 'tini') for both, so many speakers say 'he' for a woman. Examiners notice it at once, especially in Part 2 when you describe a person. Decide before you start: if the person is a woman, it is 'she' and 'her' every time.

x: My mother is a teacher. He teaches at a school.
My mother's a teacher. She teaches at a primary school.
My sister is very kind. I love him.
My sister's really kind. I love her.
My grandfather, she was a farmer.
My grandfather was a farmer.

blocks.x: In your one minute of preparation for Part 2, write 'she' or 'he' at the top of your notes. It is a simple reminder that prevents the error.

blocks.q: Correct this: 'My aunt lives in London and his children go to school there.'
blocks.a: 'My aunt lives in London and her children go to school there.'

blocks.x: **Question forms.** In Part 1 and Part 3 you sometimes ask the examiner to repeat or explain something, and you may ask questions inside a story. Direct questions need an auxiliary before the subject. Indirect questions ('Could you tell me what ...') use normal word order.

x: What you mean?
What do you mean?
Can you tell me what does this word mean?
Could you tell me what this word means?
Why you are asking?
Why are you asking?
Where he went?
Where did he go?
Sorry, you can repeat?
Sorry, could you repeat the question?

blocks.q: Correct this: 'Do you know where is the library?'
blocks.a: 'Do you know where the library is?'

blocks.x: **'I am agree'.** 'Agree' is a verb, not an adjective, so it does not need 'am'. This is probably the single most common error in Part 3. The same applies to 'I am disagree' and 'I am not agree'.

x: I am agree with you.
I agree with you.
I am not agree with this idea.
I don't agree with this idea.
I am totally agree.
I totally agree.
Most people are agree that ...
Most people agree that ...

blocks.q: Correct this: 'I am not agree, because I am not believe it is true.'
blocks.a: 'I don't agree, because I don't believe it's true.'

pages.h: Comparatives, too and very, double subjects

blocks.x: **Double comparatives.** One-syllable adjectives take '-er' and two-syllable adjectives ending in '-y' change to '-ier'. Longer adjectives take 'more'. Never use both. To make the difference stronger, use 'much', 'far' or 'a lot'.

x: My new phone is more better.
My new phone is much better.
Dhaka is more bigger than Sylhet.
Dhaka's much bigger than Sylhet.
It is more easier to study at night.
It's easier to study at night.
This is the most cheapest shop.
This is the cheapest shop.

blocks.q: Correct this: 'Life in the village is more peacefuller.'
blocks.a: 'Life in the village is more peaceful.' (or 'much more peaceful')

blocks.x: **Too and very.** 'Very' simply makes an adjective stronger. 'Too' means more than is acceptable, so it usually has a negative result. Saying 'The food was too good' sounds like a complaint to a native speaker.

x: The biryani was too delicious.
The biryani was really delicious.
My teacher is too nice.
My teacher is very nice.
It was very hot, so I couldn't go out.
It was too hot to go out.

blocks.x: **Double subjects.** In English the subject appears once. 'My father, he works in a bank' repeats the subject, which sounds like a band 6 habit. Drop the pronoun.

x: My father, he works in a bank.
My father works in a bank.
My best friend, she is studying medicine.
My best friend is studying medicine.
The people in my area, they are very friendly.
People in my area are really friendly.

blocks.q: Correct both errors: 'My cousin, he is too clever, he always gets top marks.'
blocks.a: 'My cousin's really clever, and he always gets top marks.'

blocks.x: Even band 8 speakers make mistakes. What matters is how you deal with them. If you notice an error, **correct it quickly and keep going**. A smooth self-correction shows the examiner that you know the rule. A long pause or a string of apologies hurts your fluency score instead.

head: Situation
What to say
Example
rows: He's my uncle, sorry, I mean my cousin.
I go there, or rather, I went there every summer.
My mother said he, she said I should rest.
It was quite hard. What I mean is, it was tiring rather than difficult.
let me put that another way ...
Let me put that another way: it's cheaper, but it takes longer.

x: Notice the error, but do not stop for long.
Use a short phrase such as 'sorry' or 'I mean', or simply repeat the corrected word.
Say the corrected version clearly.
Continue the sentence as if nothing happened.
I am agree, oh sorry sorry, my English, I mean, I agree.
I am, I mean, I agree with that.
He, no, no, wait, she, sorry, she is my teacher.
He, sorry, she's my teacher.
I go, um, um, I went, sorry for mistake, to Sylhet.
I go, or rather, I went to Sylhet last winter.

blocks.x: Do not correct every tiny slip. If you go back for each one, you sound hesitant and the examiner hears more problems, not fewer. Fix errors that change the meaning (he/she, wrong tense) and let small ones go.
Self-correction is a safety net, not a strategy. The real aim is to practise your personal error list until the correct form comes out first.
These answers are not especially complex, but every sentence is accurate. Look at the bold items: they are the exact places where band 6 speakers usually make the errors from this chapter.

blocks.q: Do you prefer to get news from the internet or from newspapers?
x: Mostly from **the internet**, to be honest. **I agree** that newspapers are more reliable, but I don't **have the time** to read one every morning. I usually check **a news app** on the bus, and if there's **some important information**, I look it up on two or three **different sites** to make sure it's accurate.
notes: 'the internet' uses the article correctly.
'I agree' avoids the common 'I am agree'.
'some important information' keeps 'information' uncountable.
'look it up' is a natural phrasal verb with the object in the right place.

blocks.q: Who in your family are you closest to?
x: Probably my older sister. **She lives** in Chattogram now, but **we talk on the phone** almost every day. **She's been working** as a doctor for three years, so she **gives me a lot of advice** about health and studying. She's **much better at** handling stress than I am, so I usually listen to her.
notes: 'She lives' and 'She's been working' use the correct pronoun and verb agreement throughout.
'a lot of advice' treats 'advice' as uncountable.
'much better at' avoids 'more better' and uses the right preposition.
'She's been working ... for three years' uses the present perfect continuous, not 'She is working since'.

blocks.q: Is it important for students to discuss problems with their teachers?
x: Yes, I think **it's very important**. When students **discuss their problems** with a teacher, they often find out that **the issue** is smaller than **it seemed**. The trouble is that **many students are** too shy, especially in **the first year** at university.

A friend of mine, for example, failed a course because he never **told anyone** he was struggling. If his teachers had known, they could have **helped him** much earlier. So I'd say universities should make teachers **easier to approach**.
notes: 'discuss their problems' has no 'about' after 'discuss'.
'it's very important' uses 'very', not 'too', for a positive meaning.
'many students are' shows correct plural agreement.
'A friend of mine ... failed' keeps one subject and stays in the past tense.
'If his teachers had known, they could have helped' is an accurate third conditional.

title: Part 1 strategy: short answers that sound natural
bn: How to handle the first four to five minutes of the test
goal: In this chapter you will learn what the examiner listens for in Part 1 and how to build short, natural answers to every common question type.

blocks.x: Part 1 lasts four to five minutes. The examiner checks your name and ID, then asks questions on two or three familiar topics, such as your studies, your hometown or your free time. The questions come from a script, so the examiner cannot rephrase them much or chat with you. Your job is to give **short, complete answers** that show range without turning each one into a speech.

x: Fluency and Coherence: do you answer without long pauses, and do your sentences link together?
Lexical Resource: do you use topic words precisely, with a few less common words and natural collocations such as 'a hectic schedule' or 'grab a quick bite'?
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: do you mix simple and complex sentences, and are most of them free of errors?
Pronunciation: can the examiner understand you easily, and do your stress and intonation sound like you mean what you say?

blocks.x: The four criteria are weighted equally, and the examiner rates the whole test, not each part separately. Part 1 is still important. It is your chance to settle in and show that everyday topics are easy for you.

Band 7 vocabulary in Part 1 does not mean rare words. It means precise everyday words: 'commute' instead of 'go to university', 'cosy' instead of 'nice', 'I'm not much of a reader' instead of 'I don't like reading'.

blocks.q: Do you work or are you a student?
x: I'm a student at the moment. I'm in my final year of a software engineering degree at a private university in Savar, so things are **pretty hectic** right now. I'm **juggling my thesis with** a part-time internship, but I'm **looking forward to graduating** next year and, hopefully, **landing a job** in data science.
notes: 'Juggling my thesis with a part-time internship' is a natural, less common verb collocation.
'Pretty hectic' is informal but suits a personal question.
'Looking forward to graduating' uses the -ing form after 'to', a point many candidates get wrong.

pages.h: The basic shape of a good answer

blocks.x: Most Part 1 answers work well with three moves. First, answer the question directly. Second, add a reason or a detail. Third, add an example, a contrast or a short comment about the past or the future. That gives you two to four sentences, or **about 20 to 30 seconds** of speech.

x: Answer: 'Yes, I do.' / 'Not really.' / 'Mostly at home.'
Reason or detail: 'because ...', 'mainly since ...', 'the thing is, ...'
Extend: an example ('Last week, for instance, ...'), a contrast ('When I was younger, though, ...') or a comment about the future ('I'd like to ... one day').
Yes, I like cooking. It is good.
Yes, I really enjoy it. I find it quite relaxing after a long day, and I've recently started making a few simple Thai dishes.
My hometown is Cumilla. It is a nice place.
I'm from Cumilla, a mid-sized city about two hours from Dhaka. It's much calmer than the capital, which is why I still miss it.
I don't read books much. I have no time.
Not as much as I'd like. Between classes and assignments I rarely get the chance, so most of my reading happens on my phone.

blocks.q: Do you like cooking?
x: Yes, I do, although I'm **far from an expert**. I live in a university hall, so I mostly **throw together** simple things like rice, dal and an omelette. My mother's a brilliant cook, though, and whenever I go home I try to **pick up** one of her recipes. Last month I **finally got the hang of** her chicken korma, which I was **quite proud of**.
notes: The answer comes first ('Yes, I do'), then a detail (hall life), then an example (learning a recipe): the full three-move shape.
'Throw together', 'pick up' and 'get the hang of' are natural phrasal and idiomatic items.
'Which I was quite proud of' is a relative clause ending in a preposition, which is normal in speech.

blocks.q: Do you prefer studying in the morning or at night?
x: Definitely at night. I've always been **a bit of a night owl**, and the hall is much quieter after about eleven, so it's easier to concentrate. In the morning my brain just **doesn't switch on** properly until I've had tea. **The only downside** is that I sometimes **end up staying awake** far too late before an exam.
notes: A direct answer ('Definitely at night') is followed by two reasons and a contrast.
'A bit of a night owl' is a common idiom that fits the topic exactly.
'Until I've had tea' uses the present perfect after 'until' for a completed action.

pages.h: How long to speak and how to sound natural

blocks.x: Aim for about 20 to 30 seconds per answer. A one-word reply gives the examiner nothing to rate. A one-minute speech sounds rehearsed, uses up the time, and the examiner may stop you halfway. If the examiner moves to the next question while you are still talking, that is normal. It means the script is moving on, not that you did badly.

Memorised answers are easy to spot. The speaker's rhythm changes, the vocabulary suddenly jumps a level, and the answer often doesn't quite fit the question. Examiners are trained to notice this, and they don't give credit for language that isn't your own. Prepare **ideas and phrases**, not whole answers.

x: Start with a short, natural opener: 'Yes, quite a lot, actually.' / 'Hmm, not really.' / 'It depends.'
Use contractions: 'I'd', 'it's', 'wasn't', 'I've'.
Use soft hedges: 'I'd say', 'I suppose', 'to be honest', 'kind of'.
Refer to your real life: a real place, a real habit, a real time ('last Eid', 'during the monsoon').

blocks.x: Many Bangladeshi candidates open every answer with 'Actually' or 'Basically'. Once, they sound fine. In every answer, they become a verbal habit the examiner notices. Vary your openers: 'Well,', 'To be honest,', 'Not really,', 'Yes, definitely,'. Also, 'actually' signals a small surprise or correction in English. It does not mean 'currently'.

x: I would like to say that my hometown is a place of great natural beauty and historical significance.
My hometown's quite pretty, to be honest, especially in the monsoon when everything turns green.
Reading is my passion and I read books every single day of my life.
I read most days, usually just before bed, though it's often articles rather than books.

blocks.q: Do you enjoy your studies?
x: Mostly, yes. I chose software engineering because I'd **always been into** computers, and I still **get a real kick out of** solving a tricky problem. Some of the theory courses are **pretty dry**, I have to admit, but the project work **makes up for it**, especially when we work in teams.
notes: 'I'd always been into' uses the past perfect for an interest that started before the choice.
'Get a real kick out of' is an informal idiom that sounds spontaneous, not memorised.
'Makes up for it' (phrasal verb) balances a negative point with a positive one.

pages.h: Yes/no questions and likes and dislikes

blocks.x: A yes/no question still needs more than 'yes' or 'no'. Give the answer, then the reason. If the honest answer is in between, say so: 'Sort of', 'It depends', 'Not as much as I used to'. These are often **the most natural answers** of all.

head: Instead of
Try
rows: I'm really into it / I'm a big fan of it / I absolutely love it.
I'm not a big fan of it / It's not really my thing / I can't stand it (strong).
I don't mind it / It's all right, I suppose.
I'd rather ... / I much prefer ... / I tend to go for ...

blocks.x: 'I am very much fond of it' is a common error. Say 'I'm very fond of it' or 'I'm really fond of it'. Also avoid 'I like it too much' when you mean 'a lot': 'too much' means more than is good. Say 'I like it a lot' or 'I really love it'.

blocks.q: Do you like going to the cinema?
x: Not really, to be honest. Tickets in Dhaka have become **quite pricey**, and getting to a cinema through the traffic can take **the best part of an hour**. I'd **much rather** stream something at home with friends. **That said**, if a big film **comes out**, like a new Marvel movie, I'll **make the effort** to go.
notes: 'Not really, to be honest' gives a clear but polite negative answer.
'The best part of an hour' is a natural idiom meaning almost an hour.
'That said' introduces a contrast, and 'if a big film comes out, I'll...' is a first conditional.

blocks.q: What kind of food do you dislike?
x: I'm **not a big fan of** very sweet things, which is **a bit unusual** in Bangladesh, because people here love their sweets. I can manage one rosogolla at a wedding, but after that it just feels **too sickly**. I **much prefer** **savoury snacks**, like singara or chotpoti, especially on a rainy evening.
notes: 'Not a big fan of' is the natural way to express a mild dislike.
'Which is a bit unusual in Bangladesh' is a relative clause commenting on the whole idea.
'Sickly' (unpleasantly sweet) and 'savoury' are precise food words.

pages.h: Frequency, past and present, and 'Do you think' questions

blocks.x: Three more question types come up again and again. 'How often do you...?' needs a frequency expression. 'Did you... when you were a child?' or 'Has this changed?' invites a contrast between past and present, which is an easy way to show tense control. 'Do you think...?' asks for a short opinion, and **a reason makes it believable**.

head: Question type
Useful language
rows: every now and then, once in a blue moon, a couple of times a week, hardly ever, whenever I get the chance
I used to ..., but these days ...; when I was a kid I'd ...; I've recently started ...; I don't ... as much as I used to
I'd say so, mainly because ...; I doubt it, to be honest; it depends on ...; probably, although ...

blocks.q: How often do you go swimming?
x: **Hardly ever**, these days. When I was a kid in my village, I **used to swim** in the pond almost every afternoon, and I was **pretty confident** in the water. Since I moved to Dhaka, though, I **haven't had the chance**, because there aren't many public pools, and the ones that exist **cost a fortune**.
notes: 'Hardly ever' answers the frequency question immediately.
'Used to swim' contrasts with 'haven't had the chance' (present perfect): two tenses for past and now.
'Cost a fortune' is a common informal idiom.

blocks.q: Did you play outside a lot when you were a child?
x: Yes, **all the time**. There was an empty field behind our building, and **as soon as** school finished, **we'd rush out** to play cricket until it got dark. Kids today don't seem to do that as much. My younger cousins **spend most of their time** on tablets, which I think is **a bit of a shame**.
notes: 'We'd rush out' uses 'would' for a repeated past habit.
'As soon as school finished' is a time clause that adds detail.
'Which I think is a bit of a shame' adds a personal comment with a relative clause.

blocks.q: Do you think you'll live in your hometown in the future?
x: I **doubt it**, to be honest. My hometown's lovely, but **there aren't many opportunities** for someone in tech. I'm planning to do a master's abroad, and **if that works out**, I'll probably **settle wherever I find** a good job. I'd **definitely go back** to visit, though, especially for Eid.
notes: 'I doubt it' is a natural, polite way to say no to a 'Do you think' question.
'If that works out, I'll probably settle' is a first conditional with a phrasal verb.
'Wherever I find a good job' uses a less common conjunction.

pages.h: When you have nothing to say

blocks.x: Sometimes the question is about something you never do or know nothing about, such as 'Do you like jazz?' or 'How often do you visit museums?'. Do not panic, and do not invent a long fake story. Say honestly that it is not part of your life, explain why, and then **talk about something close to it**. The examiner rates your English, not your hobbies.

x: Admit it: 'Honestly, I've never really thought about it.' / 'I don't know much about it, to be honest.'
Give a reason: 'It's not very common where I'm from.' / 'I've never had the chance.'
Move to something related: 'But I do enjoy ...' / 'The closest thing would be ...' / 'I'd like to try it one day, because ...'

blocks.x: Saying 'I have no idea' and stopping is the biggest mistake here. A long silence hurts your fluency score. Also, do not ask the examiner to explain the topic: in Part 1 they can only repeat the question. If you did not hear it, say 'Sorry, could you repeat the question?'.

blocks.q: Do you like jazz music?
x: Honestly, **I've never really listened to** much jazz. It's not very common in Bangladesh, so I **haven't been exposed to** it. **The closest thing I enjoy** would be some of the **fusion bands** here that mix folk music with guitars and drums. I'd like to **give jazz a proper try** one day, though.
notes: 'Haven't been exposed to' is a present perfect passive, used naturally.
'The closest thing I enjoy would be' moves to a related topic smoothly.
'Give jazz a proper try' is an informal collocation that ends on a positive note.

blocks.q: How often do you visit museums?
x: **Almost never**, I'm afraid. I think the last time was a school trip to the National Museum in Shahbag, **which must have been** about ten years ago. **It's not that** I'm not interested. It's more that museums **aren't really part of** student life here. **If there were** interactive exhibits on technology, **I'd probably go** more often.
notes: 'Which must have been about ten years ago' is a modal of past speculation.
'It's not that... It's more that...' is a natural way to explain a reason.
'If there were interactive exhibits, I'd probably go' is a second conditional.

blocks.q: Upgrade this answer to 'Do you like gardening?': 'No. I have no garden.'
blocks.a: Possible answer: 'Not really, to be honest. I live in a flat in Dhaka, so there's no space for a garden. My mother grows a few chillies and herbs on our balcony, though, and I sometimes help her water them.'

title: Part 1 sample answers, set A: you and your everyday life
bn: Model answers on studies, hometown, home, routine, free time, food, friends and family
goal: In this chapter you will learn how band 7 answers sound on the eight topics that come up most often in Part 1.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'in my final year', 'a heavy workload', 'fall behind', 'specialise in', 'in high demand', 'get some hands-on experience'.

blocks.q: What subject are you studying?
x: I'm studying software engineering, and I'm **in my final semester** now. It's a mix of programming, maths and project management, but **over the last year or so** I've **specialised in** data science. That's the part I **find most rewarding**, because you can actually see a model **make sense of** messy real-world data.
notes: 'Over the last year or so' with the present perfect 'I've specialised' shows tense control.
'Find most rewarding' follows the pattern find + adjective.
'Make sense of' is a useful fixed expression.

blocks.q: Why did you choose that subject?
x: **To be honest**, it was partly practical. Everyone told me IT jobs were **in high demand**, and my parents were keen on it. But I'd also **been messing around with** coding since school, so it **felt like a natural fit**. Looking back, I'm **glad I went for it**, even though the first year was tough.
notes: 'I'd been messing around with' is the past perfect continuous for an earlier ongoing activity.
'In high demand' and 'a natural fit' are strong collocations.
'Looking back, I'm glad I went for it' combines a participle phrase with a phrasal verb.

blocks.q: Is your subject popular in your country?
x: Very much so. Computer science and software engineering are **among the most competitive** subjects at Bangladeshi universities right now. A lot of students **are drawn to** them because of freelancing and remote work, which often **pay better than** local jobs. The downside is that the job market's **getting quite crowded**.
notes: 'Very much so' is a natural, emphatic yes.
'Are drawn to' is a passive structure meaning 'are attracted by'.
'Getting quite crowded' uses the present continuous for a changing situation.

blocks.q: What do you find difficult about your studies?
x: **Time management**, mainly. In the final year you've got a thesis, coursework and, in my case, an internship **all at once**, so it's easy to **fall behind**. I've learnt to **break big tasks down** into small daily goals. It doesn't always work, but it **stops me from panicking** the night before a deadline.
notes: 'Fall behind' and 'break big tasks down' are useful phrasal verbs.
'Stops me from panicking' uses the pattern stop + object + from + -ing.
'I've learnt to' (present perfect) shows a change over time.

blocks.q: What would you like to do after you graduate?
x: Ideally, I'd like to do a master's in AI abroad, **preferably on a scholarship**, since it would be **hard to afford otherwise**. After that, I'd love to work on projects that **deal with** environmental problems, like air quality or flooding. It's **a bit of a long-term plan**, but I'm **working towards it** step by step.
notes: 'Since it would be hard to afford otherwise' uses 'would' for a hypothetical situation.
'Deal with environmental problems' is an accurate verb and noun collocation.
'Working towards it' (present continuous) shows an ongoing effort.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'the pace of life', 'a fairly quiet town', 'has changed beyond recognition', 'be well worth a visit', 'move away for work', 'think of it as home'.

blocks.q: Where is your hometown?
x: I'm from Cumilla, which is **in the east of the country**, about **two hours' drive** from Dhaka **if the traffic's kind**. It's a fairly old city, **famous for** its sweets and for an ancient Buddhist site called Mainamati. I moved away for university, but I still **think of it as home**.
notes: 'Two hours' drive' uses the possessive apostrophe correctly with a time expression.
'If the traffic's kind' is a light, natural conditional.
'Think of it as home' is a natural verb pattern.

blocks.q: What do you like most about your hometown?
x: I'd say **the pace of life**. People aren't **in such a rush** as they are in Dhaka, and you can actually **stroll around** in the evening without **dodging** rickshaws and buses. I also love that everyone seems to know each other. **Whenever I go back**, the shopkeeper near our house still asks about my studies.
notes: 'The pace of life' is a precise collocation for this topic.
'Stroll' and 'dodging' are specific verbs instead of 'walk' and 'avoid'.
'Whenever I go back' introduces a real example.

blocks.q: Has your hometown changed much in recent years?
x: Yes, **quite dramatically**. When I was little, most of the buildings were two or three storeys high, but now there are **apartment blocks springing up** everywhere. The roads have been widened too, which **has made a big difference** to travel times. **On the downside**, a lot of the old ponds and green spaces **have been filled in**.
notes: 'Have been filled in' is a present perfect passive, ideal for describing change.
'Springing up' is a vivid phrasal verb for new buildings.
'On the downside' signals a contrast clearly.

blocks.q: Is your hometown a good place for young people?
x: **It depends on** what they want. If you're looking for a calm, safe place to **grow up**, it's great. But for jobs and higher education, **most young people end up** moving to Dhaka or Chattogram, because the opportunities are **concentrated in** the big cities. That's exactly what I did, actually.
notes: 'It depends on what they want' is an honest, natural opener.
'End up moving' uses the pattern end up + -ing.
'Concentrated in the big cities' is a formal collocation used naturally.

blocks.q: Would you recommend your hometown to visitors?
x: Yes, **for a day or two**, definitely. There's the Mainamati site, which **is well worth seeing** if you're **into history**, and of course the rasmalai, which is **the real reason** most people visit. I wouldn't **plan a whole week** there, but it makes **a nice break** from Dhaka.
notes: 'Well worth seeing' is a natural fixed phrase for recommending a place.
'If you're into history' is an informal conditional.
'I wouldn't plan a whole week there' uses 'would' to give hypothetical advice.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'share a room with', 'a bit cramped', 'a rented flat', 'within walking distance', 'plenty of natural light', 'have some privacy'.

blocks.q: Do you live in a house or a flat?
x: At the moment I live in a university hall in Savar, so it's **neither, really**. I **share a room with** three other students, which can be **a bit cramped**. My family, though, lives in a **rented flat** in Dhaka, on the fourth floor of a fairly old building **with no lift**.
notes: 'Neither, really' answers an either/or question honestly.
'A bit cramped' is the precise adjective for a small, crowded room.
'Which can be a bit cramped' is a relative clause with a modal.

blocks.q: What do you like about where you live?
x: The best thing is **the sense of community**. There's always someone around to **chat to** or eat with, and if I'm **stuck on** an assignment, I can just knock on a friend's door. It's also **within walking distance of** my department, so I never have to **worry about** traffic.
notes: 'The sense of community' is a natural noun phrase for hall or neighbourhood life.
'Stuck on an assignment' is an informal, accurate collocation.
'Within walking distance of' is a useful fixed phrase for location.

blocks.q: Is there anything you would like to change about your home?
x: **If I could change one thing**, it would be the noise. The walls are quite thin, and people **stay up** playing games or watching cricket until two in the morning. I'd also love a bit more **natural light**, because our window **faces** another building, so the room **feels gloomy** even at midday.
notes: 'If I could change one thing, it would be' is a second conditional.
'Natural light' and 'feels gloomy' are precise words for describing a room.
'Faces another building' uses 'face' as a verb.

pages.h: Home and accommodation (continued) and daily routine

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'a fixed routine', 'grab a quick breakfast', 'sleep in', 'catch up with friends', 'wind down', 'my day revolves around'.

blocks.q: Would you like to live in a different kind of home in the future?
x: Definitely. **Ideally**, I'd like a small flat of my own, **somewhere quiet** with a balcony, where I could **grow a few plants**. I've shared rooms **for most of my life**, first with my brother and now with roommates, so having **some privacy** would feel like **a real luxury**.
notes: 'Where I could grow a few plants' is a relative clause with a modal.
'For most of my life' with the present perfect 'I've shared' shows tense control.
'Would feel like a real luxury' expresses a hypothetical result.

blocks.q: What is your daily routine like?
x: On weekdays it's **pretty predictable**. I get up around seven, **grab a quick breakfast** in the canteen and have classes until about two. After lunch I usually work on my thesis in the library, and in the evening I either **catch up with** friends or watch something online. I try to **be in bed by** midnight, though I don't always **manage it**.
notes: 'Grab a quick breakfast' is a natural informal collocation.
'Catch up with friends' is a common phrasal verb.
'Though I don't always manage it' adds an honest contrast.

blocks.q: Do you usually have the same routine every day?
x: **More or less**, during the semester. **Having a fixed routine** actually helps me, because I **don't have to waste energy** deciding what to do next. Weekends are different, though. I tend to **sleep in**, and if I go home to Dhaka, the whole day **is built around** family.
notes: 'Having a fixed routine' uses an -ing phrase as the subject of the sentence.
'Waste energy deciding' follows the pattern waste + noun + -ing.
'The whole day is built around family' is a passive structure.

blocks.q: What is your favourite part of the day?
x: I'd say the late evening, after dinner. The day's work is **out of the way**, the hall gets a bit quieter, and I can **finally unwind**. I usually make a cup of tea and either read or call my parents. It's the only time I don't **feel under pressure** **to be productive**.
notes: 'Out of the way' is an idiom meaning finished.
'Unwind' is a less common verb for relaxing.
'The only time I don't feel under pressure' is a reduced relative clause.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'have a lie-in', 'hang out with friends', 'switch off', 'squeeze in', 'a quiet weekend', 'spend the whole day'.

blocks.q: Has your routine changed since you were a child?
x: Completely. As a child, my day **revolved around** school and private tuition, and my mother **kept a close eye on** everything I did. Now **I'm in charge of** my own time, which is great, but it also means **there's no one to blame** if I waste a whole afternoon on my phone.
notes: 'Revolved around' is a precise phrasal verb for what controls your time.
'Kept a close eye on' is a natural idiom for careful supervision.
'Which is great, but it also means...' uses a relative clause to comment on the whole situation.

blocks.q: What do you usually do at the weekend?
x: It **varies quite a lot**. If I'm staying in the hall, I usually **have a lie-in**, do my laundry and then **hang out with** friends in the evening, maybe at a tea stall near the campus. **Once or twice a month**, I take the bus home to Dhaka to see my family, which **takes up** most of Friday.
notes: 'Have a lie-in' is a natural British expression for sleeping late.
'Once or twice a month' is a precise frequency expression.
'Which takes up most of Friday' is a relative clause with a phrasal verb.

blocks.q: What did you do last weekend?
x: Last weekend was **fairly quiet**, actually. I had a deadline on Sunday, so I **spent most of** Saturday in the library. On Friday evening, though, a few of us went out for fuchka at a local market, which was **a nice way to switch off** before the work started.
notes: 'Spent most of Saturday in the library' uses the past simple accurately.
'A nice way to switch off' is a natural phrase for relaxing.
'Though' in the middle of the sentence adds a contrast smoothly.

blocks.q: Do you prefer to relax or be active in your free time?
x: **A bit of both**, really. **After a long week** I usually just want to relax and watch a series, but if I **spend the whole weekend** on the sofa, I feel **sluggish** by Saturday night. So I try to **squeeze in** a game of badminton or a long walk at some point.
notes: 'A bit of both' is a natural answer to a preference question.
'Sluggish' is a less common, precise adjective.
'Squeeze in' is a phrasal verb for finding time for something.

blocks.q: Do you think people have enough free time these days?
x: **Not really**, at least not in Dhaka. People **spend hours stuck in traffic** every day, and a lot of jobs expect you to **stay late** or answer messages at night. **Even when** people do have free time, they often **end up scrolling** on their phones instead of actually resting.
notes: 'Spend hours stuck in traffic' is a natural collocation.
'Even when people do have free time' uses emphatic 'do'.
'End up scrolling' uses the pattern end up + -ing.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'a balanced diet', 'eat out', 'pretty filling', 'a home-cooked meal', 'can't stand', 'have a sweet tooth'.

blocks.q: What is your favourite food?
x: That's an easy one: biryani, especially kacchi biryani, where the mutton and rice **are cooked together** slowly. **There's nothing quite like** a plate of it at a wedding. I try not to have it too often, because it's **pretty heavy**, but I'd **never say no** to it.
notes: 'Where the mutton and rice are cooked together' is a relative clause with a passive verb.
'There's nothing quite like' is a natural expression of strong preference.
'I'd never say no to it' is an informal idiom.

blocks.q: Do you often eat out?
x: **More than I should**, probably. The food in our hall canteen is **fairly basic**, so a few times a week my friends and I **head to** a small restaurant near the campus. It's cheap and **filling**, though not exactly healthy. **Now that** food delivery apps are everywhere, it's even more **tempting**.
notes: 'More than I should' is an honest, natural opener.
'Filling' and 'tempting' are precise food adjectives.
'Now that' introduces a reason linked to a recent change.

blocks.q: Did you learn to cook when you were young?
x: Not really. In a lot of Bangladeshi families, boys **aren't expected to** help in the kitchen, so my mother did almost everything. I only started cooking when I moved into the hall and **got tired of** canteen food. I'm **still a beginner**, but I can now **make a decent** egg curry.
notes: 'Aren't expected to' is a passive structure for social norms.
'Got tired of canteen food' is a natural collocation.
'Make a decent egg curry' uses 'decent' in its informal sense of good enough.

blocks.q: Is there any food you didn't like as a child but like now?
x: Yes, bitter gourd. As a kid I **couldn't stand** it, and I **used to hide it** under my rice. These days I actually **quite like** it fried with onions, and my mother loves reminding me how much I **made a fuss** about it. I suppose **your taste changes** as you get older.
notes: 'Couldn't stand' is a strong, natural way to express dislike.
'Used to hide it' shows a past habit.
'Made a fuss about it' is a common idiom.

blocks.q: Do you think people in your country eat healthily?
x: **On the whole**, not as healthily as they used to. Traditional meals of rice, fish, dal and vegetables are **pretty balanced**, but young people especially **are eating more** fast food and fried snacks. **On top of that**, a lot of people **don't get much exercise**, so problems like diabetes are **becoming more common**.
notes: 'On the whole' is a natural way to give a general opinion.
'Are eating more' and 'are becoming more common' use the present continuous for trends.
'On top of that' adds a second point in a spoken style.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'a close friend', 'keep in touch', 'get on well with', 'drift apart', 'have a lot in common', 'someone I can rely on'.

blocks.q: Do you have a lot of friends?
x: I've got a lot of people I'd call **acquaintances**, but only **a handful of** close friends. Two of them I've known **since primary school**, and the others I met at university. I'd **rather have** a few friends I can really **rely on** than a big group I barely know.
notes: 'Acquaintances' contrasts precisely with 'close friends'.
'Two of them I've known since primary school' fronts the object for emphasis.
'I'd rather have... than...' is a natural preference structure.

blocks.q: How often do you see your friends?
x: My university friends I see **pretty much every day**, since we live in the same hall. My old school friends are **a different story**, because they're **scattered** across different cities now. We **keep in touch** on WhatsApp, and we **try to meet up** whenever we're all home for Eid.
notes: 'A different story' is an idiom that signals a contrast.
'Scattered across different cities' is a precise passive participle.
'Keep in touch' and 'meet up' are common phrasal expressions.

blocks.q: What do you usually do with your friends?
x: Nothing very exciting, to be honest. We mostly **hang out** at a tea stall, **chat about anything and everything**, and sometimes play cricket on the field behind the hall. **Every so often** we **plan a day trip** somewhere like Sonargaon, but those plans usually **fall through** because someone's busy.
notes: 'Chat about anything and everything' is a natural fixed phrase.
'Every so often' is a less common frequency expression.
'Fall through' is a phrasal verb for plans that fail.

blocks.q: Is it easy to make new friends as an adult?
x: **I'd say it's harder**. At school you're **thrown together** with the same people every day, so friendships **happen naturally**. Once you start working, people are busier and **more guarded**, so it **takes more effort**. Shared interests help a lot, though. I made two good friends through a coding club last year.
notes: 'Thrown together' is a passive phrasal verb used naturally.
'More guarded' is a less common adjective for describing people.
'Once you start working' is a time clause that sets up the contrast.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'my immediate family', 'extended family', 'take after', 'get along with', 'a close-knit family', 'family gatherings'.

blocks.q: Do you have a large family?
x: My immediate family's quite small: just my parents, my younger sister and me. But my **extended family** is **huge**. My father **is one of six** siblings, so I've got **more cousins than I can count**. **Whenever there's a wedding**, the house **is packed with** relatives.
notes: 'Immediate family' and 'extended family' are the precise terms for this topic.
'More cousins than I can count' is a natural exaggeration.
'Is packed with relatives' is a strong informal collocation.

blocks.q: Who are you closest to in your family?
x: Probably my mother. She's the one I call **when something's on my mind**, and she **has a knack for** knowing when I'm stressed **without me saying** anything. My father's **more reserved**, so we don't talk as much, but I know he'd **do anything** for us.
notes: 'When something's on my mind' is a natural idiom.
'Has a knack for knowing' is a less common expression for a natural skill.
'He'd do anything for us' uses 'would' for a hypothetical willingness.

blocks.q: Do you spend much time with your family?
x: Not as much as I'd like **these days**. Since I moved into the hall, I only **get to see them** a couple of times a month. When I do go home, though, we **make the most of it**: we eat together, watch the news and **catch up on** all the neighbourhood gossip.
notes: 'Get to see them' means having the chance to see them.
'When I do go home' uses emphatic 'do'.
'Make the most of it' is a common idiom.

blocks.q: Do you think families are becoming smaller in your country?
x: Yes, **without a doubt**, especially in cities. My grandparents had seven children, but most couples now **stop at** one or two. Raising children in Dhaka **has become really expensive**, with school fees and rents, so people **can't afford** large families. **It's a big shift** in just two generations.
notes: 'Without a doubt' gives a confident answer.
'Has become really expensive' uses the present perfect for change up to now.
'Stop at one or two' is a natural spoken use of 'stop at'.

title: Part 1 sample answers, set B: things you use and do
bn: Model answers on technology, reading, music, weather, transport, shopping, sport and travel
goal: In this chapter you will learn model answers and useful phrases for eight more Part 1 topics that examiners use all the time.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'screen time', 'cut back on', 'can't live without', 'back up my files', 'rely on', 'keep in touch'.

blocks.q: How often do you use your phone?
x: **Far too often**, if I'm honest. It's the first thing I check when I wake up and the last thing I look at before I sleep. I use it for classes, banking and **keeping in touch** with family, so it's **hard to cut back**. My weekly **screen time report** usually **makes me feel guilty**.
notes: 'Far too often' is a strong, natural frequency answer.
'The first thing I check when I wake up' uses a reduced relative clause.
'Makes me feel guilty' follows the pattern make + object + verb.

blocks.q: What do you mainly use your phone for?
x: Apart from calls and messages, I mostly use it for studying and paying for things. Mobile banking apps like bKash **have become essential** in Bangladesh, so I **rarely carry cash** now. I also listen to podcasts **on my commute**, which **makes the bus ride go faster**.
notes: 'Have become essential' uses the present perfect for a recent change.
'On my commute' is the precise noun for a regular journey.
'Which makes the bus ride go faster' is a relative clause commenting on the whole idea.

blocks.q: Did you have a phone when you were a child?
x: No, I didn't **get my own phone** until I was about fifteen, and it was a basic one that **could only** make calls and send texts. My parents were **quite strict** about it. Looking back, I think **that was a sensible decision**, because I **spent far more time** outdoors than kids do now.
notes: 'Didn't... until I was about fifteen' is an accurate time structure.
'Looking back' is a participle phrase that introduces reflection.
'Spent far more time outdoors than kids do now' is a comparison across tenses.

blocks.q: Is there any technology you couldn't live without?
x: My laptop, **hands down**. All my coursework, my thesis and my internship work **are stored on** it, so if it **stopped working**, **I'd be in serious trouble**. I've **learnt my lesson**, though, after losing an assignment last year, and now I **back everything up** to the cloud every week.
notes: 'Hands down' is an informal idiom meaning without question.
'If it stopped working, I'd be in serious trouble' is a second conditional.
'Are stored on it' is a passive structure.

blocks.q: Do you think people rely too much on technology?
x: **In some ways**, yes. I've noticed that I can't remember phone numbers anymore, and I **struggle to find my way** without Google Maps. **On the other hand**, technology **has made life much easier** for a lot of people, especially in rural areas, where farmers can now **check crop prices** online.
notes: 'Struggle to find my way' is a natural collocation.
'On the other hand' gives a balanced answer.
'Where farmers can now check crop prices' is a relative clause of place.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'a bookworm', 'can't put it down', 'a page-turner', 'I'm not much of a reader', 'read for pleasure', 'lose interest'.

blocks.q: Do you like reading?
x: Yes, although I don't read **as much as I used to**. As a teenager I **devoured** detective novels, especially Feluda and Sherlock Holmes. These days most of my reading is **academic papers** for my thesis, which **isn't quite the same**. I try to read at least one novel **over the holidays**.
notes: 'As much as I used to' contrasts past and present habits.
'Devoured' is a vivid, less common verb for reading eagerly.
'Which isn't quite the same' is a relative clause that adds a personal comment.

blocks.q: What kind of books do you enjoy?
x: **Mostly non-fiction** these days, things like popular science or biographies. I like books that **teach me something** without feeling like a textbook. I recently read one about the history of the internet, and it was **surprisingly gripping**. Fiction is fine too, but I **tend to lose interest** if the story **moves too slowly**.
notes: 'Without feeling like a textbook' is a preposition followed by an -ing form.
'Surprisingly gripping' is a precise adverb and adjective pair.
'Tend to lose interest' is a natural way to describe a habit.

blocks.q: Do you prefer reading on paper or on a screen?
x: **I much prefer** paper, to be honest. When I read on a screen, I **get distracted by notifications**, and my eyes **get tired** quite quickly. A printed book **feels more relaxing**. **That said**, I read on my phone all the time, simply because it's **more convenient** when I'm travelling.
notes: 'Get distracted by notifications' is a passive-style collocation.
'That said' introduces a contrast naturally.
'Simply because' adds emphasis to a reason.

blocks.q: Did your parents read to you as a child?
x: My mother did, yes, mostly Bengali folk tales **at bedtime**. I **can still remember** some of them **almost word for word**, like the one about the clever fox and the crocodile. I think that's **where my love of stories** came from, even if I don't have **much time for** novels now.
notes: 'Word for word' is a fixed phrase meaning exactly.
'That's where my love of stories came from' is a cleft-style structure.
'Even if I don't have much time' adds a concession.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'have varied taste in music', 'put on some music', 'bring back memories', 'pick up an instrument', 'catchy', 'lose my train of thought'.

blocks.q: What kind of music do you like?
x: I've got **quite varied taste**, really. I listen to a lot of Bangladeshi rock bands, the ones my father **grew up with**, but I also like **lo-fi music** when I'm studying, because it **helps me focus**. **The only thing I can't get into** is heavy metal. It's just too loud for me.
notes: 'Varied taste' is the natural collocation (not 'many tastes').
'The ones my father grew up with' is a relative clause ending in a preposition.
'Can't get into' is an informal phrasal verb for not enjoying something.

blocks.q: When do you usually listen to music?
x: Mostly **when I'm on the move**. I've always got my earphones in on the bus to Dhaka, because they **block out** the horns and the traffic. I also **put on** some music when I'm doing chores like laundry. The one time I can't listen is when I'm writing, because I **lose my train of thought**.
notes: 'On the move' is an idiom for travelling.
'Block out' and 'put on' are precise phrasal verbs.
'Lose my train of thought' is a natural idiom.

blocks.q: Have you ever learnt to play a musical instrument?
x: I **had a go at** the guitar when I was about sixteen. I **took lessons** for a few months, but I **gave up** when my exams got closer. I **regret that a bit** now, because I can only play three or four chords. **If I had more time**, I'd **pick it up again**.
notes: 'Had a go at' is an informal phrase for trying something.
'If I had more time, I'd pick it up again' is a second conditional.
'Took lessons' is the right collocation (not 'did lessons').

blocks.q: Has your taste in music changed over the years?
x: Yes, **quite a lot**. As a teenager I **was really into** Western pop, mostly because my friends were. Now I **appreciate** older Bangladeshi songs much more, especially the ones my parents **used to play** on long car journeys. I suppose **I've grown into** them, and they **bring back** a lot of memories.
notes: 'Was really into... because my friends were' uses ellipsis naturally.
'Used to play' marks a past habit.
'Grown into them' and 'bring back memories' are idiomatic phrasal verbs.

blocks.q: Do you think music is important for children?
x: **Definitely**. Learning songs **helps kids pick up** language and rhythm, and singing with others **builds their confidence**. In a lot of schools here, though, music **is treated as** a minor subject, which is a pity. **I wish I'd had** more music lessons at school myself.
notes: 'Helps kids pick up language' follows the pattern help + object + verb.
'Is treated as a minor subject' is a passive structure.
'I wish I'd had' is a past regret structure.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'hot and humid', 'pouring with rain', 'for days on end', 'a cold snap', 'drenched in sweat', 'the monsoon season'.

blocks.q: What's the weather like in your country?
x: It's **hot and humid** for most of the year. We have a long summer, then **the monsoon** from around June to October, when it can rain **for days on end**. Winter is short but **really pleasant**: dry, sunny and **cool enough** for a light jacket in the mornings.
notes: 'Hot and humid' is the standard collocation for this climate.
'For days on end' is a natural idiom meaning many days without a break.
'Cool enough for a light jacket' uses 'enough' correctly after the adjective.

blocks.q: What's your favourite season?
x: Winter, **without question**. The air's cool and dry, the sky's clear, and you don't **wake up drenched in sweat**. It's also the season for pitha, the rice cakes people make at home, and for weddings and picnics. It **only lasts** about two months, though, so I **try to make the most of** it.
notes: 'Without question' is a confident, less common opener.
'Wake up drenched in sweat' is a vivid collocation.
'The rice cakes people make at home' is a relative clause with the pronoun left out.

blocks.q: Do you like rainy days?
x: **It depends on** where I am. If I'm at home with nothing to do, I love them, because the sound of rain on a tin roof is **incredibly soothing**. But if I have to get to class, it's **a different matter**. The roads **flood within minutes**, and you **end up soaked** **no matter what** you wear.
notes: 'Incredibly soothing' is a precise adjective with an intensifier.
'It's a different matter' signals contrast.
'No matter what you wear' is a less common concessive structure.

blocks.q: Has the weather in your country changed in recent years?
x: **It seems that way**, yes. Older people often say summers **didn't use to be** this hot, and the rains **have become less predictable**. Some years the monsoon **arrives late**, and then we get sudden heavy floods. I'm not an expert, but **it's hard not to** link it to climate change.
notes: 'Didn't use to be' is the correct negative form of 'used to'.
'Have become less predictable' uses the present perfect for change.
'It's hard not to link it' is a natural hedged opinion.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'rush hour', 'get stuck in traffic', 'hop on a bus', 'a long-distance journey', 'sell out', 'public transport'.

blocks.q: How do you usually travel around?
x: **Mostly by bus**. Around the campus I just walk, but **whenever I head into** Dhaka, I take a bus, which can be **a real ordeal** in **rush hour**. For short trips in the city I **hop on** a rickshaw, or I book a motorbike ride through an app if I'm **in a hurry**.
notes: 'A real ordeal' is a strong noun for a bad experience.
'Hop on a rickshaw' is an informal phrasal verb.
'Whenever I head into Dhaka' uses a less common conjunction.

blocks.q: Is public transport good in your city?
x: **It's improving**, but there's still **a long way to go**. The metro rail in Dhaka **is a huge step forward**: it's clean, fast and almost always on time. The problem is that it only covers **a limited area** so far, so most people **still rely on** crowded buses that stop wherever they like.
notes: 'A long way to go' is a natural idiom for something unfinished.
'A huge step forward' is a strong collocation for progress.
'Buses that stop wherever they like' is a relative clause.

blocks.q: Did you use public transport much as a child?
x: Not really. My school was **only ten minutes away**, so my father **used to drop me off** on his motorbike. The first time I took a long-distance bus on my own was when I came to Savar for university, and I **remember being quite nervous** about **getting off** at the wrong stop.
notes: 'Used to drop me off' combines a past habit with a phrasal verb.
'Remember being nervous' uses remember + -ing for a past memory.
'The first time I took... was when...' is a complex sentence.

blocks.q: Do you prefer travelling by bus or by train?
x: **By train, given the choice**. Trains are **more comfortable**, you can walk around, and you don't **get stuck** in traffic jams. The only problem is that tickets **sell out** really quickly, especially before Eid. So **in practice**, I **end up taking** the bus most of the time.
notes: 'Given the choice' is a concise conditional phrase.
'Sell out' is the precise phrasal verb for tickets.
'In practice' contrasts a preference with reality.

blocks.q: What would make transport in your city better?
x: **The obvious answer** is more metro lines, but I think **better traffic management** would help just as much. At the moment, buses, rickshaws and cars all **compete for** the same space, and hardly anyone **sticks to** their lane. **If buses had their own lanes**, journeys **would be much faster**.
notes: 'Compete for the same space' is a precise verb and preposition pair.
'If buses had their own lanes, journeys would be much faster' is a second conditional.
'Hardly anyone sticks to their lane' uses a negative adverb naturally.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'go window shopping', 'compare prices', 'a real hassle', 'a good bargain', 'impulse buying', 'pay on delivery'.

blocks.q: Do you enjoy shopping?
x: **Not particularly**. I find crowded markets **quite exhausting**, especially before Eid, when you can **barely move**. I **tend to** buy only what I need and get out quickly. My sister's **the complete opposite**: she can spend a whole afternoon in a shopping mall and **come back with** nothing.
notes: 'I find crowded markets quite exhausting' uses the pattern find + object + adjective.
'When you can barely move' is a relative clause of time.
'The complete opposite' is a natural phrase for contrast.

blocks.q: Do you prefer shopping online or in shops?
x: For most things, online. It **saves a lot of time**, and you can **compare prices** easily. For clothes, though, I still go to a shop, because sizes **vary a lot** between brands, and **sending things back** can be **a real hassle** here. I've **been caught out** a couple of times.
notes: 'Compare prices' and 'saves a lot of time' are natural collocations.
'Sending things back' uses an -ing phrase as the subject.
'Been caught out' is a present perfect passive idiom.

blocks.q: What was the last thing you bought?
x: **A pair of** running shoes, about two weeks ago. My old ones **had completely worn out**, and I'd **been putting off** replacing them for months. I finally ordered a pair online during a sale, so I **got a decent discount**. **So far**, they've been really comfortable.
notes: 'Had completely worn out' is past perfect with a phrasal verb.
'I'd been putting off replacing them' is past perfect continuous with put off + -ing.
'So far, they've been' uses the present perfect for up to now.

blocks.q: Has shopping changed in your country in recent years?
x: **Massively**. Ten years ago almost everyone shopped at local markets, but now online shopping **has really taken off**, especially among young people. You can order almost anything, from groceries to furniture, and **pay on delivery**. Local markets **are still popular**, though, because people **enjoy bargaining**.
notes: 'Has really taken off' is a phrasal verb for rapid growth.
'From groceries to furniture' shows range with a from... to... structure.
'Pay on delivery' is the precise term for this payment method.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'keep fit', 'a huge fan of', 'stick to a routine', 'work up a sweat', 'drag on', 'get some exercise'.

blocks.q: Do you like sport?
x: Yes, **I'm a huge cricket fan**, like most people in Bangladesh. I **follow the national team** closely, even though they **can be frustrating** to watch. I also play myself, mostly **tape-ball cricket** with friends on the field behind our hall. It's **nothing serious**, but it's great fun.
notes: 'Follow the national team' is the precise collocation for supporting a team.
'Even though they can be frustrating to watch' is a concessive clause with a modal.
'Nothing serious' is a natural phrase for something casual.

blocks.q: How do you keep fit?
x: **I try to**, at least. I go for a jog around the campus **three or four times a week**, usually early in the morning **before it gets too hot**. I've also started doing **simple bodyweight exercises** in my room. I'm not exactly an athlete, but I feel much better **when I stick to it**.
notes: 'I try to, at least' is an honest, natural hedge.
'Before it gets too hot' is a time clause.
'Stick to it' is a phrasal verb for continuing a habit.

blocks.q: Did you do much sport at school?
x: **Not as much as I would have liked**. Our school in Dhaka didn't have a proper playground, so PE lessons **were pretty limited**. We **made do with** a small courtyard, where we played football with **a half-flat ball**. City schools **really need** more space for sport, in my opinion.
notes: 'Not as much as I would have liked' is a third-conditional-style regret.
'Made do with' is an idiom for managing with something not good enough.
'Where we played football' is a relative clause of place.

blocks.q: Do you prefer playing sport or watching it?
x: **Playing, definitely**, although I watch a lot too. Watching cricket on TV is fun, but it's **pretty passive**, and a test match can **drag on** for days. When you play, you're **completely absorbed** in the moment, and you **forget about** deadlines and exams.
notes: 'Drag on' is a phrasal verb for something that lasts too long.
'Completely absorbed in the moment' is a precise collocation.
'Watching cricket on TV is fun' uses an -ing phrase as the subject.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'go sightseeing', 'off the beaten track', 'a solo trip', 'split the costs', 'absolutely stunning', 'as far as the eye can see'.

blocks.q: Do you like travelling?
x: I love it, although I **haven't had the chance** to travel much yet. **So far** I've only been to a few places in Bangladesh, like Cox's Bazar and Sylhet. What I enjoy most is **trying the local food** and seeing **how people live** in different places. **I'm hoping to** go abroad for my master's.
notes: 'So far I've only been to' uses the present perfect for life experience.
'What I enjoy most is...' is a cleft sentence that adds emphasis.
'How people live' is an embedded question used correctly.

blocks.q: What's the best place you've visited?
x: Probably Sylhet, in the north-east. I went there with friends last winter, and the tea gardens were **absolutely stunning**, with green hills **as far as the eye can see**. We also **took a boat** through a swamp forest called Ratargul, which was **unlike anything** I'd seen before.
notes: 'Absolutely stunning' uses the right intensifier with a strong adjective.
'As far as the eye can see' is a natural fixed phrase.
'Unlike anything I'd seen before' uses the past perfect for earlier experience.

blocks.q: Do you prefer travelling alone or with others?
x: With others, **for sure**. **Part of the fun** of travelling is sharing it with someone, and it's also safer and cheaper when you **split the costs**. **That said**, I'd like to try **a solo trip** at some point, just to see whether I could **cope on my own**.
notes: 'Part of the fun' is a natural noun phrase.
'Split the costs' is the precise collocation for sharing expenses.
'Whether I could cope on my own' is an embedded question with a modal.

blocks.q: Where would you like to travel in the future?
x: **If I could go anywhere**, I'd choose Japan. I've always been **fascinated by** the way it mixes modern technology with old traditions. I'd love to see Kyoto in spring, when the cherry blossoms **are out**. It's quite expensive, though, so it'll have to **wait until** I'm **earning a proper salary**.
notes: 'If I could go anywhere, I'd choose Japan' is a second conditional.
'Fascinated by the way it mixes' is a precise adjective and preposition pattern.
'Wait until I'm earning' uses the present continuous after 'until' for the future.

title: Part 1 sample answers, set C: less common topics
bn: Model answers on sleep, noise, plants, clothes, social media, happiness, patience, festivals and art
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to answer the less familiar Part 1 topics that have appeared in recent tests, so none of them catch you off guard.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'a light sleeper', 'doze off', 'short on sleep', 'fix my sleep schedule', 'take a nap', 'toss and turn'.

blocks.q: How many hours do you usually sleep?
x: **Not as many as I should**. **On a good night** I get about seven hours, but during exams it can **drop to** four or five. I'm trying to **fix my sleep schedule**, because I've noticed that when I'm **short on sleep**, I can't focus in class at all.
notes: 'On a good night' is a natural phrase for the best case.
'Short on sleep' is an informal collocation.
'I've noticed that when I'm short on sleep, I can't focus' combines a present perfect and a time clause.

blocks.q: Do you ever take naps during the day?
x: **Every now and then**, mostly on Fridays. After a big lunch I sometimes **doze off** for half an hour, and I **wake up feeling** much fresher. On weekdays, though, I avoid it, because if I nap for too long, I **struggle to fall asleep** at night.
notes: 'Doze off' is a precise phrasal verb for falling asleep lightly.
'Wake up feeling much fresher' uses a participle after the verb.
'If I nap for too long, I struggle' is a zero conditional for a general truth.

blocks.q: What do you do if you can't sleep?
x: **The worst thing I can do** is pick up my phone, but **I'm guilty of** that quite often. **When I'm being sensible**, I read a few pages of a book or listen to a podcast with a timer. Sometimes I just get up and make a cup of warm milk, which **usually does the trick**.
notes: 'I'm guilty of that' is a natural way to admit a bad habit.
'When I'm being sensible' uses the present continuous for temporary behaviour.
'Does the trick' is an idiom meaning it works.

blocks.q: Do you think people sleep less now than in the past?
x: **I'd imagine so**. My grandparents **used to go to bed** soon after dark and get up at dawn. Now, with phones and long working hours, people **stay up far later**. In Dhaka a lot of people also **lose sleep** because of noise and heat, **which doesn't help**.
notes: 'I'd imagine so' is a soft, natural way to agree.
'Used to go to bed' contrasts the past with 'stay up far later' now.
'Which doesn't help' is a relative clause commenting on the whole situation.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'background noise', 'lean on the horn', 'get used to', 'can't hear myself think', 'a bit of buzz', 'noise pollution'.

blocks.q: Is your home noisy?
x: **Quite noisy**, yes, especially in the evening. There are about two hundred students in our hall, so there's **always something going on**: music, phone calls, people **arguing about** cricket. **I've got used to it**, mostly, but I **keep a pair of earplugs** for exam weeks.
notes: 'Always something going on' is a natural spoken phrase.
'I've got used to it' uses get used to + noun correctly.
'Arguing about cricket' is a reduced relative clause.

blocks.q: What kinds of noise do you dislike?
x: Car horns, **more than anything**. Drivers in Dhaka **lean on the horn** for no reason, even when the traffic **isn't moving at all**. I also **can't stand** construction noise early in the morning. **It's hard to think straight** when someone's drilling next door.
notes: 'Lean on the horn' is an idiomatic phrase for honking for a long time.
'Even when the traffic isn't moving at all' is a concessive time clause.
'It's hard to think straight' is a natural idiom.

blocks.q: Do you prefer a quiet or a lively environment?
x: **For studying**, it has to be quiet. Even a little **background chatter** breaks my concentration. Socially, though, I like **a bit of buzz**. A busy café or a crowded tea stall **has a nice atmosphere**, and silence in those places **would feel a bit strange**.
notes: 'For studying... Socially, though...' divides the answer clearly.
'Background chatter' and 'a bit of buzz' are precise, informal nouns.
'Would feel a bit strange' is a hypothetical with 'would'.

blocks.q: Do you think cities are getting noisier?
x: Dhaka **certainly is**. There are **far more vehicles** on the road than there were ten years ago, and **construction never seems to stop**. I've read that noise levels in parts of the city are **well above** safe limits. People complain about it constantly, but nobody **seems to do much** about it.
notes: 'Dhaka certainly is' uses ellipsis to answer briefly.
'Far more vehicles than there were' is a comparative across tenses.
'Well above safe limits' is a precise collocation.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'have green fingers', 'a rooftop garden', 'potted plants', 'grow wild', 'in full bloom', 'water the plants'.

blocks.q: Do you have any plants at home?
x: Not in the hall, because there's **hardly any sunlight** in our room. At my parents' flat, though, my mother **keeps a small rooftop garden** with chillies, tomatoes and **a few potted roses**. Whenever I'm home, she **puts me in charge of** watering them, which I don't mind.
notes: 'Hardly any sunlight' uses a negative adverb accurately.
'Puts me in charge of watering them' is a natural phrase with a gerund.
'Which I don't mind' is a relative clause with a mild opinion.

blocks.q: Did you grow plants as a child?
x: Yes, **in a small way**. At primary school we each **had to grow** a bean plant in a plastic cup for a science project. I remember **checking on** mine every morning and **being thrilled** when the first leaves appeared. Unfortunately, it **didn't survive** the summer holidays.
notes: 'Remember checking on mine' uses remember + -ing for a past memory.
'Being thrilled' is a stronger choice than 'being happy'.
'Didn't survive the summer holidays' adds light humour.

blocks.q: What's your favourite flower?
x: **I'd have to say** the water lily, which we call shapla. It's our national flower, and it **grows wild** in ponds all over the countryside. I love seeing **whole ponds covered** in pink and white flowers during the monsoon. **It reminds me of** my grandparents' village.
notes: 'I'd have to say' is a natural opener for choosing one thing.
'Whole ponds covered in pink and white flowers' is a participle phrase.
'It reminds me of' links the topic to a personal memory.

blocks.q: Do people in your country give flowers as gifts?
x: Yes, **more and more**. Flowers **used to be** mainly for weddings and festivals like Pohela Falgun, when women **wear flowers in their hair**. Now, though, people give bouquets for birthdays and graduations too. Shahbag in Dhaka **is famous for** its flower market, which **stays open** late.
notes: 'More and more' describes a growing trend.
'Used to be mainly for' contrasts past and present.
'Which stays open late' is a relative clause with useful detail.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'dress up', 'smart casual', 'keep up with trends', 'designer labels', 'loose and comfortable', 'give it a modern twist'.

blocks.q: What kind of clothes do you usually wear?
x: **Pretty casual** stuff, mostly: jeans or chinos with a T-shirt or a shirt. **When it's really hot**, I'll wear a cotton panjabi, because it's **loose and comfortable**. I **dress up** a bit more for presentations, but **I'm not really one for** suits and ties.
notes: 'I'll wear' uses 'will' for a typical habit.
'Loose and comfortable' is a natural pair of adjectives for clothes.
'Not really one for' is an idiomatic way to say you don't like something.

blocks.q: Is fashion important to you?
x: **Not hugely**, to be honest. I like to look **neat and presentable**, but I don't **follow trends** closely. I'd **rather spend** my money on books or travel than on **designer labels**. My younger sister, on the other hand, **keeps up with** every new style on Instagram.
notes: 'Neat and presentable' is a precise pair of adjectives.
'I'd rather spend... than...' is a natural preference structure.
'Keeps up with every new style' is a phrasal verb.

blocks.q: Do you wear traditional clothes?
x: Yes, **on special occasions**. For Eid I always wear a new panjabi, and for weddings I **go for** something a bit more formal. On Pohela Boishakh almost everyone wears red and white, which **makes the streets look amazing**. **In everyday life**, though, I **stick to** Western clothes.
notes: 'Go for' is a phrasal verb meaning choose.
'Which makes the streets look amazing' follows the pattern make + object + verb.
'Stick to Western clothes' is a natural phrasal verb.

blocks.q: Have clothes in your country changed in recent years?
x: Yes, **noticeably**. Young people **wear far more** Western-style clothes than our parents did, partly because of social media. **At the same time**, there's been **a revival of** local fabrics like jamdani, and quite a few young designers are **giving traditional styles a modern twist**.
notes: 'Wear far more... than our parents did' is a comparison across tenses.
'There's been a revival of' uses the present perfect for a recent trend.
'Giving traditional styles a modern twist' is an idiomatic collocation.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'scroll through my feed', 'waste hours', 'fake news', 'stay connected', 'go viral', 'take a break from'.

blocks.q: Do you use social media much?
x: **More than I'd like to admit**. I'm on Facebook mainly because **that's where** university groups and announcements are, and I check Instagram a few times a day. I recently deleted TikTok, though, because I was **losing hours** to it **without even noticing**.
notes: 'More than I'd like to admit' is an honest, natural opener.
'That's where university groups are' is a cleft-style structure.
'Was losing hours to it' uses the past continuous for an ongoing habit.

blocks.q: What do you like about social media?
x: **The main thing** is staying connected. My school friends are **spread across** the country, and some are abroad, so it's the easiest way to **see what they're up to**. It's also **really handy** for finding events and internships that **I'd otherwise miss**.
notes: 'The main thing is staying connected' uses an -ing form after 'is'.
'See what they're up to' is an informal idiom.
'That I'd otherwise miss' is a relative clause with a hypothetical meaning.

blocks.q: Is there anything you dislike about social media?
x: Yes, **the amount of** fake news. **Every time** something big happens in Bangladesh, **rumours spread** on Facebook **within minutes**, and a lot of people share them **without checking**. I also think it **makes people compare themselves** to others, which can't be good for anyone.
notes: 'The amount of fake news' uses 'amount' correctly with an uncountable noun.
'Every time something big happens' is a time clause.
'Which can't be good for anyone' is a modal of deduction in a relative clause.

blocks.q: Do you think children should use social media?
x: **Not until** they're in their teens, in my view. Young children **aren't mature enough** to deal with strangers or online bullying. **If I had kids**, I'd probably **let them** use messaging apps to talk to family, but I'd **hold off on** Instagram and TikTok for as long as I could.
notes: 'Not until they're in their teens' is a concise, clear opinion.
'If I had kids, I'd probably let them' is a second conditional.
'Hold off on' is a less common phrasal verb meaning delay.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'in a good mood', 'clear my head', 'not have a care in the world', 'up to a point', 'talk things through', 'bottle things up'.

blocks.q: What makes you happy?
x: **Simple things**, mostly. A long chat with my parents, a good cup of tea, or **finally fixing** a bug in my code **after hours of trying**. I've noticed that I'm happiest when I've **made progress** on something, even if it's small. Big events are nice, but the feeling **doesn't last**.
notes: 'After hours of trying' is a preposition followed by an -ing form.
'I'm happiest when I've made progress' combines a superlative with the present perfect.
'Even if it's small' adds a concession.

blocks.q: Were you happier as a child?
x: **In some ways**, yes. **I didn't have a care in the world**: no deadlines, no job applications, no worries about money. But I think I **appreciate things more** now. As an adult, you **make your own choices**, and **there's a real satisfaction** in that.
notes: 'I didn't have a care in the world' is a natural idiom.
'Appreciate things more' is a precise verb choice.
'There's a real satisfaction in that' ends with a reflective comment.

blocks.q: Do you think money can make people happy?
x: **Up to a point**. If you can't afford food or rent, money obviously **makes a huge difference**. But **once your basic needs are taken care of**, I don't think more money makes you much happier. Some of the happiest people I know **don't earn much** at all.
notes: 'Up to a point' is a natural way to partly agree.
'Once your basic needs are taken care of' is a time clause with a passive.
'Some of the happiest people I know' is a superlative with a reduced relative clause.

blocks.q: What do you do when you feel unhappy?
x: I usually **go for a long walk**, on my own if possible. Walking **helps me clear my head**, and I come back **in a better mood**. **If something's really bothering me**, I call a close friend and **talk it through**. **Bottling things up** never works for me.
notes: 'Helps me clear my head' is a natural idiom.
'Talk it through' is a phrasal verb for discussing a problem.
'Bottling things up' is an -ing phrase used as the subject.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'lose patience', 'get restless', 'stay calm under pressure', 'things don't go to plan', 'in their own time', 'it pays to be patient'.

blocks.q: Are you a patient person?
x: **It depends on the situation**. With people, I'm **fairly patient**: I don't mind explaining things to classmates **more than once**. But I'm **hopeless** in traffic. If I'm stuck in a jam for an hour, I **get really restless**, even though I know there's nothing I can do about it.
notes: 'Hopeless in traffic' is an informal, precise use of 'hopeless'.
'I don't mind explaining' uses mind + -ing.
'Even though I know there's nothing I can do' is a concessive clause.

blocks.q: When do you find it hard to be patient?
x: Mostly **when I'm waiting for** results. After an exam or a job application, I **keep refreshing** my email, even though I know it'll **take weeks**. I also **lose patience** with slow internet, which, in our hall, happens **far too often**.
