notes: 'Keep refreshing' uses keep + -ing for a repeated action.
'Lose patience with' is the right collocation (not 'lose my patient').
'Which, in our hall, happens far too often' is a relative clause with an inserted phrase.

blocks.q: Do you think you were more patient as a child?
x: **Probably less**, actually. As a kid I **wanted everything right away**, and I **used to sulk** if my parents said no. **Over time**, I've learnt that most good things, like learning a skill, **take a long time**. University **has taught me that**, if nothing else.
notes: 'Used to sulk' is a precise verb for a child's behaviour.
'Over time, I've learnt that' uses the present perfect for gradual change.
'If nothing else' is a natural fixed phrase.

blocks.q: Is patience important at work?
x: **Very much so**. In most jobs, things **don't go to plan**, and you have to deal with people who **work at their own pace**. **During my internship**, I noticed that the people who **stayed calm under pressure** usually **solved problems faster** than the ones who panicked.
notes: 'Don't go to plan' is a natural idiom.
'Work at their own pace' is a precise collocation.
'The people who stayed calm under pressure' is a defining relative clause.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'get together', 'a family tradition', 'soak up the atmosphere', 'go all out', 'a low-key celebration', 'it's worth it'.

blocks.q: What's the most important festival in your country?
x: **For most people**, it's Eid ul-Fitr, at the end of Ramadan. Millions of people **travel back to** their villages, so Dhaka **becomes almost empty** for a week. **Families get together**, everyone wears new clothes, and there's **far more food** than anyone can eat.
notes: 'Travel back to their villages' is an accurate verb and preposition pair.
'Becomes almost empty' describes a change with 'become'.
'Far more food than anyone can eat' is a natural exaggeration.

blocks.q: How do you usually celebrate your birthday?
x: **Quite quietly** these days. My friends in the hall usually **surprise me** with a cake at midnight, which **has become a bit of a tradition**. If I'm home, my mother makes payesh, a kind of rice pudding, because she knows it's my favourite. **I've never been one for** big parties.
notes: 'Which has become a bit of a tradition' is a relative clause with the present perfect.
'A kind of rice pudding' explains a local word clearly.
'I've never been one for' is an idiomatic way to express dislike.

blocks.q: Do you enjoy Pohela Boishakh?
x: Yes, **it's one of my favourite days** of the year. It's the Bengali New Year, in mid-April, and the whole country celebrates it **regardless of religion**. I usually go to a fair with friends, eat panta bhat with fried hilsa and **soak up the atmosphere**. It's hot, but **it's well worth it**.
notes: 'Regardless of religion' is a less common prepositional phrase.
'Soak up the atmosphere' is a natural idiom for enjoying a place.
'It's well worth it' is a fixed phrase that ends the answer neatly.

blocks.q: Have celebrations changed since you were a child?
x: **Somewhat**. When I was young, Eid was **all about** visiting relatives **from house to house**. Now a lot of greetings happen **over video calls**, because families **are more spread out**. The heart of it, getting together and sharing food, **hasn't changed**, though.
notes: 'All about visiting relatives' is a natural informal phrase.
'Are more spread out' is a passive-style adjective phrase.
'The heart of it... hasn't changed' uses the present perfect to contrast with the past.

blocks.x: Useful phrases for this topic: 'I'm no expert', 'go over my head', 'really striking', 'an exhibition', 'be put off by', 'well worth a visit'.

blocks.q: Do you like art?
x: **I appreciate it**, but **I'm no expert**. I like **paintings that tell a story**, especially ones about village life or the Liberation War. Abstract art usually **goes over my head**, to be honest. I can **see the skill** involved, but I don't feel much when I look at it.
notes: 'Paintings that tell a story' is a defining relative clause.
'Goes over my head' is an idiom meaning too hard to understand.
'The skill involved' is a reduced relative clause.

blocks.q: Did you learn art at school?
x: Yes, **up until** Class Eight. We had drawing lessons once a week, and I was **pretty average** at it. I was fine with colours, but **anything involving** people or faces **turned out badly**. I still **remember being embarrassed** when my teacher held up my portrait of my mother.
notes: 'Anything involving people or faces' is a reduced relative clause.
'Turned out badly' is a phrasal verb for a result.
'Remember being embarrassed' uses remember + -ing for a past memory.

blocks.q: Have you been to an art gallery recently?
x: Yes, actually. A few months ago I went to an exhibition at the Shilpakala Academy in Dhaka with a friend who **studies fine arts**. **I wasn't expecting much**, but some of the photography was **really striking**, especially the pictures of the floods in Sylhet. It **made me want to** go more often.
notes: 'A friend who studies fine arts' is a defining relative clause.
'I wasn't expecting much' uses the past continuous for an earlier attitude.
'Really striking' is a precise adjective for visual art.

blocks.q: Should museums be free to enter?
x: **Ideally, yes**, or at least very cheap for students. **If entry were free**, more families might **take their children along** at weekends. Museums **hold a lot of** history, and **it'd be a shame** if people **were put off** by the price.
notes: 'If entry were free, more families might...' is a second conditional with 'might'.
'Take their children along' is a phrasal verb with an object in the middle.
'Were put off by the price' is a passive phrasal verb.

title: Part 2 strategy: planning and telling your story
bn: How to use your minute, shape your talk and keep going for two minutes
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to plan a Part 2 talk in one minute and keep speaking naturally for the full two minutes.

blocks.x: Part 2 is the long turn. The examiner gives you a task card with a topic and three or four prompts, plus a pencil and some paper. You have one minute to prepare. Then you speak for one to two minutes without interruption. When the time is up, the examiner stops you and may ask one or two short **rounding-off questions** before moving on to Part 3.

The whole Speaking test lasts 11 to 14 minutes, and Part 2 takes about three or four of them, including the preparation. It is the only part of the test where you control the talk completely. You choose the story, the vocabulary and the grammar. It is also where many candidates lose marks, because they stop after 50 seconds or simply list facts.

head: Criterion
What it means in Part 2
rows: You keep talking with few long pauses, and your ideas follow a clear order.
You use some less common words and natural collocations, and you paraphrase when you cannot find a word.
You mix simple and complex sentences, and most of your sentences have no errors.
The examiner understands you easily, and your stress and intonation sound natural.

blocks.x: The four criteria carry equal weight. Part 2 is where the examiner hears your longest stretch of speech, so it gives a clear picture of all four at once.
Aim for the full two minutes. If the examiner stops you in the middle of a sentence, that is fine. It simply means you still had more to say.

Many candidates treat the prompts as four separate questions and give one sentence for each. That gives you about 40 seconds and very little to assess. Use the prompts as a guide for a story, not as a questionnaire.

One minute is very short. You cannot write sentences, and you should not try. Write **key words only**: nouns, a few verbs and one or two good phrases you want to use. Your notes are there to remind you, not to be read aloud.

x: Read the card for about ten seconds. Choose your topic at once, and take the first real example that comes to mind.
Write one line for each prompt, using two or three words.
Add a story line: when, where, and one thing that happened.
Write down two or three band 7 phrases you want to use, such as a collocation or an idiom.
Note one feeling or reflection for the ending.
Use any seconds left to plan your first sentence in your head.

blocks.x: Imagine the card says 'Describe a time when you had to wait for something important', with prompts on what you were waiting for, how long you waited, what you did while you were waiting, and how you felt when the wait was over. Here are one candidate's real notes. There is not a single full sentence.

x: HSC results, after exams
nearly 3 months, monsoon
busy: helping Ammu, cricket, computer course
nervous, rumours, checking phone
result day: whole family, uncle's laptop, website crashed
SMS!! forgot I registered
phrases: easier said than done / couldn't sit still / weight off my shoulders
end: worrying changes nothing

blocks.x: Writing full sentences such as 'I was waiting for my HSC result' uses up half your minute, and you will be tempted to read them out. Reading sounds flat, and the examiner will notice.

blocks.q: Turn this sentence into key-word notes: 'I went to Cox's Bazar with my cousins last winter and we stayed in a small hotel near the beach.'
blocks.a: Cox's Bazar, cousins, last winter, small hotel near beach.

blocks.x: A clear shape helps you keep going, and it helps the examiner follow you. You do not need to say 'firstly' and 'secondly'. Instead, move through four stages and let the story carry you from one to the next.

head: Stage
What you do
Rough time
rows: Say what you are going to talk about and give the background: when, where and who.
Answer the prompts, adding a detail or a reason to each one.
Tell one moment in detail: what happened, what someone said, what went wrong.
Say how you felt then and how you see it now. This answers the 'explain' line.

blocks.x: Here is the card from the previous page in full, followed by a talk built on those notes. Listen for the moment each stage begins.

Describe a time when you had to wait for something important.
You should say:
- what you were waiting for
- how long you had to wait
- what you did while you were waiting
and explain how you felt when the wait was over.

x: I'm going to talk about the time I was waiting for my HSC results, which was probably the longest three months of my life. I'd just finished my exams, and everyone kept telling me to relax and enjoy the break, but honestly, that was **easier said than done**.

For the first few weeks I **kept myself busy**. I helped my mother at home, watched far too many cricket matches and started a short computer course near our house. But as the date got closer, I **couldn't sit still**. I was checking Facebook groups every few hours, because there were always rumours that the results **were about to be published**. My father, who's normally very calm, kept asking whether I'd heard anything, which didn't help at all.

The day itself was quite dramatic. The results were supposed to come out at two o'clock, and by half past one the whole family **had gathered around** my uncle's laptop. Of course, the moment the website opened, it crashed, because thousands of students were trying to log in at the same time. **While we were refreshing the page** for the tenth time, my phone buzzed. I'd registered for the SMS service and **completely forgotten about it**. I'd got the grade I was hoping for, and my mother actually started crying.

Looking back, it was **a huge weight off my shoulders**. What I learned is that worrying doesn't change anything. **If I'd spent less time** checking rumours, I'd have enjoyed that summer a lot more. These days, when I'm waiting for something, I try to **focus on what I can control**.
notes: Each stage is clear: the background, the waiting period, the story of results day, and finally a lesson.
'had gathered around' (past perfect) and 'While we were refreshing the page' (past continuous) put the events in a clear time order.
'If I'd spent less time ... I'd have enjoyed' is a third conditional used for reflection.
'easier said than done' and 'a huge weight off my shoulders' are idioms native speakers really use, and they fit the story naturally.

blocks.q: Do you think young people today are more patient than in the past?
x: Probably less patient, to be honest. We're **used to getting things instantly**, whether it's food delivery or a reply on Messenger, so waiting feels strange. That said, I don't think it's entirely our fault. **If you grow up with** fast internet, you **naturally come to expect** speed. My grandparents waited weeks for a letter, so they had no choice.
notes: 'be used to getting' (be used to + -ing) is a structure many band 6 speakers get wrong.
'That said' signals a contrast in a natural spoken way.
The answer is short and direct, which suits a rounding-off question.

blocks.x: If you finish stage 4 and the examiner has not stopped you, go back and add one more detail to the story, such as what someone said or what the weather was like.

pages.h: Telling the story in the past

blocks.x: Most Part 2 cards ask about the past: a time you did something, a person you met, a trip you took. This is your best chance to show **grammatical range**. A band 6 speaker usually tells the whole story in the past simple. A band 7 speaker mixes tenses, so the listener knows what happened first and what was going on in the background.

head: Tense
What it does
Example
rows: The main events, one after another
'We got on the bus and found our seats.'
Background action, or an action interrupted by another one
'It was raining heavily when we arrived.'
An action that happened before another past action
'I realised I had left my wallet at home.'
An action in progress up to a past moment
'I had been studying for six hours, so I was exhausted.'
'My grandfather would take me to the river every Friday.'

x: I studied for six hours. Then I was very tired.
I'd been studying for six hours, so I was completely exhausted.
I left my phone at home. I noticed it at the station.
When I got to the station, I realised I'd left my phone at home.
It rained. We waited under a shop.
It was pouring with rain, so we took shelter in a tea stall.
Every Friday my grandfather took me to the river.
Every Friday my grandfather would take me down to the river.
I met Rafi. He was my classmate before.
I bumped into Rafi, who I'd been at school with years earlier.

blocks.x: A common slip is drifting into the present tense once the story gets exciting: 'Then my friend come and he say ...'. It happens when you focus on the story and forget the grammar. Practise the irregular past forms you need most often: 'came', 'said', 'told', 'brought', 'thought', 'caught'.
Do not use the past perfect for every past action. 'Yesterday I had gone to the market' is wrong when there is no later past event to compare it with. Use it only when you jump further back in time.

blocks.q: Fill in the gaps: When we _____ (reach) the stadium, the match _____ (already / start), and people _____ (shout) everywhere.
blocks.a: When we reached the stadium, the match had already started, and people were shouting everywhere.

pages.h: When you run out of things to say

blocks.x: Almost everyone dries up at some point. The examiner does not expect a perfect two minutes, but long silences lower your fluency score. The answer is to have a few ways of **opening up new material** ready before you walk in.

x: Go back to a prompt and add a reason: 'The main reason I chose it was ...'
Zoom in on one detail of the story: the weather, a smell, what someone was wearing.
Add what someone said, in reported speech: 'My friend told me he'd never seen anything like it.'
Compare then and now: 'At the time I thought ..., but now I realise ...'
Imagine a different outcome: 'If it hadn't rained, we would probably have ...'
Say what you would do differently, or what you would like to do next.
Umm ... umm ... and that's all.
Actually, there's one more thing I should mention.
I don't know what more to say.
Thinking about it now, what really stays with me is ...
It was very good. Very very good.
It was one of those experiences I'll probably remember for years.
Yes, so, that is my answer.
Anyway, if I had the chance, I'd definitely do it again.

blocks.x: Fillers such as 'Let me think' or 'How can I put it?' are fine once or twice. They give you two seconds. Used every few sentences, they start to sound like stalling.

Do not switch to a new topic when you run out. Moving from your best friend to a different friend halfway through looks as if you have lost control of the talk. Stay with the same story and go deeper.

blocks.q: You are talking about a park and run out of ideas after one minute. Give two sentences that open up new material.
blocks.a: Possible answers: 'The thing I remember most is the smell of the grass after the rain.' 'If they built a park like that near my hall, I'd probably go there every evening.'

blocks.x: You cannot prepare for every card, but you can prepare five or six **flexible stories**: real experiences with plenty of detail that you can bend to fit different topics. One good story about a trip can answer cards about a journey, a happy time, a time something went wrong, a place you visited or a person you spent time with.

head: Cue card
Story: a trip to Sylhet with hall friends. What to put in the centre
rows: The tea gardens, the boat ride and the food
The bus breaking down on the way
A time you laughed a lot
The friend who turned the breakdown into a joke
A place you would like to visit again
Ratargul, and why you want to go back in the monsoon
A time you tried something new
Swimming in a river for the first time

blocks.x: Below is a card that looks hard at first. The talk uses the same Sylhet trip and puts the funny moment at the centre.

Describe a time when you laughed a lot with other people.
You should say:
- when and where it happened
- who you were with
- what made you laugh
and explain why you remember it so well.

x: I'd like to talk about a trip I took to Sylhet with four friends from my university hall last year. It was the first time we'd travelled anywhere together without any family, so we were all **in high spirits** from the start.

The funniest part happened on the way there. We'd booked the cheapest bus we could find, and somewhere near Srimangal it **broke down in the middle of nowhere**. It was nearly midnight and **it was pouring with rain**. Most people would have been annoyed, but my friend Tanvir decided this was the perfect moment to give a speech. He stood up and started **impersonating our hall provost**, telling the other passengers off for being late with their fees. Even the driver, who **had been looking pretty miserable**, ended up laughing so hard he had to sit down.

After that, the joke just kept going. Every time something went slightly wrong, like when our boat at Ratargul **got stuck among the trees**, or when we ordered far too much food, someone would do the provost voice again. By the third day we were **in stitches** over things that weren't really funny at all.

I think I remember it so well because it **turned a bad situation into the best part** of the trip. **If the bus hadn't broken down**, we'd probably have slept the whole way and forgotten about it. It also **brought us much closer** as a group. We still message each other in that voice whenever one of us is stressed before an exam.
notes: 'in high spirits' and 'in stitches' are natural idioms for happiness and laughter, used once each so they do not sound forced.
'had been looking pretty miserable' (past perfect continuous) inside a relative clause shows grammatical range.
'If the bus hadn't broken down, we'd probably have slept' is an accurate third conditional.
The same Sylhet story could answer at least four other cards, which is the point of a flexible story.

blocks.q: Do you think it's important to laugh at work or at school?
x: Yes, I'd say it's really important, as long as it doesn't **get out of hand**. A bit of humour **breaks the tension**, especially before exams or deadlines. Some of my best teachers used jokes to **keep us engaged** in long classes. Of course, there's **a time and a place** for it, and you wouldn't joke during a serious meeting.
notes: 'get out of hand' and 'a time and a place' are fixed expressions that sound natural here.
'as long as' introduces a condition without a full if-clause.
The answer gives a view, a reason and a limit in under a minute.

blocks.x: Before the test, write down five stories you could tell for two minutes: a trip, a celebration, a problem you solved, a person who matters to you, and something you bought or were given. Practise each one with three different cue cards.

After your talk, the examiner may ask one or two short questions linked to your topic, such as 'Would you do it again?' or 'Do your friends feel the same way?'. Everything you say still counts, so answer properly. Give a **short, direct answer** of two or three sentences. Part 3 is about to start, so this is not the place for another long speech.

x: Would you like to go there again?
Do other people in your family feel the same way?
Is this a common thing to do in your country?
Have you ever told anyone else about it?
Yes.
Yes, definitely, although I'd probably go in winter next time.
No, I don't think so.
Not really. My brother's much more practical than me, so he'd probably find it boring.
Yes, it is common.
It's becoming more common, especially among younger people in Dhaka.

blocks.q: Would you like to go on another trip with the same friends?
x: Definitely, and we've **already started planning** one to Bandarban in the winter. The only problem is that **we've all got different schedules** now, because two of them have part-time jobs. **Assuming we can find** a free week, though, I'm sure it'll happen. I'd just choose a better bus this time.
notes: 'we've already started planning' (present perfect) links the past trip to the present.
'Assuming we can find' is a less common way to express a condition.
The final sentence links back to the talk with a touch of humour.

blocks.x: Some candidates think a rounding-off question means their talk went badly. It does not. It is a normal part of Part 2, so answer it calmly and naturally.

blocks.q: Upgrade this answer to 'Would you recommend this place to a friend?': 'Yes, I like it. It is good.'
blocks.a: Possible answer: 'Yes, I'd definitely recommend it, especially to anyone who likes quiet places. I'd just tell them to avoid the weekends, when it gets crowded.'

title: Sample talks: people
bn: Six model talks about people you know, admire or would like to meet
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to describe a person's character, habits and influence with band 7 vocabulary and grammar.

blocks.x:
Describe a person who inspired you to do something.
You should say:
- who the person is
- how you know this person
- what this person inspired you to do
and explain why this person had such an effect on you.

x: The person I'd like to talk about is a senior student from my department called Mitu. She was in her final year when I joined university, and I first met her at a club orientation, where she was **in charge of** recruiting new members for a volunteer group.

What she inspired me to do was get involved in community work. Before I met her, I'd **never really thought about** volunteering. I was quite shy, and I spent most of my free time in my room playing games. Mitu, on the other hand, **seemed to have endless energy**. She was organising a winter clothes drive for families living near the river outside Savar, and she asked me to help sort the donations. I agreed mainly because I **found it hard to say no** to her.

That first weekend changed things. We **ended up collecting** over three hundred blankets, and when we handed them out, an old man held my hand and thanked me for nearly a minute. I'd **never felt so useful** in my life. After that, I went to every event, and by my second year I was **running the social media side** of the group myself.

I think she had such an effect on me because she **led by example**. She never lectured anyone. She just worked harder than everyone else, and people wanted to keep up with her. She's graduated now and works for an NGO, but we're still in touch. **If I hadn't met her**, I'd probably still be the quiet student who **kept himself to himself**.
notes: 'in charge of', 'ended up collecting' and 'led by example' are natural collocations that a band 6 speaker rarely uses.
'I'd never really thought about' and 'I'd never felt so useful' use the past perfect to compare before and after.
'If I hadn't met her, I'd probably still be' is a mixed conditional: past cause, present result.
'kept himself to himself' is an everyday idiom for a reserved person.

blocks.q: Do you think famous people or ordinary people inspire us more?
x: For me, it's ordinary people, without a doubt. Famous people can **seem a bit out of reach**, because their lives are so different from ours. Someone like a teacher or a senior student is **much more relatable**. You can actually see how they **got where they are**, so success feels possible for you too.
notes: 'out of reach' and 'relatable' paraphrase the idea of distance and closeness.
'how they got where they are' is an embedded question, a sign of grammatical range.
The answer is direct and gives one clear reason.

x: She is a very good person.
She's genuinely warm and easy to talk to.
She motivated me a lot.
She really pushed me out of my comfort zone.
I started to do volunteer work.
I got involved in volunteering.
She was an example for me.
She led by example.
I changed a lot because of her.
She had a lasting effect on me.

blocks.x: With a person card, one short story about something the person did is worth more than a long list of their good qualities.

pages.h: A friend you enjoy spending time with

blocks.x:
Describe a friend you enjoy spending time with.
You should say:
- who this friend is
- how you met
- what you usually do together
and explain why you enjoy spending time with this friend.

x: I'm going to talk about my friend Fahim, who I've known since we were about twelve. We were **put in the same section** in class seven, and the teacher made us share a bench. To be honest, we didn't get on at first, because he talked non-stop. But after a few weeks we **discovered we had a lot in common**, especially our obsession with cricket, and we've been close ever since.

These days we're at different universities, so we don't see each other **as often as we'd like**. Even so, we try to meet up at least twice a month. Usually we go to Dhanmondi Lake in the evening, walk around for an hour and then **grab some fuchka** from one of the stalls. If there's a big match on, we watch it at his place, and his mother always **insists on feeding us** far too much.

What I enjoy most about him is that he's **completely down to earth**. He doesn't care about brands or showing off, and he's the kind of person you can **sit in silence with** without it feeling awkward. He's also very honest. Last year, when I was thinking about **dropping out of** a course I'd already paid for, he told me straight that I'd regret it. I didn't want to hear it, but he was absolutely right.

I suppose I value him because he **knows me better than** almost anyone. With most people I feel I have to make an effort, but with Fahim I can just be myself. I think that's quite rare, and I'm lucky to **have found it so early**.
notes: 'who I've known since' (present perfect with since) is accurate, and it avoids the common error 'I know him since'.
'discovered we had a lot in common' and 'completely down to earth' are natural, idiomatic ways to describe friendship and character.
'the kind of person you can sit in silence with' is a relative clause ending in a preposition, which sounds natural in speech.
'insists on feeding us' uses the verb + preposition + -ing pattern correctly.

blocks.q: Is it easy to make new friends at university?
x: It depends on the person, I think. For me it was fairly easy, because living in a hall means you're **surrounded by people** all the time. But I know some students who commute from far away, and they **find it harder to fit in**. Joining a club usually helps, because you **meet people with similar interests**.
notes: 'It depends on the person' is a natural way to start a balanced answer.
'fit in' is an everyday phrasal verb used accurately.
The answer compares two groups of students and offers a solution.

x: We are friends for a long time.
We've been close friends for years.
He is very simple.
He's completely down to earth.
We have the same interests.
We've got a lot in common.
We meet sometimes.
We meet up whenever we get the chance.
He tells me the truth directly.
He tells me straight, even when I don't want to hear it.

blocks.x: Avoid 'He is very simple' to praise someone. In English it can sound as if the person is not very clever. Say 'down to earth' or 'easy-going' instead.

Describe a family member you admire.
You should say:
- who this person is
- what this person does
- what qualities this person has
and explain why you admire this person.

x: The family member I admire most is my grandmother on my father's side. She's in her late seventies now and lives with my uncle in our village near Cumilla. Whenever I go home for Eid, she's the first person I visit.

Her life hasn't been easy at all. My grandfather passed away when she was only in her thirties, and she **was left to raise** five children on her own with very little money. She **kept the family going** by growing vegetables, raising chickens and selling homemade pickles at the local market. **Somehow she managed to** send all five children to school, which was quite unusual for a family like ours at that time.

The quality I admire most is her **sheer determination**. She never **felt sorry for herself**, at least not in front of anyone. She's also incredibly curious. She **had never learned to read** as a child, but when she was about sixty, she asked my cousin to teach her. Now she reads the newspaper every morning and **has strong opinions about** politics, which makes family dinners quite lively.

I suppose I admire her because she **puts my own problems into perspective**. When I'm stressed about an assignment, I remember what she went through, and it seems much smaller. She's also taught me that **it's never too late** to learn something new. **If she could learn to read at sixty**, I really have no excuse for giving up on things just because they're difficult.
notes: 'was left to raise' is a passive structure that shows the situation was forced on her.
'sheer determination' and 'puts my own problems into perspective' are strong collocations.
'had never learned to read as a child' (past perfect) moves the story further back in time.
'If she could learn to read at sixty, I really have no excuse' uses a real past ability in a conditional, a flexible use of if.

blocks.q: Do you think older people get enough respect in your country?
x: Mostly yes, especially in villages, where elders are still **looked up to**. In cities it's changing a bit. People are busier, and some older people **end up feeling quite lonely**, even when they live with their children. I don't think it's a lack of respect exactly. It's more that **families spend less time together** than they used to.
notes: 'looked up to' is a passive phrasal verb used naturally.
'end up feeling' expresses an unplanned result.
'It's more that ...' corrects the idea in the question politely.

x: She is very strong.
She's got real determination.
Her life was very hard.
She's had a really tough life.
She did not stop trying.
She never gave up, however hard things got.
She helped the family to survive.
She kept the family going.
My problems look small.
It puts my own problems into perspective.

blocks.x: Use 'passed away' for a death in the family. It is gentler than 'died' and sounds respectful in an exam.

Describe a teacher who helped you a lot.
You should say:
- who the teacher was
- what subject this teacher taught
- how this teacher helped you
and explain why you still remember this teacher.

x: I'd like to talk about my maths teacher from secondary school. Everyone called him Mizan Sir, and he taught us in classes nine and ten. He was a small, quiet man who **wore the same grey sweater** every winter, and at first nobody took him very seriously.

I was **struggling badly with maths** at that time. I'd done well in primary school, but once we got to algebra, I **completely lost track**. In the first term test of class nine, I got thirty-one out of a hundred, and I **was too embarrassed to** show the paper to my parents. Mizan Sir must have noticed, because he asked me to stay behind after class. I thought he was going to **tell me off**, but instead he asked me to come to the staff room twice a week at lunchtime.

He never charged me a single taka for those sessions, which was unusual, since most teachers **ran private coaching on the side**. What he did was **break every problem down** into tiny steps and make me explain each step back to him. By the end of the year, I'd **gone from failing to** getting one of the highest marks in the class.

I still remember him because he **saw something in me** that I couldn't see myself. He also taught me a way of working that I still use. Whenever a topic **seems overwhelming**, I split it into small pieces, just as he showed me. I visited him last year, and he remembered my test score before I'd even sat down.
notes: 'struggling badly with maths' and 'completely lost track' describe difficulty precisely.
'must have noticed' is a modal of deduction about the past.
'ran private coaching on the side' is a natural phrase for a second job, and it fits the Bangladeshi context.
'I'd gone from failing to getting' (past perfect with from ... to) shows clear progress in one structure.

blocks.q: Would you like to be a teacher yourself?
x: Maybe one day, but not right now. I think teaching **takes a lot of patience**, and I'm not sure I have enough yet. **What appeals to me** is the idea of making a difference, like Mizan Sir did for me. Perhaps I'll **do some part-time tutoring** first and see whether I enjoy it.
notes: 'What appeals to me is ...' is a cleft sentence that puts focus on the reason.
'takes a lot of patience' is a common collocation.
The answer links back to the talk, which keeps it coherent.

x: I was weak in maths.
I was really struggling with maths.
I could not understand anything.
I completely lost track.
He did not take money.
He never charged me a single taka.
He made the problems easy.
He broke every problem down into small steps.
He believed in me.
He saw something in me that I couldn't see myself.

blocks.x: Say 'I was weak at maths' or, better, 'I struggled with maths'. 'Weak in maths' is a common local form, but 'at' is the usual preposition.

pages.h: A person who is good at their job

blocks.x:
Describe a person you know who is very good at their job.
You should say:
- who the person is
- what job this person does
- how you know this person
and explain why you think this person is good at the job.

x: The person I'm going to describe runs a small tea stall just outside my university hall in Savar. Everyone calls him Kamal Bhai, and I've been buying tea from him almost every evening for about three years, so I suppose I **know him quite well** by now.

On the surface, his job looks simple. He makes tea, sells biscuits and bananas and keeps the stall open until about midnight. But he's **remarkably good at it**. The first thing you notice is his memory. There might be thirty students crowded around the stall, all shouting at once, and he'll **remember exactly how** each person likes their tea: less sugar, extra ginger, no milk. **I've never once seen him** get an order wrong.

He's also **brilliant with people**. He knows which students are from which district, who has exams coming up and who's **going through a hard time**. During the exam period last year, when I was studying late every night, he started **putting aside** a packet of biscuits for me, because he'd noticed I always arrived after the stall had run out.

I think he's good at his job because he **takes real pride in** it. A lot of people would see a tea stall as just a way to earn a living, but he treats it almost like a profession. He keeps the place spotless, he's never rude, and he **gets through hundreds of cups** a night without looking stressed. **If I end up being half as organised** as him in my career, I'll be very happy.
notes: 'remarkably good at it' and 'brilliant with people' are natural intensifier collocations.
'I've never once seen him get an order wrong' uses the present perfect with emphasis.
'because he'd noticed I always arrived after the stall had run out' contains two past perfect verbs, used accurately.
'If I end up being half as organised as him' is a first conditional with a comparison structure.

blocks.q: Should people choose a job they enjoy or one that pays well?
x: Ideally both, but if I had to choose, I'd **go for enjoyment**, within reason. You **spend most of your waking hours** at work, so hating your job would be miserable. Having said that, in Bangladesh many people **don't have the luxury of choosing**, because they need to support their families first.
notes: 'if I had to choose, I'd ...' is a second conditional for a hypothetical choice.
'Having said that' introduces a contrast naturally.
'don't have the luxury of choosing' is a less common, idiomatic phrase.

x: He is very good in his work.
He's remarkably good at his job.
He never forgets the orders.
I've never once seen him get an order wrong.
He is friendly with everyone.
He's brilliant with people.
He likes his job.
He takes real pride in his work.
He does a lot of work without stress.
He gets through hundreds of cups a night without breaking a sweat.

blocks.x: You do not need to choose someone with an impressive job. An ordinary person described in vivid detail makes a stronger talk than a doctor described in general terms.

pages.h: A famous person you would like to meet

blocks.x:
Describe a famous person you would like to meet.
You should say:
- who this person is
- what this person is famous for
- what you would ask this person
and explain why you would like to meet this person.

x: If I could meet any famous person, I'd choose a well-known spin bowler who plays for the Bangladesh national team. He's been playing at the top level for over ten years, and he's **something of a hero** in my family.

He's famous mainly for his bowling, obviously, but also for his background. He grew up in a small town in the north, and he **didn't have access to** proper equipment as a child. Apparently he practised with a tennis ball **wrapped in electrical tape** on a field that flooded every monsoon. **Despite all that**, he made it into the national team before he was twenty, and he's **won us several matches** almost single-handedly.

If I met him, the first thing I'd ask is how he **copes with the pressure**. Imagine walking out in front of thirty thousand people, knowing the whole country is watching and that one bad over could **turn everyone against you**. I'd also like to know what he does on the days when nothing goes right, because I think that's when you find out what a person is really like.

The main reason I'd like to meet him is that he **came from nothing**, more or less, and still reached the top. A lot of young people here feel that **the odds are stacked against them** because they aren't from Dhaka or from a rich family. He shows that isn't always true. Even a ten-minute conversation would probably **stay with me for years**.
notes: 'the odds are stacked against them' and 'came from nothing' are idioms used in the right context.
'If I met him, the first thing I'd ask is how ...' combines a second conditional with an embedded question.
'Imagine walking out ..., knowing that ...' uses -ing clauses to build a vivid picture.
'Despite all that' links the hardship to the success without a simple 'but'.

blocks.q: Do you think famous people have a responsibility to be good role models?
x: To some extent, yes. Whether they like it or not, **millions of children copy them**, so their behaviour matters. But I also think we **expect too much** of them sometimes. They're human, and they're bound to **make the odd mistake** like anyone else. Parents and teachers are more important role models, in my opinion.
notes: 'Whether they like it or not' is a natural concessive phrase.
'they're bound to make the odd mistake' uses 'be bound to' for something certain.
The answer agrees partly and then adds a limit, which shows flexible thinking.

x: He is from a poor family.
He came from nothing, more or less.
He had many problems but he succeeded.
Despite all the obstacles, he made it to the top.
Everyone knows him.
He's a household name here.
I want to ask how he handles pressure.
I'd ask him how he copes with the pressure.
Young people from villages have less chance.
Young people from small towns often feel the odds are stacked against them.

blocks.x: This card uses 'would' throughout because the meeting is imagined. Keep the conditional going: 'I'd ask', 'I'd like to know', 'it would probably stay with me'.

title: Sample talks: places and objects
bn: Six model talks about places you know and things you own, give or keep
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to describe places and objects in vivid detail and connect them to your own memories.

pages.h: A place where you like to relax

blocks.x:
Describe a place where you like to relax.
You should say:
- where it is
- how often you go there
- what you do there
and explain why this place helps you relax.

x: The place where I relax most is the rooftop of our building in Mirpur, where my family lives. It's only a six-storey building, so the roof isn't particularly high, but on a clear night you can see **across a sea of rooftops** all the way to the stadium lights.

I go up there whenever I'm home from university, which is usually every second weekend. My mother **has turned one corner** of it into a little garden, with chillies, tomatoes and a couple of rose bushes growing in old paint buckets, and there's a plastic chair that **nobody else seems to use** except me.

What I do there is very simple. Most evenings I take a cup of tea up just before sunset and sit there for half an hour or so. Sometimes I water the plants, sometimes I call a friend, and sometimes I **just sit and watch** the kites that children fly from the other roofs. In winter, a few neighbours put up a badminton net, and we **play until it gets too dark** to see the shuttle.

I think it helps me relax because it's **one of the few places** in Dhaka where you can **get away from the noise**, at least a little. Down on the street it's all horns and traffic, but up there you mostly hear birds and the call to prayer. I've **got into the habit** of going up whenever I'm stressed, and **by the time I come down**, I can usually think clearly again.
notes: 'across a sea of rooftops' is a vivid image that a band 6 speaker would describe as 'many buildings'.
'has turned one corner of it into a little garden' uses the present perfect with turn ... into.
'one of the few places where you can get away from the noise' combines a superlative-style phrase with a relative clause.
'by the time I come down' is a time clause that adds grammatical variety.

blocks.q: Do you think people in cities find it harder to relax?
x: Yes, I'd say so. In a city like Dhaka you're **constantly surrounded by** noise and crowds, so your mind **never really switches off**. People in villages have more open space and a slower pace of life. That said, a lot of city people **have found their own ways** to cope, like rooftop gardens.
notes: 'never really switches off' is a natural phrasal verb about the mind.
'a slower pace of life' is a standard collocation.
'That said' adds a balanced second point.

x: It is a very peaceful place.
It's one of the few places where you can get away from the noise.
I go there many times.
I go up there whenever I get the chance.
I don't do anything special.
I just sit and watch the world go by.
It makes me calm.
It helps me unwind.
I go there when I am stressed. It is my habit.
I've got into the habit of going up there whenever I'm stressed.

blocks.x: Sounds and smells are an easy way to add detail to a place talk: 'all horns and traffic', 'the smell of wet soil', 'the call to prayer'.

Describe a city you have visited.
You should say:
- which city it was
- when and why you went there
- what you did there
and explain how you felt about this city.

x: I'd like to talk about Kolkata, which I visited with my father about two years ago. The main reason for the trip was a medical check-up. My father **had been having problems** with his back for a while, and a relative recommended a specialist there. We **ended up staying** for about ten days, and since his appointments only took a few hours, we had plenty of time to explore.

The thing I enjoyed most was walking around the old parts of the city. We spent a whole afternoon on College Street, which is **lined with** tiny bookshops, some of them no bigger than a cupboard. I **picked up** a second-hand copy of a Bangla novel I'd been looking for for years, and it cost less than a cup of coffee in Dhaka. We also rode one of the old trams, which **move at a snail's pace** but give you a great view of the street.

The food was another highlight. On our last evening we had biryani at an old restaurant, and I have to admit it was **on a par with** anything in Old Dhaka, although my friends will never forgive me for saying so.

I felt surprisingly **at home** there. People speak the same language, of course, so it never felt completely foreign, but there were **enough differences to keep it interesting**. The pace of life seemed slower than in Dhaka, and the traffic, **believe it or not**, felt more organised. **If I get the chance**, I'd like to go back on my own and spend more time in the bookshops.
notes: 'had been having problems' (past perfect continuous) explains the background to the trip.
'lined with', 'picked up' and 'move at a snail's pace' are natural, everyday phrases for describing a city.
'on a par with' is a less common expression for equal quality.
'believe it or not' adds a personal, spoken tone without sounding memorised.

blocks.q: Would you prefer to live in a big city or a small town?
x: For now, a big city, because that's **where the opportunities are**, especially for jobs in tech. In the long run, though, I can see myself **settling down** somewhere smaller. The idea of a short commute and **a bit of green space** sounds very appealing after years of Dhaka traffic.
notes: 'For now ... In the long run' contrasts the present and the future clearly.
'settling down' is a common phrasal verb for starting a stable life.
The answer gives a preference and a reason for each choice.

x: The street has many bookshops.
The street is lined with tiny bookshops.
The tram is very slow.
The trams move at a snail's pace.
The biryani was same as Dhaka.
The biryani was on a par with anything in Old Dhaka.
I felt comfortable there.
I felt surprisingly at home there.
I bought an old book.
I picked up a second-hand copy of a novel.

blocks.x: If the reason for a trip was ordinary, such as a medical visit, say so. Real reasons sound natural, and you can still talk about what you enjoyed.

Describe a building you find interesting.
You should say:
- where it is
- what it looks like
- what it is used for
and explain why you find this building interesting.

x: The building I find most interesting is the National Parliament House in Dhaka, in the Sher-e-Bangla Nagar area. Most people in Bangladesh have seen it on TV, but I think you only **really appreciate it** when you stand in front of it.

From a distance it looks like a huge grey fortress. It's made almost entirely of concrete, and the walls **are cut through with** enormous circles, triangles and rectangles instead of normal windows. The whole building **is surrounded by** an artificial lake, so on a calm day you can see its reflection in the water, which looks really **striking**, especially in the late afternoon.

It's where the parliament meets, so ordinary people can't just walk in. I've only been inside the grounds once, on a university trip, but plenty of people go jogging or walking on the roads nearby every morning, and families come at the weekend to sit on the grass and take photos.

What I find interesting is that it **doesn't look like** any other government building I've seen. It was designed by a famous American architect, and **it took about twenty years** to build, partly because of the war. He actually died before it **was completed**. Somehow, a building made of plain concrete **manages to feel** calm rather than cold. The shapes let in light without letting in too much heat, which **makes a lot of sense** in our climate. I'm not an architecture student, but **every time I pass it**, I notice something new.
notes: 'are cut through with' and 'is surrounded by' are passive forms used for description, which is exactly where the passive is natural.
'striking' is a precise adjective for a building that catches the eye.
'He actually died before it was completed' combines past simple and a passive in one sentence.
'manages to feel calm rather than cold' expresses contrast without relying on 'but'.

blocks.q: Should old buildings be protected or replaced with new ones?
x: I think the important ones should **definitely be preserved**. Old Dhaka has some beautiful buildings that are **falling apart** because nobody looks after them, which is a real shame. Of course, not every old building is worth saving. **If something is unsafe**, it may be better to replace it.
notes: 'should definitely be preserved' is a passive with a modal.
'falling apart' is a natural phrasal verb for a building in poor condition.
The answer gives a view and then a sensible exception.

x: It is a very big and grey building.
It looks like a huge grey fortress.
It has many big holes in the walls.
The walls are cut through with enormous geometric shapes.
There is water around it.
It's surrounded by an artificial lake.
It looks very nice.
It looks really striking, especially in the late afternoon.
The design is good for hot weather.
The design makes a lot of sense in our climate.

blocks.x: When you describe how something looks, use the passive: 'it is made of', 'it is surrounded by', 'it was designed by'. It is natural, accurate and easy to plan.

Describe a useful object or gadget you own.
You should say:
- what it is
- when and how you got it
- how you use it
and explain why it is so useful to you.

x: The object I'm going to talk about isn't very exciting, but it's probably the most useful thing I own: a small rechargeable fan. It's about the size of a dinner plate, it's bright blue, and it **clips onto** the edge of a desk or the frame of a bed.

I got it last summer, during a period when we **were having power cuts** several times a day in Savar. The heat was unbearable, especially at night, and I **hadn't slept properly** for nearly a week. One of my roommates had a similar fan, and after borrowing it a few times, I **gave in** and bought my own from an electronics shop in the local market. It cost about two thousand taka, which felt like a lot at the time.

I use it almost every day from April to October. When the electricity is on, I keep it **plugged in** so the battery stays full, and as soon as the power goes off, I switch it on. The battery **lasts for around six hours** on the lowest setting, which is usually enough to get me through a power cut. It's also handy in the library, because the ceiling fans there **barely make a difference**.

It's useful because it **solves a very real problem**. In our climate, heat affects your sleep, your concentration and even your mood. Before I had the fan, I'd **lie awake** half the night and then struggle through morning classes. Now I can actually rest. **Looking back**, it's probably the best two thousand taka I've ever spent.
notes: 'were having power cuts' (past continuous) sets up the background situation.
'hadn't slept properly for nearly a week' uses the past perfect with a time phrase accurately.
Phrasal verbs such as 'clips onto', 'gave in' and 'plugged in' make the description sound natural.
'barely make a difference' and 'solves a very real problem' are useful collocations for any object card.

blocks.q: Do you think people depend too much on gadgets these days?
x: In some ways, yes. Most of us **would be lost without** our phones, and that's a bit worrying. But many gadgets genuinely **make life easier**, like my fan. I think the problem isn't the gadgets themselves. It's when we use them **out of habit** rather than because we actually need them.
notes: 'would be lost without' is an idiomatic way to show dependence.
'It's when we ...' focuses the answer on the real issue.
'out of habit rather than because ...' contrasts two reasons in one sentence.

x: The weather was very hot.
The heat was unbearable.
I did not sleep well many days.
I hadn't slept properly for nearly a week.
Finally I bought one.
In the end, I gave in and bought my own.
The battery runs six hours.
The battery lasts for around six hours.
The library fans are useless.
The ceiling fans in the library barely make a difference.

blocks.x: A simple object with a clear problem behind it is easier to talk about for two minutes than an expensive gadget you can only describe in technical terms.

Describe a gift you gave to someone.
You should say:
- what the gift was
- who you gave it to
- why you chose this gift
and explain how the person felt about it.

x: I'd like to talk about a smartphone I gave my mother about a year and a half ago. It wasn't an expensive one, just a mid-range Android phone, but it **meant a lot** to both of us, because I bought it with the money from my first tutoring job.

At that time, I'd been tutoring a class eight student for about four months, and I'd **managed to save up** most of what I earned. My mother was still using an old button phone that she'd had for nearly ten years. The main reason I chose a smartphone was my older sister, who'd moved to Canada for her master's the year before. My mother **missed her terribly**, and the only way she could see her was by borrowing my phone for video calls.

I gave it to her on her birthday. At first she **wasn't very keen**. She said it was a waste of money and that she'd never learn to use it. So I spent the whole evening **showing her the basics**: how to unlock it, how to open WhatsApp and how to answer a video call. I even **stuck little paper labels** on the screen protector so she'd remember which app was which.

The real moment came the next morning, when she called my sister **all by herself** for the first time. I could hear her laughing from the other room. These days she uses it **far more than I expected**. She watches cooking videos, sends me voice messages and **keeps up with** all our relatives. **If I'd known** how happy it would make her, I'd have bought it much sooner.
notes: 'I'd been tutoring ... and I'd managed to save up' uses two past perfect forms to explain the background.
'missed her terribly' and 'wasn't very keen' are natural ways to express strong and weak feelings.
'so she'd remember which app was which' is a purpose clause with an embedded question.
'If I'd known how happy it would make her, I'd have bought it' is an accurate third conditional.

blocks.q: Do you prefer giving gifts or receiving them?
x: Giving, I think, although it's **more stressful**. When you receive something, you just have to say thank you. When you give something, you have to **put real thought into** what the person needs. But seeing my mother's reaction **made it all worthwhile**, so I'd choose giving any day.
notes: 'put real thought into' is a natural collocation.
'made it all worthwhile' expresses a reward after effort.
The answer contrasts giving and receiving in two parallel sentences.

x: It was not expensive but it was important.
It wasn't expensive, but it meant a lot to both of us.
I saved money from my job.
I managed to save up most of what I earned.
She did not like it at first.
At first she wasn't very keen on it.
I taught her how to use it.
I spent the evening showing her the basics.
She uses it a lot.
She uses it far more than I expected.

blocks.x: The 'how the person felt' line is the easiest place to add a story. Describe the moment they first used or opened the gift.

pages.h: A photograph that is special to you

blocks.x:
Describe a photograph that is special to you.
You should say:
- what the photograph shows
- when and where it was taken
- who took it
and explain why this photograph is special to you.

x: The photograph that's most special to me is an old printed one that sits in a frame on my desk in the hall. It shows me at about six years old, sitting on my grandfather's shoulders at a Pohela Boishakh fair in our village. I'm wearing a red and white panjabi that's **far too big for me**, and I'm holding a clay horse that he'd just bought me.

It was taken by my uncle, who'd **just got hold of** a film camera and was photographing absolutely everything that day. The colours have **faded quite a bit**, and there's a crease in one corner, because my mother **kept it in her purse** for years. In the background **you can just make out** the fair: stalls selling sweets, a small Ferris wheel and crowds of people in red and white.

It's special because my grandfather passed away when I was nine, and this is one of the very few photos of the two of us together. I don't remember that particular day very clearly, but whenever I look at the picture, **it brings back** other memories of him, like the way he hummed old songs and how he **used to slip me** a few taka when my parents weren't looking.

It also reminds me of a time when life **felt much simpler**. Now everyone takes hundreds of photos on their phones, and **most of them are never looked at** again. This one is different, because it's the only copy. I've scanned it so it won't be lost, but I still prefer the paper version. **If there were ever a fire**, it's the first thing I'd grab.
notes: 'It was taken by my uncle' and 'most of them are never looked at' are passives used naturally.
'you can just make out' is a precise phrasal verb for seeing something with difficulty.
'used to slip me a few taka' describes a past habit with a vivid, informal verb.
'If there were ever a fire, it's the first thing I'd grab' is a second conditional using 'were', which sounds polished.

blocks.q: Do you think printed photos will disappear in the future?
x: Not completely, I don't think. They'll probably **become more of a luxury**, something people print only for special occasions like weddings. Digital photos are convenient, but they're **easy to lose** when a phone breaks. I think many people will **keep printing their favourite ones**, just to have something they can hold.
notes: 'become more of a luxury' is a natural comparative phrase.
'will probably' expresses a careful prediction.
The answer gives both sides before a final view.

x: The colours are not bright now.
The colours have faded quite a bit.
You can see the fair a little bit.
In the background you can just make out the fair.
When I see it, I remember him.
Whenever I look at it, it brings back memories of him.
He gave me money secretly.
He used to slip me a few taka when my parents weren't looking.
People do not see their photos again.
Most photos are never looked at again.

blocks.x: Describe a photo from the foreground to the background: who is in front, what they are wearing and holding, then what you can see behind them.

title: Sample talks: events and experiences
bn: Seven model talks about things that happened to you and things you did
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to tell a story about an event or experience using a mix of past tenses and natural, idiomatic language.

blocks.x:
Describe a time when you helped someone.
You should say:
- who you helped
- what the situation was
- how you helped this person
and explain how you felt about helping this person.

x: I'd like to talk about a time I helped an elderly woman at Gabtoli bus terminal in Dhaka. It was about six months ago, just before Eid, and I was on my way home to visit my family.

The terminal **was absolutely packed**, as it always is before a holiday. While I was waiting for my bus, I noticed an old woman sitting on her bag near the ticket counters, looking very confused. She **must have been** in her seventies. At first I walked past, but something **made me turn back**, and when I asked if she was all right, she told me she was going to Rajshahi, where her daughter lived. The problem was that her son, who **was supposed to** put her on the bus, had been called away for work, and she couldn't read the names on the counters.

So I took her ticket, which luckily she **hadn't lost**, and went from counter to counter until I found the right company. Her bus wasn't leaving for another hour, so I bought her some tea and biscuits and we chatted for a while. I also called her daughter on my phone so she wouldn't worry. When the bus finally arrived, I carried her bag on and **made sure she had** a seat near the front.

I felt **genuinely good** about it afterwards, but also a bit guilty, because I'd **nearly ignored her**. It made me realise how easily people **slip through the cracks** in a busy place like that. Since then, I've tried to **pay more attention** to the people around me, especially older people travelling alone.
notes: 'She must have been in her seventies' is a modal of deduction about the past.
'who was supposed to put her on the bus' is a relative clause with 'be supposed to' for an expected action that did not happen.
'slip through the cracks' is an idiom used in exactly the right context.
The talk moves from past continuous ('While I was waiting') to past simple to past perfect, so the order of events is always clear.

blocks.q: Do you think people help strangers less than they used to?
x: In big cities, probably yes. People are **in such a hurry** that they don't notice what's happening around them. There's also more fear of **getting involved**, because of scams. But I've seen plenty of kindness too, especially during floods, when complete strangers **come together** to help.
notes: 'in such a hurry that ...' is a such ... that result structure.
'getting involved' is a natural phrase for helping in a situation.
The answer accepts the idea but then gives a counter-example.

x: The bus station was very crowded.
The terminal was absolutely packed.
I think she was seventy years old.
She must have been in her seventies.
Her son had to put her on the bus.
Her son was supposed to put her on the bus.
I almost did not help her.
I nearly ignored her, to be honest.
Some people get no help from anyone.
Some people slip through the cracks.

blocks.x: Admitting a small weakness, such as nearly walking past, makes your story sound real. Examiners hear many talks where the speaker is a perfect hero.

Describe a celebration you enjoyed.
You should say:
- what the celebration was
- where and when it took place
- who was there
and explain why you enjoyed it.

x: The celebration I'd like to describe is my cousin Ruma's gaye holud, which is the turmeric ceremony that takes place a day or two before a wedding. It happened last December at my aunt's house in Chattogram.

The whole family **had been preparing for weeks**. The house was decorated with marigolds and fairy lights, and the rooftop **had been turned into** a stage, with yellow and orange cloth everywhere. Nearly a hundred people turned up, mostly relatives, but also Ruma's friends from university and a lot of neighbours, who I **suspect came mainly for the food**.

The ceremony started in the late afternoon. Ruma sat on the stage, and one by one, people went up to **put turmeric paste** on her face and feed her sweets. By the time everyone **had had their turn**, she was completely yellow. After that, things **got pretty lively**. My cousins and I had secretly practised a dance for nearly two weeks, and when we performed it, the whole crowd **burst out laughing**, partly because my younger brother forgot the steps and just **made it up as he went along**.

I enjoyed it so much because it was the first time in years that the whole extended family **was in one place**. Normally we only see each other in small groups at Eid. **We stayed up talking** on the rooftop until about three in the morning. It reminded me how much I **take my family for granted** when I'm busy at university.
notes: 'had been preparing for weeks' and 'had been turned into' show the past perfect continuous and the past perfect passive.
'By the time everyone had had their turn' uses 'had had' correctly, which many learners avoid.
'burst out laughing' and 'made it up as he went along' are natural idioms for a lively scene.
'take my family for granted' adds a personal reflection at the end.

blocks.q: Are traditional celebrations becoming less important to young people?
x: I don't think so, actually. If anything, young people in Bangladesh seem **more enthusiastic** about things like Pohela Boishakh than ever, partly because of social media. What's changed is the style. Weddings, for example, have **become far more elaborate**, with photographers and themed outfits, which **some older people aren't too happy about**.
notes: 'If anything' introduces a point that goes against the question.
'What's changed is the style' is a cleft sentence for focus.
'which some older people aren't too happy about' is a relative clause that refers to a whole idea.

x: The family prepared for a long time.
The family had been preparing for weeks.
The rooftop became a stage.
The rooftop had been turned into a stage.
After that it was very fun.
After that, things got pretty lively.
Everyone laughed suddenly.
The whole crowd burst out laughing.
He forgot the dance so he did anything.
He forgot the steps and just made it up as he went along.

blocks.x: If you use a local word such as 'gaye holud', explain it in one short phrase. It shows you can paraphrase, which is part of Lexical Resource.

Describe a time when you were late for something important.
You should say:
- what you were late for
- why you were late
- what happened as a result
and explain how you felt about being late.

x: I'm going to talk about a time I was late for an interview for a part-time job at a software company in Gulshan. This was in my second year at university, and I'd **been looking forward to it** for weeks, because the job would have given me real experience as well as some income.

The interview was at ten in the morning, so I left Savar at seven, thinking three hours would be **more than enough**. Unfortunately, that was the day of a big political rally, and several main roads **had been closed** without much warning. My bus **sat in a jam** near Gabtoli for nearly an hour. At about half past nine, I **gave up on** the bus and tried to find a CNG, but every driver wanted three times the normal fare. In the end, I booked a motorbike through an app, and we **weaved through the traffic** as fast as we could.

I arrived about twenty-five minutes late, **drenched in sweat**, with my shirt looking as if I'd slept in it. I apologised and explained what had happened. The interviewer was polite, but she said they'd **already moved on** to the next candidate. They gave me ten minutes at the end of the day, but the interview felt rushed, and I didn't get the job.

At the time I felt **absolutely terrible**, partly embarrassed and partly angry with myself. **I should have stayed** with a friend in Dhaka the night before, which is what I'd do now. It taught me to **always allow for** the worst possible traffic, because in Dhaka it usually happens.
notes: 'the job would have given me' expresses a result that did not happen.
'several main roads had been closed' is a past perfect passive explaining the cause.
'sat in a jam', 'weaved through the traffic' and 'drenched in sweat' are vivid, natural collocations.
'I should have stayed' is a modal of past regret, used accurately.

blocks.q: Is being on time important in your culture?
x: It depends on the situation. For exams, flights and job interviews, people **take it very seriously**. For social events, though, it's much more relaxed. If a wedding invitation says seven o'clock, **hardly anyone turns up** before eight. Traffic is partly to blame, but I think it's also **just the way things are** here.
notes: 'hardly anyone turns up' uses a negative adverb with a phrasal verb.
'is partly to blame' is a natural way to give a partial cause.
The answer gives two contrasting situations with a clear example.

x: I left early. I thought it was enough time.
I left at seven, thinking three hours would be more than enough.
The bus did not move for one hour.
My bus sat in a jam for nearly an hour.
I stopped waiting for the bus.
In the end, I gave up on the bus.
I was very sweaty.
I arrived drenched in sweat.
It was wrong that I did not stay in Dhaka.
I should have stayed with a friend in Dhaka the night before.

blocks.x: Stories with a bad ending are fine. The examiner scores your language, not whether the story was a success.

Describe a useful skill you learned.
You should say:
- what the skill is
- when and how you learned it
- how difficult it was to learn
and explain why you think this skill is useful.

x: The skill I'd like to talk about is cooking. It might sound like a basic thing, but until I moved into a university hall, I **genuinely couldn't make** anything more complicated than an omelette.

I learned mainly during my first year. The food in the hall dining room was cheap, but it was **pretty much the same** every day: thin dal, rice and a small piece of chicken. After a few months I **was sick of it**, so my roommate and I bought a small electric cooker and started experimenting. Most of what I know comes from YouTube videos and from my mother, who I'd video call while I was cooking so she could **tell me what I was doing wrong**.

It was harder than I'd expected. The first time I tried to make chicken curry, I burned the onions, added far too much chilli and **nearly set off** the fire alarm in the corridor. Getting the spices right was the hardest part, because my mother never measures anything. She just tells me to add a little, and I had to **work out** how much a little actually meant. It **took me a good few months** before I could cook something I'd happily serve to other people.

I think it's useful for a few reasons. The obvious one is money. Cooking for ourselves **works out much cheaper** than eating out every night. It's also healthier, because I can control how much oil goes in. But the main thing is independence. I'm planning to study abroad, and **knowing that I can feed myself** properly makes the idea **a lot less scary**.
notes: 'genuinely couldn't make anything more complicated than' is an emphatic comparative structure.
'was sick of it', 'nearly set off' and 'work out' are common informal phrases that suit spoken English.
'It was harder than I'd expected' compares with an earlier past expectation using the past perfect.
'knowing that I can feed myself ... makes the idea a lot less scary' uses an -ing clause as the subject.

blocks.q: Do you think schools should teach practical skills like cooking?
x: Yes, I really do. Schools in Bangladesh **focus heavily on exams**, and a lot of students **leave home without** knowing how to cook, manage money or fix simple things. Even a short weekly class would help. It doesn't have to **replace academic subjects**, just sit alongside them.
notes: 'focus heavily on' is a strong verb and adverb collocation.
'leave home without knowing' uses a preposition followed by -ing correctly.
'just sit alongside them' offers a balanced solution.

x: I could only make an omelette.
I genuinely couldn't make anything more complicated than an omelette.
The food was same every day.
The food was pretty much the same every day.
I did not like the hall food anymore.
After a few months, I was sick of it.
I had to understand how much is a little.
I had to work out how much a little actually meant.
Cooking is cheaper.
Cooking for ourselves works out much cheaper.

blocks.x: Funny mistakes make a skill story easy to tell. Describe one disaster in detail before you explain how you improved.

pages.h: A trip that did not go as planned

blocks.x:
Describe a trip that did not go as planned.
You should say:
- where you were going
- who you went with
- what went wrong
and explain how you felt about the trip in the end.

x: I'd like to talk about a trip to Saint Martin's Island that I planned with three classmates last November. We'd been talking about it for nearly a year, and we'd **saved up for months**, so we were really excited.

The plan was simple. We'd take an overnight bus from Dhaka to Teknaf, catch the morning ship to the island and spend two nights in a small resort we'd **booked in advance**. Everything went fine until we reached Teknaf. When we got to the jetty, we found out that all the ships **had been cancelled** because of a depression in the Bay of Bengal. Nobody could tell us when they'd **start running again**. Some people said one day, others said a week.

We **hung around** Teknaf for a day, hoping the weather would clear, but it only got worse. It **was bucketing down**, and the wind was so strong you could hardly stand up near the river. On top of that, the resort refused to give us our deposit back. In the end, we **cut our losses**, took a bus to Cox's Bazar and spent the remaining days there instead.

**Strangely enough**, I ended up enjoying it. Cox's Bazar was almost empty because of the weather, so we **had the beach to ourselves**, and the hotels were offering huge discounts. We ate fried fish at a tiny restaurant every night and played cards until late. **If everything had gone to plan**, I don't think we'd have laughed as much. We still **haven't made it to** Saint Martin's, but we've promised each other we'll try again next winter.
notes: 'We'd take ... catch ... and spend' uses 'would' for a plan seen from the past.
'had been cancelled' is a past perfect passive that explains the problem clearly.
'cut our losses', 'hung around' and 'had the beach to ourselves' are natural idiomatic phrases.
'If everything had gone to plan, I don't think we'd have laughed as much' is a third conditional with a negative opinion verb.

blocks.q: Do you prefer to plan trips carefully or be spontaneous?
x: I used to plan everything in detail, but after that trip I've **become a lot more flexible**. I still book the basics, like transport and somewhere to stay, but I **leave the rest open**. Some of the best moments **happen by accident**, and too much planning just makes you disappointed when things change.
notes: 'I used to ..., but I've become ...' contrasts a past habit with a present change.
'leave the rest open' is a natural expression for flexible plans.
The answer gives a clear preference with a reason.

x: The ships stopped because of bad weather.
All the ships had been cancelled because of the storm.
We waited in Teknaf doing nothing.
We hung around Teknaf for a day.
It rained very much.
It was bucketing down.
We stopped trying and went to Cox's Bazar.
In the end, we cut our losses and went to Cox's Bazar.
The beach was empty, only us.
We had the beach to ourselves.

blocks.x: A story where a problem turns into something good gives you a natural ending: say how you felt at the time and how you feel about it now.

pages.h: A decision that changed your life

blocks.x:
Describe an important decision you made that changed your life.
You should say:
- what the decision was
- when you made it
- how you made it
and explain how this decision changed your life.

x: The decision I'd like to talk about is choosing to study computer science instead of medicine. I made it about four years ago, just after my HSC exams, and it's **without a doubt** the biggest decision I've made so far.

For most of my school life, everyone **assumed I'd become a doctor**. My grades in biology were good, my parents had always wanted a doctor in the family, and I'd even **enrolled in** a medical admission coaching centre. The problem was that I **wasn't enjoying it at all**. I was memorising hundreds of facts every week, and I **dreaded every class**. Meanwhile, in my free time, I was teaching myself basic programming from online courses, and **I'd lose track of time** completely.

Making the decision wasn't easy. I spent about two weeks **weighing up the pros and cons**. I talked to a cousin who works as a software engineer, and I looked at the jobs I could get after each degree. The hardest part was telling my parents. My father **didn't say a word** for about a minute, which was worse than shouting. But after a long conversation, he agreed to let me try, **on the condition that** I took it seriously.

It changed my life in quite a few ways. I'm now studying something I **actually care about**, so I work much harder than I ever did at school. I've also become more confident, because I **stood up for** what I wanted. My father has **come round to it** completely now. He even asks me to fix his phone.
notes: 'everyone assumed I'd become a doctor' uses 'would' as future in the past.
'I'd lose track of time' uses 'would' for a repeated past habit, a structure band 6 speakers rarely use.
'weighing up the pros and cons' and 'on the condition that' are less common phrases used accurately.
'stood up for' and 'come round to it' are phrasal verbs that show idiomatic control.

blocks.q: Should parents make important decisions for their children?
x: Up to a certain age, yes, but not for things like careers or marriage. Parents usually **have their children's best interests at heart**, but they don't always know what their children are good at. I think the best approach is for parents to **give their advice** and then **step back**, even if it's hard for them.
notes: 'have their children's best interests at heart' is an idiomatic phrase used correctly.
'the best approach is for parents to ...' is a for + object + infinitive structure.
The answer gives a limit, a reason and a solution.

x: Everyone thought I will be a doctor.
Everyone assumed I'd become a doctor.
I did not like the coaching classes.
I dreaded every class.
I thought about good and bad points.
I spent two weeks weighing up the pros and cons.
He agreed but with one condition.
He agreed, on the condition that I took it seriously.
Now my father accepts it.
My father has come round to it completely.

blocks.x: For a decision card, the 'how you made it' prompt is where you show range: compare options, mention who you asked, and describe the moment you told someone.

pages.h: A time you used technology to solve a problem

blocks.x:
Describe a time when you used technology to solve a problem.
You should say:
- what the problem was
- what technology you used
- how you used it
and explain how you felt about the result.

x: I'd like to talk about the time I used a simple online spreadsheet to fix the meal system in our university hall.
