Our floor runs its own mess, which means about thirty students share the cost of cooking, and every month one person **takes on the role** of mess manager. Last spring, it was my turn.

The problem was that everything **was recorded by hand** in a notebook. Students had to tell the manager each day whether they'd be eating lunch and dinner, and at the end of the month, the manager **worked out** what everyone owed. In practice, people forgot to tell anyone, the notebook **went missing** twice, and there were constant arguments about money. The previous manager **had been accused of** overcharging people, which I definitely wanted to avoid.

So I set up a free online form and linked it to a shared spreadsheet. Every evening, each student filled in the form on their phone, which took about ten seconds, and the spreadsheet **automatically added up** the meals and the cost per person. I also made the sheet visible to everyone, so nobody could say the numbers were being hidden. A few people **complained at first**, mostly because they had to change their habits, but within a week almost everyone was using it.

I felt **really proud of the result**. The arguments **more or less stopped**, and I saved myself hours of calculations. **What surprised me most** was how simple the solution was. I didn't need to write any code or spend any money. Even now, **long after my turn ended**, the floor is still using the same system.
notes: 'was recorded by hand', 'had been accused of' and 'were being hidden' show three different passive forms.
'takes on the role', 'worked out' and 'went missing' are natural phrasal verbs and collocations.
'What surprised me most was how simple the solution was' is a cleft sentence with an embedded clause.
The talk explains the technology in plain words, which keeps it clear for a listener with no technical background.

blocks.q: Do you think older people find it hard to use new technology?
x: Some do, definitely, but I think it's often about confidence rather than ability. My mother, for example, was **terrified of breaking** her smartphone at first. Once someone **took the time to** show her the basics, she **picked it up quite quickly**. Younger people sometimes forget how much patience it takes to teach.
notes: 'about confidence rather than ability' contrasts two nouns neatly.
'terrified of breaking' uses adjective + preposition + -ing correctly.
'picked it up' is a natural phrasal verb for learning a skill.

x: Everything was written in a notebook.
Everything was recorded by hand in a notebook.
People said he took extra money.
He'd been accused of overcharging people.
The sheet calculates by itself.
The spreadsheet automatically added up the meals.
The fighting stopped mostly.
The arguments more or less stopped.
I was surprised the solution was simple.
What surprised me most was how simple the solution was.

blocks.x: You do not need advanced technology for this card. A simple app, a phone feature or an online form is enough, as long as the problem and the result are clear.

title: Part 3 strategy
bn: How to handle the discussion section with confidence
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to recognise each type of Part 3 question and give a clear, well-organised answer to it.

pages.h: What Part 3 is and how it is marked

blocks.x: Part 3 is the last part of the Speaking test and lasts four to five minutes. The examiner asks questions linked to the topic of your Part 2 talk, but the questions are more general. If you talked about a teacher in Part 2, Part 3 might ask about education systems, exams or the role of technology in schools.

The big shift is from your own life to **society in general**. In Part 1 you say 'I like rice'. In Part 3 you say 'People in Bangladesh tend to eat rice at almost every meal, partly because it is cheap and partly because of tradition'.

You are marked on the same four criteria as in the rest of the test, and they carry equal weight: Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and Pronunciation. Part 3 is where the examiner checks whether you can keep going on abstract topics, so it often decides between band 6 and band 7.

x: Band 7 vocabulary: you use words flexibly, including some less common and idiomatic items, you choose natural collocations, and you can paraphrase when you do not know a word. A few wrong choices are allowed.
Band 7 grammar: you use a range of complex structures with some flexibility, many of your sentences have no errors, and a few mistakes still appear.
Band 7 fluency: you can speak at length without obvious effort, and you use a variety of linking words, though you may sometimes hesitate or repeat yourself.

blocks.x: The examiner may stop you in the middle of an answer and ask a new question. This is normal in Part 3. It means time is limited, not that your answer was wrong.
Many candidates answer Part 3 questions in one sentence, as if they were Part 1 questions. 'Yes, I think so' is not an answer at this level. Always give at least a reason and an example.
Most Part 3 questions belong to one of seven types. If you can recognise the type in the first second, you already know how to start your answer and which phrases to use.

head: Question type
Typical question
Ready phrases to start
rows: Do you think children should wear school uniforms?
'I'd say ...', 'Personally, I think ...', 'On balance, I'm in favour of ...'
How is shopping different now from in the past?
'A generation ago, people used to ...', 'These days, by contrast, ...', 'The biggest change is ...'
Will people still read printed books in the future?
'I imagine ...', 'It's quite likely that ...', 'I doubt ... will ever ...'
Why are so many people moving to cities?
'The main reason is ...', 'This is partly because ...', 'As a result, ...'
What are the pros and cons of working from home?
'The obvious advantage is ...', 'On the downside, ...', 'The drawback is that ...'
'The most effective thing would be to ...', 'One option is to ...', 'In the long run, ...'
Some people say success is just luck. Do you agree?
'I partly agree, but ...', 'There's some truth in that, although ...', 'I'd put it slightly differently ...'

blocks.x: Listen for the key words: 'why' means causes, 'how has ... changed' means past and present, 'will' or 'in the future' means prediction, 'what can be done' means solutions.

blocks.q: Which type is this question? 'What effect has the internet had on family life?'
blocks.a: Causes and effects. Start with the main effect, explain it, then give an example.

blocks.q: Which type is this question? 'Do you think robots will look after old people one day?'
blocks.a: Predict the future. Start with 'I imagine ...' or 'I doubt ...' and give a reason.

pages.h: A simple shape for every answer

blocks.x: You do not need a new plan for every question. One shape works for almost all of them: give a direct answer, explain why, add an example, and if you have time, **consider the other side**. This keeps you organised and stops you from running out of things to say.

x: Answer: say your view in the first sentence. 'Yes, I think they should, at least the basics.'
Explain: give the main reason. 'The main reason is that ...'
Example: make it real with something from Bangladesh, your city, or people you know. 'In my hall, for example, ...'
Other side: show you can see a different view. 'That said, I can see why some people would disagree ...'

blocks.q: Do you think children should learn to cook at school?
x: Yes, I think they should, at least the basics. The main reason is that a lot of young people **leave home without** being able to make a simple meal, and they end up **living on instant noodles** and takeaway food. If schools taught a few practical skills, students **would be far better prepared** for life on their own. In my hall, for example, the students **who'd learnt to cook** at home spend much less and eat better. That said, I can see **why some parents would object**. Timetables are already packed, and they might argue that cooking is something families **should be responsible for**, not teachers.
notes: The answer follows the full shape: answer, reason, example from hall life, then the other side.
'would be far better prepared' is a second conditional with an intensifier, a clear sign of grammatical range.
'who'd learnt to cook' is a defining relative clause containing a past perfect.
'That said' moves smoothly to the opposite view, which helps coherence.
'living on instant noodles' is a natural, slightly informal collocation that suits spoken English.

x: Yes. Because it is useful.
Yes, I think they should, mainly because it's a useful life skill.
For example my friend.
In my hall, for example, a friend of mine ...
But some people say no.
That said, I can see why some people would disagree.

blocks.x: Do not memorise the four steps as fixed sentences. If every answer begins 'In my opinion' and ends 'On the other hand', the examiner will notice the pattern. Vary your openings and do not always use all four steps.

Opinion questions ask what you think. Evaluate-a-statement questions give you somebody else's view and ask you to react. In both cases, take a clear position early. A balanced answer is good, but an answer with no position at all sounds weak.

blocks.q: Is it important for people to have hobbies?
x: Yes, I'd say it's really important, mainly for **mental health**. Most adults spend their days at work or studying, and a hobby gives them **something to look forward to** that has nothing to do with deadlines. It also **helps people switch off**. My uncle, for example, took up gardening after he retired, and he says it **keeps him sane**. Having said that, I don't think hobbies **have to be** anything serious. Even something simple like watching cricket with friends **counts as a hobby**, as long as it's **genuinely relaxing** rather than another thing you feel obliged to do.
notes: 'something to look forward to' and 'switch off' are natural, idiomatic phrases about free time.
'keeps him sane' is an informal idiom used correctly about a real person.
'as long as' introduces a condition, and 'rather than' makes a contrast inside one sentence.
'Having said that' signals a limit to the main opinion.

blocks.q: Some people say that success is mainly a matter of luck. What do you think?
x: I **partly agree**, but I think luck is only one piece of it. Obviously, **where you're born** and the family you grow up in **make a huge difference**. A child in a well-off family in Dhaka has opportunities that a child in a remote village **simply doesn't have**. But I'd argue that **hard work and persistence** matter more in the long run. Luck might **open a door** for you, but if you're not prepared, you won't be able to **make the most of** it. So I'd put it this way: luck gives you the chance, and effort decides what you do with it.
notes: 'I partly agree' answers the statement directly and shows a careful position.
'where you're born' is a noun clause used as a subject, which is a less common structure.
'open a door' and 'make the most of' are idiomatic and used naturally.
The final sentence rephrases the idea instead of repeating the question, which is effective paraphrase.

head: To agree
To partly agree
To disagree
rows: 'I'm not sure I'd go along with that.'
'I don't think that's really the case.'

blocks.x: 'I am agree' is a very common error. 'Agree' is a verb, so say 'I agree' or 'I don't agree', never 'I am agree' or 'I am not agree'.

Comparison and prediction questions test your control of tenses. When you compare, move between the past ('used to', 'would', past simple) and the present ('these days', present simple or present perfect). When you predict, use a mix of 'will', 'might', 'is likely to' and future continuous.

blocks.q: How has the way people communicate changed compared to the past?
x: It's changed enormously. **A generation ago**, if you wanted to talk to a relative abroad, you'd have to **book an expensive phone call** or write a letter that **took weeks to arrive**. Now almost everyone has a smartphone, so we **stay in touch** through WhatsApp or Messenger, often several times a day. I think the biggest change is speed. **Messages are expected** to be answered almost instantly, which wasn't the case before. I'm not sure it's all positive, though. People **used to put more thought into** what they wrote, whereas now a lot of communication is quick and a bit **shallow**.
notes: 'A generation ago' sets the time frame clearly, and 'you'd have to' uses 'would' for past habits.
'Messages are expected to be answered' is a passive structure used naturally.
'used to put more thought into' contrasts past and present with 'whereas'.
'which wasn't the case before' is a relative clause that comments on the whole idea.

blocks.q: How do you think shopping will change in the future?
x: I **expect online shopping will keep growing**, especially for everyday things like groceries. In Dhaka, grocery apps have already **taken off**, and I imagine that within ten years most young people **will be ordering** food and household items from their phones. I also think **shops will have to reinvent themselves**. They **might become** places where you go for an experience, such as trying clothes on or getting advice, rather than just buying things. That said, I doubt traditional markets **will disappear altogether**. Bargaining in a bazaar is **part of the culture**, and older people in particular enjoy it.
notes: 'will be ordering' is the future continuous, used for an activity in progress at a future time.
'expect', 'imagine', 'might' and 'doubt' show different degrees of certainty about the future.
'reinvent themselves' and 'taken off' are less common but natural vocabulary for business change.
'disappear altogether' is a strong collocation, softened by 'I doubt'.

x: In the past people write letters.
In the past, people used to write letters.
Now people are using phone always.
These days, almost everyone relies on their phone.
In future online shopping will increase.
I imagine online shopping will keep growing.
Maybe shops will close.
Some shops might struggle to survive.

blocks.x: With 'How has ... changed?' questions, use the present perfect at least once: 'It has changed a lot', 'Prices have gone up'. Many band 6 speakers only use the past simple.

Cause and effect questions often start with 'why' or 'what effect'. Solution questions ask 'what can be done' or 'how can we'. For both, give one main idea and develop it well. Two clear points are better than five short ones.

blocks.q: Why are so many young people moving from villages to cities?
x: The main reason is jobs. There simply **aren't enough opportunities** in rural areas, especially for people with an education, so cities like Dhaka and Chattogram **act as a magnet**. Education is another factor. Most good universities are in big cities, and once students **have settled there**, very few go back. As for the effects, villages are **left with an ageing population**, and farms **are struggling to find workers**. Meanwhile, cities **become overcrowded**, and the pressure on housing and transport **gets worse every year**. I suppose the only real solution would be to **create decent jobs** outside the capital.
notes: 'act as a magnet' is a vivid but natural metaphor for attraction.
'once students have settled there' uses a time clause with the present perfect.
'As for the effects' and 'Meanwhile' organise the answer clearly.
'left with an ageing population' is a precise collocation for this topic.

blocks.q: What can governments do to reduce traffic congestion in big cities?
x: I think the most effective thing would be to **invest heavily in public transport**. The Dhaka Metro Rail is a good example. Since it opened, a lot of office workers **have switched from** buses and private cars, at least on that route. If the network **were extended** to more parts of the city, I'm sure the effect would be much bigger. Another option is to **discourage private car use**, for example by charging for parking in the city centre. That **wouldn't be popular**, of course, but it's worked in other countries. Long term, the government should also **move some offices and industries** out of the capital, so fewer people **need to travel** into the centre.
notes: 'If the network were extended' combines a second conditional with a passive.
'invest heavily in' and 'discourage private car use' are strong topic collocations.
'Since it opened' is followed correctly by the present perfect 'have switched'.
'Another option is' and 'Long term' move between solutions clearly.

head: Function
Phrases
rows: 'As a result, ...', 'This means that ...', 'This leads to ...'
'One thing that could help is ...', 'The most effective thing would be ...'

blocks.x: Avoid 'The reason is because ...'. Say 'The reason is that ...' or simply 'It's because ...'.

For advantages and disadvantages, give one or two of each and show the link between them. You do not need a long list. Then add a short judgement at the end, for example 'So I think a mix works best'.

blocks.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of working from home?
x: The obvious advantage is that you **save time on commuting**, which in a city like Dhaka **can easily be** two or three hours a day. People also have **more control over their schedule**, so they can fit work around family life. On the downside, it's **harder to draw a line** between work and home. A lot of people end up **working longer hours**, not shorter ones, because the laptop is always there. There's also the social side. You **miss out on** the casual conversations with colleagues, and for new employees, that's **often how they learn** the job. So I think a mix of office and home works best.
notes: 'The obvious advantage' and 'On the downside' structure the answer clearly.
'draw a line between work and home' is an idiomatic collocation.
'miss out on' is a natural phrasal verb.
The final sentence gives a short, clear judgement.

blocks.x: Part 3 asks about things nobody knows for certain, so **hedging language** is natural and expected. It makes you sound thoughtful, not unsure. It also lets you talk about people in general without making claims you cannot prove.

x: All young people are addicted to phones.
A lot of young people seem to spend far too long on their phones.
Old people don't like technology.
Older people tend to be a bit more cautious about new technology.
This will happen.
This is quite likely to happen, I'd say.
I don't know about this.
I can't be sure, but I'd guess that ...
I like online classes.
Many students find online classes more convenient.
Tend to: 'People tend to eat out more at weekends.'
Seem to: 'Young people seem to care more about the environment.'
Modals of speculation: 'It might be because ...', 'That could be one reason.', 'It must be hard for ...'
Softeners: 'I'd say', 'I suppose', 'to some extent', 'in a way'
General subjects: 'most people', 'a lot of families', 'people in my generation', 'in Bangladesh'

blocks.x: Do not keep talking only about yourself. 'I use Facebook every day' is a Part 1 answer. In Part 3, widen it: 'Most students I know use Facebook every day, and I think that's typical of young people in Bangladesh.'

pages.h: Unfamiliar questions and how long to speak

blocks.x: Sometimes you will get a question you have never thought about. This is not a knowledge test. The examiner only wants to hear your English. You are allowed to say you are not sure, as long as you then **give it a try**.

x: Buy a little time honestly: 'That's not something I've thought much about, but ...'
Connect it to something you know: your country, your city, people you know.
Give a cautious opinion with hedging: 'I suppose ...', 'I'd guess ...'
Give one reason or example and stop when you have made your point.

blocks.q: Do you think space exploration is a waste of money?
x: That's not something I've **given much thought to**, to be honest, but I'll try. On one hand, I can understand people who say it's a waste. Billions are spent on rockets while millions of people still **lack basic necessities** like clean water, so the priorities **seem a bit strange**. On the other hand, a lot of everyday technology, like satellite weather forecasts, **came out of space research**. In Bangladesh, we **rely on** those forecasts to prepare for cyclones, so in a way space programmes **have saved lives** here. So I suppose I'd say it isn't a waste, as long as it's **balanced against** more urgent needs.
notes: The speaker admits the question is unfamiliar but keeps going, which shows fluency.
'Billions are spent' and 'it's balanced against' are passive forms used naturally.
'lack basic necessities' and 'came out of space research' are precise phrases.
Linking a distant topic to cyclone forecasts in Bangladesh is a smart way to find something to say.

blocks.x: How long should each answer be? There is no fixed rule, but most strong Part 3 answers last somewhere around 30 seconds to a minute, which is roughly four to seven sentences. Shorter answers do not show enough language. Much longer ones can stop the examiner from asking the questions they need.
If you finish and the examiner says nothing, you can add one more sentence, such as an example or a short conclusion. Do not start a completely new idea.
Saying 'I don't know' and then stopping is the worst choice. Even 'I've never really thought about it, but my guess is ...' gives the examiner something to mark.

blocks.q: Make this answer more Part 3: 'I don't know. I never go to museums.'
blocks.a: Possible answer: 'I'm not really sure, because I don't go to museums much myself. But I'd guess young people find them a bit boring, mainly because they're used to getting information quickly online.'

title: Part 3 sample answers: education, work and technology
bn: Model discussion answers on study, jobs and the digital world
goal: In this chapter you will learn how band 7 and band 8 speakers answer Part 3 questions about education, careers and technology.

blocks.x: Education is one of the most common Part 3 topics. It often follows a Part 2 card about a teacher, a subject you studied or a skill you learnt. Notice how each answer moves from a direct opinion to a reason and then to a **concrete example**.

blocks.q: Why do some people say that learning should be lifelong?
x: I think it's because the world **changes so fast** now that what you learnt at school **won't be enough** for your whole life. Someone who **trained as an accountant** twenty years ago, for example, now has to use software that didn't even exist then. If they **refuse to keep learning**, they'll **fall behind** quite quickly. There's also a personal side to it. Learning a new skill, even something like cooking or a language, **keeps your mind active** as you get older. So I'd say lifelong learning is both **a practical necessity** and good for you.
notes: 'changes so fast ... that' is a so ... that structure showing result.
'Someone who trained as an accountant' is a defining relative clause.
'fall behind' and 'keeps your mind active' are natural collocations.
The first conditional 'If they refuse ..., they'll fall behind' is accurate.

blocks.q: Is it better to study alone or in a group?
x: I'd say **it depends on what you're studying**. For things that need a lot of memorising, like vocabulary or formulas, I find it's more efficient to work alone, because **there are fewer distractions**. But for subjects where you need to **discuss ideas** or solve problems, a group is usually better. When my friends and I were preparing for our final exams, we **took turns explaining** topics to each other, and I remember things much better when I've had to **put them into my own words**. The risk with groups is that they **turn into a chat** quite easily, so you need someone **to keep everyone on track**.
notes: 'it depends on what you're studying' uses a noun clause after a preposition.
'took turns explaining' and 'keep everyone on track' are idiomatic.
'subjects where you need to' is a relative clause with 'where'.
The answer compares both options before giving a judgement.

blocks.q: Do you think online learning will replace traditional classrooms?
x: I don't think it'll **replace them completely**, but it'll definitely **play a bigger role**. During the pandemic, my university **moved all its classes online** almost overnight, and to be honest, it worked better than I'd expected for lectures. But it was **pretty hopeless** for lab work and group projects. There's also the problem of access. Not every student in Bangladesh **has a reliable internet connection**, especially in rural areas, so a fully online system would **leave a lot of people behind**. I think the future is probably a **blended approach**, where theory is taught online and practical sessions happen on campus.
notes: 'better than I'd expected' uses the past perfect in a comparison.
'blended approach' is a less common, topic-specific term.
'would leave a lot of people behind' is a hypothetical with a phrasal verb.
'where theory is taught online' combines a relative clause with a passive.

blocks.q: Should university education be free?
x: In an ideal world, yes. Education **shouldn't depend on** how much money your family has, and a lot of talented students **are put off** by the cost. But realistically, I'm not sure every country **can afford it**. Somebody has to pay for teachers and buildings, so free education usually means **higher taxes**. In Bangladesh, public universities are already **heavily subsidised**, which I think is a good compromise. Instead of making everything free, governments could **offer more scholarships** to students from poorer backgrounds. That way, the money **goes to the people** who actually need it.
notes: 'In an ideal world' and 'realistically' contrast theory and practice.
'are put off by' is a passive phrasal verb used naturally.
'heavily subsidised' is a precise, less common collocation.
'which I think is a good compromise' is a relative clause commenting on a whole idea.

blocks.x: When a question asks 'Should ...?', you can start with 'In an ideal world, yes, but realistically ...'. It gives you a balanced answer straight away.
Questions about schools and teachers let you use your own school memories, but remember to widen them into general points about **the education system**.

blocks.q: What makes a good teacher?
x: For me, the most important thing is being able to **explain things clearly**. Plenty of teachers know their subject **inside out**, but they **can't get it across** to students. A good teacher also **notices when someone's struggling** and changes their approach. I had a maths teacher in Class Nine who **would stop the lesson** if even one student looked lost, and that's the only reason I **scraped a pass**. Patience matters too. Students learn at different speeds, and a teacher who **loses their temper** easily makes people too nervous to ask questions. So I'd say patience matters as much as knowledge.
notes: 'know their subject inside out' and 'get it across' are idiomatic.
'would stop the lesson' uses 'would' for a repeated past action.
'scraped a pass' is informal but natural and correct.
'too nervous to ask' is a too + adjective + infinitive structure.

blocks.q: Should schools focus more on practical skills or academic subjects?
x: I think there should be **a better balance** than there is now. In Bangladesh, the system is **very exam-oriented**, so students spend years memorising answers but leave school without knowing how to manage money or write a CV. **I'm not saying** academic subjects aren't important. Maths and science **form the foundation** for a lot of careers. But schools could easily **set aside** a few hours a week for things like basic finance, first aid or computer skills. Those are things **you'll need regardless of** what job you end up doing, and they'd **give students a head start** when they start working.
notes: 'exam-oriented' is a compound adjective typical of education topics.
'I'm not saying ... aren't important' is a natural way to accept the other side.
'set aside' and 'give students a head start' are idiomatic.
'regardless of what job you end up doing' combines a preposition with a noun clause.

blocks.q: Why do some parents send their children to private tutors?
x: Mostly because they're **worried about competition**. Getting into a good college or university **comes down to** exam results, so parents want their children **to have every advantage**. In Dhaka it's almost normal for a child to have two or three tutors after school. Some parents also feel that classes are **too big for teachers** to give individual attention, which is often true. I think tutoring **can be useful** when a child is weak in one subject. The problem is when it **becomes a habit**. Children end up **studying from morning till night** and **have no time left** for sport or just being kids.
notes: 'comes down to' is a useful phrasal verb meaning 'depends mainly on'.
'too big for teachers to give' is a less common too ... for ... to structure.
'Getting into a good college' uses a gerund phrase as the subject.
'end up studying' shows the result of a process.

blocks.x: Do not say 'take tuition from a teacher' or 'private tuition' only. Both 'have a private tutor' and 'go to coaching centres' are natural. 'Coaching centre' is understood in South Asia, but explain it briefly the first time.
Work questions often ask what people want from a job, how careers are changing, or the differences between types of employers. Use **contrast language** to compare options.

blocks.q: What do most people look for when choosing a job?
x: I'd say salary is still **the top priority** for most people, especially here, where living costs **have gone up so much**. But I think young people are starting to care about other things as well. A lot of my friends **would rather take** a slightly lower salary if the company offers **flexible hours** or good training. Job security matters too. Government jobs in Bangladesh are **hugely popular** for that reason, even though the pay isn't amazing. And then there's **work-life balance**. After seeing their parents **work long hours** for years, many people my age want a job that **leaves them some time** for family and friends.
notes: 'would rather take' shows preference correctly with a bare infinitive.
'where living costs have gone up so much' is a relative clause with the present perfect.
'even though the pay isn't amazing' is a concession clause.
'work-life balance' and 'flexible hours' are standard topic vocabulary.

blocks.q: Is it better to work for a big company or a small one?
x: Both have their advantages. A big company usually offers **a more stable income**, a proper training programme and **a clear career path**, which is attractive when you're just starting out. On the other hand, you can **feel like a small cog** in a huge machine. In a small company or a startup, you tend to **take on more responsibility** early on. I worked at a small tech startup for a few months, and I **ended up doing** everything from market research to product planning. It was stressful, but I **learnt far more** than I would have in a big firm. So I think it depends on **what stage of your career** you're at.
notes: 'feel like a small cog in a huge machine' is a well-known idiom used appropriately.
'than I would have in a big firm' is a shortened third conditional comparison.
'take on more responsibility' is a strong work collocation.
'everything from ... to ...' shows range in a natural way.

blocks.q: Why do some people change jobs frequently?
x: Often it's simply about money. In many industries, the quickest way **to get a pay rise** is to move to another company rather than wait for a promotion. Some people also get bored easily and **want a fresh challenge**. And sometimes it's the workplace itself. If people **feel undervalued** or have a difficult manager, they **won't stick around** for long. I don't think changing jobs is necessarily a bad thing, as long as people **gain new skills** each time. But if someone **has had five jobs** in three years, employers **might start to wonder** whether they're reliable.
notes: 'feel undervalued' and 'stick around' are natural workplace vocabulary.
'as long as' introduces a condition.
'has had five jobs' uses the present perfect for life experience.
'might start to wonder whether' is a modal with an embedded question.

blocks.q: Should people be allowed to retire whenever they want?
x: In principle, I think it **makes sense** to give people a choice. Some people are **worn out** by sixty, especially if they've done physical work, while others are **perfectly capable** of carrying on into their seventies. Forcing both groups to retire at the same age **doesn't seem fair**. The difficulty is money. If lots of people **retired early**, the government would have to pay more pensions while **collecting less tax**. So in practice, I think there needs to be a minimum age, with the option to **stay on longer** for those who want to.
notes: 'In principle' and 'in practice' frame a balanced view.
'worn out' and 'perfectly capable of carrying on' are natural descriptions.
'If lots of people retired early, the government would have to' is a correct second conditional.
'Forcing both groups to retire' uses a gerund as the subject.

blocks.x: Future questions test your **prediction language**. Mix 'will', 'might', 'is likely to', 'I'd imagine' and 'I doubt' so that you are not saying 'will' in every sentence.

blocks.q: What kinds of jobs do you think will be popular in the future?
x: I'd imagine anything connected to technology **will be in high demand**, especially data analysis and software development. Every company now **collects huge amounts of data**, and they need people who can **make sense of it**. I also think healthcare jobs will grow, because people **are living longer** and there'll be more elderly people to look after. Another area is renewable energy. If countries are serious about **cutting carbon emissions**, they'll need engineers and technicians to install solar panels and maintain them. Funnily enough, I think some practical jobs, like plumbers and electricians, **will still be needed**, because they're **hard to automate**.
notes: 'in high demand' and 'make sense of' are natural, high-value phrases.
'will still be needed' is a future passive.
'Funnily enough' introduces a surprising point in a natural spoken way.
'are living longer' uses the present continuous for a current trend.

blocks.q: Will people in the future need to change careers more often?
x: Probably, yes. **The pace of change** is so fast that a lot of jobs **may not exist** in twenty years, at least not in their current form. So people **will have to retrain**, maybe more than once. My father, for example, started as a typist, and **by the time he retired**, he'd moved into IT support, which nobody **could have predicted** when he started. I think the key will be **adaptability** rather than one fixed set of skills. Universities might **have to rethink** their degrees too, maybe offering shorter courses that people can take in the middle of their careers.
notes: 'by the time he retired, he'd moved' uses the past perfect correctly.
'could have predicted' is a past modal of possibility.
'adaptability' is a less common noun used precisely.
'may not exist' and 'might have to rethink' vary the prediction language.

blocks.q: What skills will young people need to succeed in the future job market?
x: I think the technical skills will **keep changing**, so the most useful thing is **the ability to learn quickly**. Beyond that, I'd say communication. Machines are getting better at routine tasks, but they **can't replace** someone who can **explain a problem clearly** to a client or **work well in a team**. English is important too, particularly for Bangladeshi graduates, because a lot of good jobs **involve working with** international clients. And I'd add basic financial skills. If more people are going to work freelance, they'll need **to manage their own income**, which isn't something most of us are taught.
notes: 'Beyond that' and 'And I'd add' link the points smoothly.
'involve working with' uses a verb followed by a gerund.
'which isn't something most of us are taught' combines a relative clause with a passive.
'work freelance' is natural, current vocabulary.

x: In future, IT jobs will be more.
I'd imagine IT jobs will be in high demand.
Many jobs will finish.
A lot of jobs may disappear, or at least change a lot.
People must learn new things always.
People will have to keep retraining throughout their careers.

blocks.x: Technology questions are easy to answer with examples from Bangladesh: mobile banking, ride-sharing apps, online classes and load-shedding. Use these to make your answers **sound real**.

blocks.q: How has technology changed the way people live?
x: It's changed **almost every part of daily life**. Even ten years ago, paying a bill meant **queuing at a bank**. Now people in Bangladesh just use bKash or Nagad and it **takes a few seconds**. The same goes for shopping, booking tickets and even getting a ride across town, since ride-sharing apps **have become so common**. I think the biggest benefit is convenience. The downside is that we've **become very dependent on** our phones. If mine **runs out of battery**, I honestly feel a bit lost, **which says a lot about** how much things have changed.
notes: 'paying a bill meant queuing at a bank' uses gerunds as subject and object.
'The same goes for' is a natural spoken linking phrase.
'become very dependent on' is a precise collocation.
'which says a lot about' comments on the whole previous idea.

blocks.q: Do you think people rely too much on technology?
x: In some ways, yes. I've noticed that I **can't remember phone numbers** anymore, not even my mother's, because they're all saved in my phone. And a lot of people **can't find their way** around without Google Maps. If the internet **went down** for a day, I think most of us **would struggle** to do our jobs. But I'm not sure relying on technology is always bad. We rely on electricity and cars too, and nobody **complains about** that. I think the problem is **when we stop thinking for ourselves**, for example when students **copy answers** from the internet without understanding them.
notes: 'If the internet went down, most of us would struggle' is a second conditional.
'find their way around' and 'went down' are natural phrasal expressions.
'when we stop thinking for ourselves' is a noun clause after 'is'.
The speaker accepts the idea partly and then challenges it, which shows balance.

blocks.q: Are there any disadvantages to smart home devices?
x: The main one, I think, is privacy. Devices like smart speakers **are constantly listening** for commands, and a lot of people **aren't really aware of** what data is being collected or who **has access to it**. There's also the cost. They're still quite expensive, so in a country like Bangladesh, only a small number of wealthy households can afford them. And they **depend on a stable connection**. If the power **cuts out**, which happens fairly often here during summer, the whole system **becomes useless**. So for now, I'd say they're **more of a luxury** than a necessity.
notes: 'what data is being collected' is an embedded question with a continuous passive.
'cuts out' is a natural phrasal verb for power failures.
'more of a luxury than a necessity' is a less common comparative pattern.
'which happens fairly often here' is a non-defining relative clause.

blocks.q: Do older people find it difficult to use new technology?
x: Many do, but I think it's more about confidence than ability. My grandmother, for instance, was **convinced she'd break** the smartphone we gave her, so she **hardly touched it** at first. Once my cousin **sat down with her** and showed her how to video call, she **picked it up** surprisingly quickly. Now she **calls us every evening**. The problem is that a lot of apps **aren't designed with** older users in mind. The text is tiny, and the menus **keep changing** with every update. If companies **made things simpler**, I'm sure more elderly people would use them.
notes: 'more about confidence than ability' is a clear, thoughtful contrast.
'convinced she'd break' uses reported thought with 'would'.
'picked it up' means 'learnt it' and is very natural.
'aren't designed with older users in mind' is a passive with an idiomatic phrase.

blocks.x: These questions often ask about social media, screen time and online safety. Avoid extreme claims like 'social media is destroying young people'. **Hedged, balanced answers** score better.

blocks.q: How does social media affect young people?
x: There are positive and negative effects, I'd say. On the positive side, it lets young people **keep in touch with friends**, find information and even **start small businesses**. A lot of students in Bangladesh sell clothes or food through Facebook pages. But the negative side worries me more. Young people **constantly compare themselves** to others, and since everyone **only posts the highlights** of their lives, it's easy to **feel inadequate**. It's also **incredibly addictive**. I know people who spend **six or seven hours a day** scrolling, which must **affect their studies** and their sleep.
notes: 'compare themselves to others' and 'feel inadequate' are precise emotional vocabulary.
'since everyone only posts the highlights' is a reason clause with 'since'.
'which must affect their studies' uses a modal of deduction.
'On the positive side' and 'But the negative side worries me more' organise the answer.

blocks.q: Should parents limit the amount of time children spend online?
x: Yes, definitely for younger children. A seven-year-old **doesn't have the self-control** to put a tablet down after an hour, so parents need **to set clear limits**. But I think the approach should **change as children get older**. With teenagers, strict rules **tend to backfire**. They just find ways **to get around them**, like using a friend's phone. It's probably better for parents **to talk openly** about the risks and agree on some rules together. And honestly, parents need to **set a good example**. It's hard to tell a child to stay off their phone if you're **glued to yours** all evening.
notes: 'tend to backfire' and 'get around them' are idiomatic.
'glued to yours' is an informal but common idiom for heavy phone use.
'It's probably better for parents to talk' uses an it + adjective + for + infinitive pattern.
The answer changes its view by age group, which shows flexible thinking.

blocks.q: What are the dangers of children using the internet?
x: The most obvious danger is **contact with strangers**. Children often **don't realise** that the person they're chatting to online might not be who they say they are. Then there's **inappropriate content**. Even with filters, it's very easy for children **to come across** violent or adult material by accident. Cyberbullying is another serious problem. In the past, if a child **was bullied at school**, they could at least escape it at home, but now it **follows them everywhere** on their phones. I think schools should **teach online safety** from an early age, in the same way they teach road safety.
notes: 'might not be who they say they are' is a complex noun clause.
'come across' means find by chance and is used naturally.
'if a child was bullied at school' is a past passive in a conditional context.
'in the same way they teach road safety' is a clear comparison.

blocks.x: Do not say 'internet addicted'. Say 'addicted to the internet' or 'internet addiction'. Also, it is 'spend time on your phone', not 'spend time in your phone'.
AI is now a very common Part 3 topic. You do not need technical knowledge. Talk about jobs, students, fairness and **everyday convenience**.

blocks.q: Do you think artificial intelligence will take away people's jobs?
x: Some jobs, yes. I think anything **repetitive and predictable**, like data entry or basic customer service, **is likely to be automated** fairly soon. Some banks **have already replaced** a lot of call centre staff with chatbots. But I don't think it'll lead to **mass unemployment**. Historically, new technology **has destroyed some jobs** and created others. Nobody **worked as an app developer** thirty years ago. What worries me more is the transition. If you're forty-five and your job **disappears overnight**, it's not easy to retrain, so governments need to support workers through that change.
notes: 'is likely to be automated' combines a prediction phrase with a passive.
'What worries me more is' is a cleft sentence, a sign of grammatical range.
'mass unemployment' and 'repetitive and predictable' are precise collocations.
'Historically' and the app developer example support the main point well.

blocks.q: Should students be allowed to use AI tools for their assignments?
x: I think **banning them completely** would be unrealistic, because students **will use them anyway**. And in most jobs, people will be expected to use these tools, so it makes sense to learn how at university. But there should be clear rules. Using AI to check grammar or **brainstorm ideas is one thing**. Getting it to write the whole essay is basically cheating, and the student learns nothing. Some of my teachers now ask us to **explain our work** in a short viva, which I think is a clever solution, because you **can't fake understanding** when someone asks you questions **face to face**.
notes: 'banning them completely would be unrealistic' uses a gerund subject with 'would'.
'X is one thing. Y is ...' is a natural pattern for drawing a line between two ideas.
'can't fake understanding' and 'face to face' are natural spoken phrases.
'people will be expected to use' is a future passive.

blocks.q: What are the benefits of automation in everyday life?
x: The biggest benefit is that it **frees people from** boring and dangerous work. In factories, robots now **handle tasks** that used to cause a lot of injuries. In daily life, it's things like automatic bill payments or washing machines, which **save hours every week**. My mother says that before we got a washing machine, laundry **took up most of her Saturday**. Automation can also **reduce human error**. Machines don't get tired, so in something like medical testing, results **tend to be more accurate**. Of course, someone still has to **keep an eye on** the machines, so I don't think humans **will ever be completely replaced**.
notes: 'frees people from' and 'reduce human error' are strong collocations.
'tasks that used to cause' is a relative clause with 'used to'.
'keep an eye on' is a natural idiom.
'will ever be completely replaced' is a future passive with an adverb.

x: AI will take all jobs.
AI is likely to replace some jobs, but it'll create others.
Using AI for homework is not good.
Getting AI to write your whole essay is basically cheating.
Machines make less mistakes.
Machines make fewer mistakes, so results tend to be more accurate.

title: Part 3 sample answers: society, environment and culture
bn: Model discussion answers on cities, family, health, media and traditions
goal: In this chapter you will learn how strong candidates discuss social, environmental and cultural questions in Part 3.

blocks.x: City and village questions are a gift for Bangladeshi candidates, because the contrast between Dhaka and rural life is so clear. Use **comparative structures** and talk about trends, not only your own experience.

blocks.q: What are the main differences between life in the city and in the countryside?
x: The pace of life is probably **the biggest difference**. In Dhaka, everyone seems to be **in a hurry**, and you **spend half your day** stuck in traffic. In villages, life **moves much more slowly**, and people have more time for each other. Neighbours actually know each other's names, which is rare in a city apartment block. On the other hand, cities **offer far more opportunities**. The best hospitals, universities and jobs **are concentrated** in urban areas, so if you're ambitious, you almost **have no choice** but to move. Village life is calmer, but it **can feel quite limited** for young people.
notes: 'moves much more slowly' and 'offer far more opportunities' use modified comparatives.
'are concentrated in urban areas' is a passive with formal topic vocabulary.
'have no choice but to' is a fixed expression used correctly.
'which is rare in a city apartment block' is a non-defining relative clause.

blocks.q: Do you think more people will move to the countryside in the future?
x: I think **a small number might**, but it won't be a big trend, at least not in Bangladesh. Since the pandemic, some people **have realised** they can work from anywhere, and a few of my relatives **have moved back** to their home districts. But for most people, the jobs **are still in the cities**. For rural life to become attractive, villages **would need** much better internet, healthcare and schools. If the government **invested in** those things, I think many families **would happily leave** the city, because nobody actually enjoys the pollution and the traffic.
notes: 'a small number might' uses an elliptical modal answer, which sounds natural.
'Since the pandemic ... have realised' pairs 'since' with the present perfect.
'For rural life to become attractive' is a less common for + object + infinitive structure.
'If the government invested ..., many families would happily leave' is a second conditional.

blocks.q: What problems do big cities face?
x: In Dhaka, the first thing that comes to mind is **traffic congestion**. It's **not unusual** to spend two hours covering a few kilometres. Then there's **air pollution**, which **has got noticeably worse** over the last decade, mostly because of brick kilns, construction and old vehicles. Housing is another problem. Rents **have gone through the roof**, so a lot of low-income families **end up living in** slums with no proper sanitation. And during the monsoon, many roads **get flooded** because the drainage system **can't cope**. Most of these problems come from the same thing, really: too many people in too little space.
notes: 'have gone through the roof' is an idiom used naturally for rising prices.
'not unusual' is a litotes, a less common way of saying 'common'.
'get flooded' is a get-passive, typical of spoken English.
The final sentence links all the problems to one cause, which shows strong coherence.

blocks.x: 'Urban' and 'rural' are useful, but do not repeat them in every sentence. Vary with 'in the cities', 'in villages', 'outside the capital' and 'in the countryside'.

Bangladesh is often mentioned in discussions of climate change, so you have real examples to use: floods, cyclones, salt water in farmland and river pollution. Learn **the key collocations** for this topic.

blocks.q: What can individuals do to protect the environment?
x: Quite a lot, actually, even if each action seems small. The easiest thing is **cutting down on** plastic. In Bangladesh, polythene bags **were banned** years ago, but you still see them everywhere, so carrying a cloth bag **makes a real difference**. People can also save electricity by switching off fans and lights, which helps with **the load-shedding problem** too. Using public transport instead of a car is another option. That said, I don't think we should **put all the responsibility** on individuals. Big companies and governments **produce most of the pollution**, so they need to **take the lead**.
notes: 'cutting down on' is a three-part phrasal verb used naturally.
'were banned years ago' is a past passive.
'take the lead' and 'make a real difference' are idiomatic collocations.
'That said' introduces a sensible limit to the main argument.

blocks.q: How is climate change affecting your country?
x: Bangladesh is **one of the most vulnerable** countries in the world, mainly because so much of it is **low-lying**. In the coastal areas, rising sea levels **are pushing salt water** into farmland, so rice won't grow properly there anymore. We're also seeing **more extreme weather**. Cyclones seem to **be getting stronger**, and the floods during the monsoon **have become harder to predict**. A lot of families from the south **have been forced to move** to Dhaka after losing their land, which adds to the pressure on the city. So for us, climate change isn't a distant problem. It's **happening right now**.
notes: 'low-lying' and 'vulnerable' are precise, less common topic words.
'seem to be getting stronger' is a continuous infinitive after 'seem'.
'have been forced to move' is a present perfect passive.
'after losing their land' uses a gerund after a preposition.

blocks.q: Should governments make laws to protect the environment, or should it be left to individuals?
x: I think laws are **absolutely necessary**. If you leave it to individuals, most people **will do whatever is cheapest** or most convenient, and that's usually not the greenest option. Look at the rivers around Dhaka. Factories **have been dumping waste** into the Buriganga for decades, and that **would never have stopped** through goodwill alone. Only **strict regulations and fines** can change that kind of behaviour. But laws only work if they're **properly enforced**, which is often the weak point here. Ideally, I'd like to see tough laws combined with education, so people **understand why** the rules matter.
notes: 'have been dumping waste for decades' is the present perfect continuous.
'would never have stopped' is a third conditional result without an if-clause.
'properly enforced' is the natural collocation for laws.
'Only strict regulations and fines can change' places emphasis at the start of the sentence.

head: Collocation
Example
rows: Most people could easily cut down on plastic.
Cars are a major source of carbon emissions.
Rising sea levels are a threat to coastal areas.
Extreme weather is becoming more common.
The law exists, but it isn't enforced.

blocks.x: Family questions often ask how families have changed and how different generations get on. Compare the past and the present and use the present perfect for **ongoing change**.

blocks.q: How have families changed in your country over the last few decades?
x: The biggest change is that **joint families** are becoming less common, especially in cities. When my father was young, he lived with his grandparents, uncles and cousins all **under one roof**. Now most couples in Dhaka live in **nuclear families**, partly because flats are small and partly because people **move for work**. Families **have also got smaller**. My grandparents had seven children, but most couples now **stop at one or two**, mainly because raising children **has become so expensive**. I think family ties are still strong, though. People still **gather together** for Eid and weddings, even if they live far apart.
notes: 'joint families' and 'nuclear families' are accurate sociology vocabulary.
'under one roof' is a common idiom.
'partly because ... and partly because' balances two reasons.
'have also got smaller' and 'has become so expensive' use the present perfect for change.

blocks.q: Do you think young people should take care of their elderly parents?
x: Yes, I do, and in Bangladesh it's **more or less expected**. Most people feel that their parents **made huge sacrifices** for them, so looking after them in old age is **a way of giving something back**. Care homes are very rare here, and I think most families **would feel ashamed** to send a parent to one. That said, it's **getting harder** for young people. If both partners work full time, or if they live abroad, they can't always **provide daily care**. In those cases, I think it's fine to **hire some help**, as long as the children **stay closely involved**.
notes: 'more or less expected' is a natural hedge.
'a way of giving something back' is an idiomatic phrase.
'would feel ashamed to send' uses 'would' for a hypothetical reaction.
'as long as the children stay closely involved' adds a condition.

blocks.q: What can grandparents teach young people?
x: Quite a lot, I think. The obvious one is **life experience**. My grandfather **lived through** the Liberation War, and hearing his stories taught me more about our history than any textbook. Grandparents also **tend to be more patient** than parents, because they're not dealing with jobs and bills, so children often **open up to them** more easily. They **pass on** practical things as well, like traditional recipes or how to grow vegetables. Sadly, a lot of that knowledge **is being lost**, because young people are too busy with their phones to sit and listen. I think families should **make a point of** spending time together across generations.
notes: 'lived through the Liberation War' is a precise phrasal verb about history.
'is being lost' is a present continuous passive.
'too busy ... to sit and listen' is a too + adjective + infinitive structure.
'make a point of spending' is an idiomatic phrase followed by a gerund.

blocks.x: 'Elder people' is wrong in most contexts. Say 'elderly people', 'older people' or 'the elderly'. 'Elder' is used mainly for siblings, as in 'my elder brother'.
Health questions usually ask about diet, exercise, stress and who is responsible. Give **balanced answers** that mention both personal choice and the role of governments.

blocks.q: Why do many people find it difficult to live a healthy lifestyle?
x: I think the main reason is time. People **work long hours**, and by the time they get home, **the last thing they want** is to go for a run or cook a healthy meal. Fast food is **cheap and quick**, so it's the easy option. In Dhaka, there's also a practical problem. There aren't many **safe places to exercise**, and the air pollution **puts people off** walking outside. And to be honest, a lot of it is habit. In Bangladeshi culture, food **is heavily linked to** hospitality, so if you visit someone, you're **expected to eat** whatever's offered, which usually means rice and something fried.
notes: 'the last thing they want is' is a natural, emphatic phrase.
'puts people off walking' uses a phrasal verb followed by a gerund.
'is heavily linked to' and 'you're expected to eat' are passive structures.
The cultural example about hospitality makes the answer original.

blocks.q: Should the government be responsible for people's health?
x: I think **it's a shared responsibility**. The government should **provide affordable healthcare** and make sure people have **access to clean water** and safe food, because individuals **can't control** those things. It can also **discourage unhealthy habits**, for example by taxing cigarettes, which Bangladesh **has already done**. But in the end, the government can't **make people exercise** or stop them eating junk food. People have to **take responsibility** for their own choices. The best a government can do, I suppose, is make the healthy option the easy option.
notes: 'a shared responsibility' gives a clear, balanced position.
'make people exercise' uses the causative 'make' correctly.
'which Bangladesh has already done' is a relative clause with the present perfect.
'The best a government can do is ...' is a less common sentence pattern.

blocks.q: Do you think people today are healthier than in the past?
x: In some ways, definitely. People **live much longer** now, and diseases that **used to kill** thousands, like cholera, **are far less common**, thanks to vaccines and clean water. Child mortality in Bangladesh **has dropped dramatically** over the last thirty years. But in other ways, I think we're less healthy. The previous generation walked everywhere and did physical work, whereas now a lot of people **sit at a desk** all day. As a result, problems like diabetes and heart disease **are on the rise**, even among young people. So we're better at **treating illness**, but our lifestyles **are making us sick** in new ways.
notes: 'diseases that used to kill thousands' is a relative clause with 'used to'.
'has dropped dramatically' combines the present perfect with a strong adverb.
'are on the rise' is a natural phrase for increasing trends.
'whereas' contrasts past and present inside one sentence.

x: People eat much junk food.
A lot of people eat far too much junk food.
Government should give hospital.
The government should provide affordable healthcare.
Diabetes is increasing day by day.
Diabetes is on the rise, even among young people.

blocks.x: Media questions ask how people get news, how advertising works and whether the media should be controlled. These topics need **careful, hedged opinions**.

blocks.q: Do you think advertising has too much influence on people?
x: Yes, I'd say it does, especially on children and young people. Adverts **are designed to make you feel** that you need something, even when you don't. On social media, it's even more powerful, because the ads **are tailored to** your interests and they **don't always look like** ads. When an influencer recommends a skincare product, a lot of their followers **assume it's an honest opinion**, when in fact they've been paid. I think that's a bit dishonest. **Having said that**, advertising isn't all bad. It helps small businesses **reach customers**, and it's how a lot of free content **gets funded**.
notes: 'are tailored to your interests' is a passive with precise vocabulary.
'when in fact they've been paid' contrasts belief and reality.
'gets funded' is a natural get-passive.
'Having said that' introduces the other side clearly.

blocks.q: How has the way people get news changed?
x: It's changed completely. My father still reads a newspaper every morning, but I can't remember the last time I bought one. Most young people **get their news** from Facebook or YouTube, often **without actively looking for it**. The advantage is that news **spreads instantly**. The problem is that **false information spreads** just as fast. During floods or political events, you see rumours **being shared thousands of times** before anyone checks whether they're true. I think people need to be more careful and **check the source** before they believe something, or worse, **pass it on**.
notes: 'without actively looking for it' uses a gerund after a preposition.
'see rumours being shared' is a verb + object + passive participle pattern.
'just as fast' is a natural comparison.
'check the source' and 'pass it on' are useful phrases for this topic.

blocks.q: Should the government control what is shown in the media?
x: To some extent, yes. I think there should be rules to **protect children** from violent or adult content, and to stop things like **hate speech**. But beyond that, I'm **quite wary of** government control. If politicians **get to decide** what's shown on TV or online, they could easily **use that power** to hide criticism of themselves. A free press is important because it **holds powerful people to account**. So I'd say the government should **set basic standards**, but an independent body, rather than the government itself, should **be in charge of** enforcing them.
notes: 'quite wary of' is a less common, precise way to express doubt.
'holds powerful people to account' is a strong idiomatic collocation.
'If politicians get to decide ..., they could easily' is a first conditional with a modal.
'rather than the government itself' adds a contrast inside the sentence.

blocks.x: 'News' is uncountable and singular. Say 'The news is ...', not 'The news are ...', and 'a piece of news', not 'a news'.
Tourism questions ask about benefits, problems and why people travel. Bangladesh gives you strong examples: Cox's Bazar, the Sundarbans, Sylhet and **Saint Martin's Island**.

blocks.q: What are the benefits of tourism for a country?
x: The most obvious benefit is economic. Tourism **brings in foreign currency** and **creates jobs** for local people, not just in hotels but also for drivers, guides and people selling handicrafts. Cox's Bazar is a good example. The whole local economy **depends on visitors**. Tourism can also **put a country on the map**. A lot of people abroad only know Bangladesh from news about floods, so if more tourists came and saw the Sundarbans or the tea gardens in Sylhet, it **would change that image**. And it **encourages governments** to protect historical sites and natural areas, because they **become a source of income**.
notes: 'put a country on the map' is a natural idiom.
'brings in foreign currency' is a precise economic collocation.
'if more tourists came ..., it would change' is a second conditional.
'people selling handicrafts' is a reduced relative clause.

blocks.q: Can tourism cause problems for local people?
x: Yes, definitely. One problem is that prices **shoot up** in popular areas, which can **price local people out** of their own neighbourhoods. Another is the damage to the environment. On Saint Martin's Island, for example, the number of tourists **has grown so fast** that the coral and beaches **have been seriously damaged**, and there's rubbish everywhere. There can be cultural problems too. Some tourists **don't respect local customs**, like dressing modestly, which **causes tension** with residents. I think the answer is **sustainable tourism**, where the number of visitors is limited and some of the money **goes back into** the local community.
notes: 'price local people out' is a less common, idiomatic phrasal verb.
'has grown so fast that' combines the present perfect with a so ... that clause.
'have been seriously damaged' is a present perfect passive.
'sustainable tourism, where ...' is topic vocabulary followed by a relative clause.

blocks.q: Why do people like to travel abroad?
x: I think the main attraction is **experiencing something different**. When you travel abroad, you **see a different way of life**, try new food and meet people who think differently, and that **broadens your mind**. For a lot of Bangladeshis, it's also about status. Having photos from Thailand or Dubai on Facebook **says something** about you. Some people go abroad for practical reasons too, like medical treatment in India or shopping. Personally, I'd love to travel more, but **visa restrictions** make it **quite a hassle** for us. You often **have to go through** a lot of paperwork just to visit a neighbouring country.
notes: 'broadens your mind' is a common collocation about travel.
'Having photos ... says something about you' uses a gerund phrase as the subject.
'quite a hassle' is informal but natural.
'have to go through a lot of paperwork' is a natural phrasal verb.

blocks.x: Festivals give you a chance to use rich cultural vocabulary. Explain local words briefly, because the examiner may not know them. For example, say 'panta ilish, which is rice soaked in water served with **fried hilsa fish**'.

blocks.q: Why are traditional festivals important?
x: I think they **bring people together** in a way that ordinary life doesn't. During Pohela Boishakh, for example, people of all religions and backgrounds **celebrate the Bengali New Year** together, wearing red and white and eating panta ilish. It **reminds us of** what we have in common. Festivals also **keep traditions alive**. Children learn songs, recipes and customs that **would otherwise be forgotten**. And for many people, especially those who **live away from home**, festivals like Eid are **the one time of year** when the whole family **gets together**.
notes: 'in a way that ordinary life doesn't' is a less common comparison.
'would otherwise be forgotten' is a passive with 'otherwise', a sign of range.
'keep traditions alive' and 'bring people together' are strong collocations.
'the one time of year when' uses a relative clause with 'when'.

blocks.q: Are traditional festivals losing their meaning?
x: To some extent, yes. A lot of festivals **have become very commercialised**. During Eid, for example, there's huge pressure to buy new clothes and expensive gifts, and some people **seem to care more about** shopping than about the religious side. Social media **plays a part** too. People are often **more focused on taking photos** than actually enjoying the moment. But I don't think the meaning **has disappeared completely**. Families still **make an effort** to visit their villages for Eid, even though the journey is exhausting. That shows the festivals **still matter deeply** to people.
notes: 'commercialised' is a precise, less common word.
'more focused on taking photos than actually enjoying' is a comparison with gerunds.
'plays a part' and 'make an effort' are natural collocations.
'even though the journey is exhausting' is a concession clause.

blocks.q: Should children learn about traditional culture at school?
x: Yes, I think so, particularly in cities, where children **grow up surrounded by** Western films, music and games. If schools don't teach traditional culture, many children **might never come across it**. It doesn't have to be dry history lessons, though. Schools could **invite local artists**, teach folk songs or organise events for festivals. My school used to **hold a cultural programme** every year on Pohela Boishakh, and those are some of my **fondest memories**. I think learning about your own culture **gives you a sense of identity**, and it actually **makes you more open** to other cultures as well.
notes: 'grow up surrounded by' is a natural participle phrase.
'might never come across it' combines a modal with a phrasal verb.
'fondest memories' and 'a sense of identity' are strong collocations.
'It doesn't have to be dry history lessons' uses 'dry' with an idiomatic meaning.

blocks.x: If you mention a festival, add one short explanation and one detail: what people eat, wear or do. This gives you more to say and shows descriptive vocabulary.
Money questions ask about spending habits, saving and the future of cash. Mobile payments are a strong example from Bangladesh, and **peer pressure** is a useful phrase for spending.

blocks.q: Why do some people buy things they don't need?
x: I'd say it's partly advertising and partly emotion. A lot of shopping **has nothing to do with need**. People buy things when they're stressed or bored, because it **gives them a quick boost**. Online shopping **makes it even easier**. You can buy something with two clicks at midnight, and you don't really feel like you're **spending real money**. There's **peer pressure** as well. If all your friends have the latest phone, you **feel left out** without one. I'm **guilty of it myself**, to be honest. I've bought clothes in sales just because they were cheap, and then **never worn them**.
notes: 'has nothing to do with need' is a natural phrase.
'feel left out' and 'peer pressure' are common topic vocabulary.
'I'm guilty of it myself' is an idiomatic personal admission.
'I've bought ... and then never worn them' uses the present perfect for life experience.

blocks.q: Is it important for young people to learn how to manage money?
x: Yes, extremely. A lot of young people leave home without any idea of how to **make a budget**, and they **run out of money** halfway through the month. I've seen it happen to friends in my hall. They spend the first two weeks eating out and then **survive on rice and dal**. It's even more important now, because it's **so easy to borrow**. Buy-now-pay-later schemes and credit cards can **get people into debt** very quickly. If schools **taught basic money skills**, like saving and understanding interest, young people **would make far fewer mistakes**.
notes: 'run out of money' and 'get people into debt' are natural collocations.
'I've seen it happen' is a verb + object + bare infinitive pattern.
'If schools taught ..., young people would make far fewer mistakes' is a second conditional.
'Buy-now-pay-later schemes' is current, precise vocabulary.

blocks.q: Do you think cash will disappear in the future?
x: In some countries, it's **already happening**, but I don't think cash will disappear in Bangladesh any time soon. Mobile payments **have spread incredibly fast**, and even rickshaw pullers and street vendors **accept bKash** now. But a lot of older people and people in rural areas still prefer cash, partly because they **don't fully trust** digital systems. There's also the issue of **network problems**. If the connection goes down, you can't pay for anything. So I think we'll **move towards** a mostly cashless system, but cash will probably **stick around** as a backup for a long time.
notes: 'any time soon' is a natural phrase for the near future.
'have spread incredibly fast' combines the present perfect with a strong adverb.
'stick around' is an informal phrasal verb used appropriately.
'partly because they don't fully trust' gives a careful reason.

x: People buy unnecessary things.
A lot of people buy things they don't really need.
They have no money at month end.
They run out of money halfway through the month.
Cash will not finish soon.
I don't think cash will disappear any time soon.

title: Fluency, coherence and pronunciation
bn: Speaking smoothly, sounding clear, and getting ready for test day
goal: In this chapter you will learn how to speak more smoothly, pronounce English more clearly and prepare yourself for the day of the test.

blocks.x: Many candidates think fluency means speaking fast. It does not. Fluency means you can keep talking **without long, unnatural pauses**, and your ideas follow each other in a clear order. A calm, steady speaker often scores higher than a fast one.

Fluency and Coherence is one of the four criteria, worth a quarter of your mark. At band 7, you can speak at length without obvious effort, you link ideas with a range of connectives, and some hesitation or self-correction is fine. At band 6, you are willing to speak at length, but you sometimes lose coherence because of repetition, self-correction or hesitation.

x: Speed: how many words per minute. Not marked directly.
Fluency: how smoothly you keep going. Marked.
Coherence: how clearly your ideas connect. Marked.
Pausing to think before a main idea: natural and acceptable.
Pausing in the middle of a phrase to search for a word: this is what lowers your score.
I think... er... the... er... traffic is... very... er... bad.
I think the traffic is, well, pretty terrible, to be honest.
Because... because... because people are many.
Mainly because there are just too many people.
He go, sorry, he went, he goes there.
He went there, I mean he goes there every week.

blocks.x: Speaking very fast to sound fluent often makes pronunciation unclear and grammar sloppy. If the examiner cannot follow you, fast speech hurts two criteria at once. Slow down to a speed where you can control your words.
Self-correction is allowed. Fix a mistake once, quickly, and move on. Repeating the correction several times breaks your fluency more than the original error did.
Spoken linking is different from written linking. Essay words like 'consequently' and 'in conclusion' sound strange in conversation. Use **spoken connectives** instead.

head: Function
Written style (avoid in speaking)
Spoken style (use these)
rows: On top of that, Also, And another thing
But, Then again, Having said that, Mind you
For example, Take ... for example, Like ...
So basically, So I'd say, All in all
Well, I'd say the main thing is ..., First of all

blocks.q: Why do people enjoy watching sport?
x: Well, I think there are a few reasons. **First of all**, it's exciting because **you never know** what's going to happen. A cricket match **can turn around** in a single over. **On top of that**, sport gives people **a sense of belonging**. When Bangladesh plays, the whole country **gets behind the team**, and complete strangers start chatting about the score in tea stalls. **What I find interesting**, though, is that people enjoy watching even when their team loses. I suppose it's because they **share the experience** with others, and that matters more than the result.
notes: 'First of all' and 'On top of that' are spoken linkers, not essay linkers.
'What I find interesting, though, is' is a cleft sentence that signals a new angle.
'gets behind the team' and 'turn around' are idiomatic.
'I suppose it's because' gives a hedged reason to close the answer.

blocks.x: Overusing 'and then' or 'also' at the start of every sentence sounds like a list. Vary with 'On top of that', 'What's more' and 'Another thing is'.

blocks.q: Replace the essay linker with a spoken one: 'Consequently, many people moved to Dhaka.'
blocks.a: 'So a lot of people ended up moving to Dhaka.' or 'That's why so many people moved to Dhaka.'

blocks.x: Everyone needs time to think. The difference between band 6 and band 7 is what you do with that time. Instead of silence or 'er', use a short **thinking phrase** that sounds natural.

head: Situation
Phrases to buy time
rows: 'That's an interesting question.' 'Let me think about that for a second.'
You need a moment in the middle
'What's the word ...' 'It's a kind of ...' 'Something like ...'
'What I mean is ...' 'Or rather ...' 'Let me put it another way.'
'Let me give you an example.' 'Take ... for example.'

blocks.q: Do you think people read fewer books these days?
x: Hmm, that's an interesting question. **I'd say so**, yes, at least printed books. **The thing is**, people still read a lot, but **it's mostly on screens**: news, posts and messages. What they don't do so much is **sit down with** a long book for an hour. **Let me think**. Among my friends, maybe two or three read regularly, and even they **tend to use** e-readers. I think it's mainly because our **attention spans have got shorter**. It's hard to concentrate on a novel when your phone **keeps buzzing** every few minutes.
notes: 'Hmm, that's an interesting question' and 'Let me think' fill thinking time naturally.
'The thing is' introduces the main point in a spoken way.
'What they don't do so much is sit down with' is a cleft sentence.
'attention spans have got shorter' is a strong collocation with the present perfect.

x: Choose two thinking phrases from the table and learn them until they come out automatically.
Answer a Part 3 question while recording yourself.
Listen back and count every 'er' and every silence longer than two seconds.
Answer the same question again and replace each pause with a phrase.
Repeat with a new question every day for a week.

blocks.x: Do not use the same filler all the time. Saying 'actually' or 'basically' in every sentence becomes very noticeable and makes you sound less fluent, not more.
If you lose a word completely, describe it. 'The thing you use to open a bottle' is better than ten seconds of silence. Paraphrasing like this is a band 7 skill.

Pronunciation is a quarter of your score. It is not about sounding British or American. It is about being **easy to understand**. A clear Bangladeshi accent is completely fine. The features below matter far more than accent.

head: Feature
What it means
Example
rows: One syllable in a word is stronger and longer.
Content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives) are stressed; small words are weak.
I WENT to the MARket to BUY some FISH.
Group words into meaningful chunks with tiny pauses between them.
I grew up / in a small town / not far from Savar.
The voice falls at the end of statements and wh-questions, and rises on yes/no questions and unfinished lists.
Where do you LIVE? (falls) Do you live NEARby? (rises)
