Small words like 'to', 'for', 'and', 'of' are often reduced.
a cup of tea sounds like 'a cuppa tea'

blocks.x: Many Bangladeshi speakers give every syllable the same stress, so 'development' sounds flat and can be hard to catch. Mark the stress when you learn a new word and say it with that stress from the start.

blocks.q: Which syllable is stressed? 'environment', 'technology', 'comfortable'
blocks.a: enVIronment, techNOlogy, COMfortable (said as three syllables: COMF-ta-ble).

blocks.x: Use stress to show contrast. 'I don't hate it, I just don't LOVE it.' Stressing the contrasting word makes your meaning clearer and your speech more natural.

pages.h: Sounds that cause problems for Bangla speakers

blocks.x: Most sound problems come from the differences between Bangla and English sound systems. You do not need to fix all of them. Focus on the ones that **change meaning** or make words hard to recognise.

head: Problem
Common error
How to fix it
rows: 'very' sounds like 'bhery', 'wine' and 'vine' sound the same
For v, touch your top teeth to your bottom lip and buzz. For w, round your lips like 'oo' without touching your teeth.
Put your tongue lightly between your teeth and blow air. 'three', 'thanks', 'the', 'other'.
'see' and 'she' or 'same' and 'shame' sound the same
For s, smile slightly and keep your tongue behind your teeth. For sh, push your lips forward.
Say z as a buzzing s, with no tongue contact on the roof of your mouth.
Start directly with the s sound. Practise: 'ssss-chool'.
Finish the word. Practise pairs like 'pass / past', 'whole / hold'.
Short vowels are quick and relaxed. Long vowels are held longer with more tension.

head: Ending
Sound
Examples
rows: -ed after p, k, f, s, sh, ch
-s after s, z, sh, ch, j

blocks.x: Dropping -ed and -s endings is a pronunciation problem and a grammar problem at the same time. If you say 'Yesterday I walk' or 'She live in Dhaka', the examiner hears a grammar error. Make these endings clear.

blocks.q: Say these words aloud. How many syllables does each one have? 'walked', 'wanted', 'watches', 'played'
blocks.a: walked (1), wanted (2), watches (2), played (1).

blocks.x: Pick only two sounds from the table, the ones your friends or teacher say you struggle with most, and practise them for a week before moving on.

**Shadowing** means listening to a speaker and repeating their words at almost the same time, copying their rhythm, stress and intonation. It is one of the fastest ways to improve fluency and pronunciation. Use the model answers in this book: read them aloud, or record a good speaker reading them, then shadow.

x: Minutes 1 to 3: Choose one model answer. Read it silently and mark the stressed words and the chunk breaks with a slash.
Minutes 4 to 8: Listen to or read the answer aloud slowly, chunk by chunk, copying the stress you marked.
Minutes 9 to 13: Shadow the full answer at natural speed three times. Do not stop if you make a mistake.
Minutes 14 to 17: Close the book and answer the same question in your own words, using at least three bold phrases from the model.
Minutes 18 to 20: Record that last answer and listen once, noting one thing to improve tomorrow.

blocks.q: What are the advantages of living in a big city?
x: For me, / the biggest advantage / is **access to opportunities**. Most of the good universities, / hospitals and companies / **are based in** big cities, / so if you want to **build a career**, / that's where you need to be. Cities are also / more **convenient in everyday life**. You can get almost anything / **delivered to your door**, / and there's always somewhere to eat, / even late at night. And there's more variety. You **come across** people / from all over the country, / which **makes life more interesting**. Of course, / you **pay for all that** / in traffic and noise, / but for young people, / I think it's worth it.
notes: The slashes show chunk breaks for shadowing practice. Pause very briefly at each one.
'access to opportunities' and 'build a career' are strong collocations to stress clearly.
'delivered to your door' is a causative get + object + participle pattern.
'which makes life more interesting' is a non-defining relative clause read as one chunk.

blocks.x: Shadow the same model for three days in a row before switching. Repetition is what moves phrases from the page into your own speech.
Do not shadow by reading only with your eyes. Say every word out loud, at full volume. Quiet mumbling does not train your mouth.

You cannot hear your own mistakes while you speak. A phone recording shows you exactly what the examiner hears. Record one full practice test a week, and **score yourself honestly** against the four criteria.

head: Criterion
Ask yourself
Band 6 sign
Band 7 sign
rows: Did I keep going? Were my ideas in a clear order?
Long pauses, repeated words, 'and' or 'also' everywhere
A few pauses to think, varied spoken linkers, clear answer shape
Did I use topic words and natural collocations? Did I paraphrase?
Same simple words repeated, some unnatural combinations
Some less common words and idioms, good collocations, paraphrase when stuck
Did I use complex sentences? How many errors?
Mostly simple sentences, frequent tense errors
Conditionals, relative clauses, passives, many error-free sentences
Could a stranger understand every word?
Some words unclear, flat stress, missing endings
Clear words, correct word stress, natural chunking, endings heard

x: Record yourself answering one Part 1 set, one Part 2 cue card and three Part 3 questions.
Listen once without stopping, and give yourself a band for each criterion.
Listen again and write down every grammar error you hear.
Write down three words you repeated too often and find a replacement for each.
Do the same test again next week and compare the two recordings.

blocks.x: Transcribe one minute of your recording word by word. It is slow, but it shows your grammar mistakes and repeated words very clearly.
Do not score yourself only on the best part of the recording. The examiner gives one band for each criterion across the whole test, so weak moments count too.

pages.h: The last week and test day

blocks.x: In the final week, stop learning large amounts of new material. **Revise and practise** what you already know so it comes out smoothly under pressure.

head: Day
What to do
rows: Record a full practice test (about 14 minutes) and score it with the checklist.
Review your three most common grammar errors. Practise sentences that avoid them.
Practise five Part 2 cue cards with a one-minute timer for notes.
Answer ten Part 3 questions, two for each question type.
Shadow two model answers and revise your best topic phrases.
Do a second full recorded test and compare it with the first.
Light practice only: talk in English for 20 minutes, check your documents, sleep early.

head: Do
Don't
rows: Arrive early and bring the same ID you used to register.
Don't memorise whole answers. Examiners are trained to notice them.
Speak in English for 15 minutes before the test to warm up.
Don't give one-word answers in Part 1.
Ask the examiner to repeat a question if you didn't catch it.
Don't ask what a whole question means in Part 3; ask about one word instead.
Use all of the one-minute preparation time in Part 2.
Don't stop speaking in Part 2 before the examiner stops you.
Don't apologise repeatedly or say 'my English is bad'.
Don't try to use a fancy word you are not sure about.

blocks.x: If your mind goes blank, say so naturally: 'Sorry, my mind's gone blank for a second. Let me think.' This is real English and it gives you time.
Some candidates try to use every idiom they have learnt. Forced idioms sound unnatural and can lower your Lexical Resource score. Use an idiom only when it really fits the meaning.

Read this page the morning of your test. It sums up the habits that move a speaker from band 6 to band 7. You do not need to think about all of them while speaking. If you have practised them, **they will be there**.

x: Part 1: answer, then add a reason or detail. Two to four sentences.
Part 2: use the minute to write keywords, not sentences. Cover every point on the card and keep going for the full two minutes.
Part 3: answer directly, explain, give an example, and consider the other side when you can.
Talk about people in general in Part 3, not only about yourself.
Use hedging: 'I'd say', 'tend to', 'might', 'it's quite likely that'.
Use at least one conditional, one relative clause and one passive in Part 3.
Use the present perfect when you talk about change: 'It has changed', 'Prices have gone up'.
Use natural collocations, not single difficult words.
Paraphrase the question instead of repeating it.
Use spoken linkers, not essay linkers.
Fill thinking time with phrases, not long silences.
Finish your word endings: -ed, -s, final consonants.
Stress the important words and speak in chunks.

blocks.q: How important is it to speak English well in your country?
x: It's **becoming more and more important**. A few years ago, you could **get by** with just Bangla in most jobs, but now a lot of companies **work with international clients**, so good English **gives you a real advantage**. It also matters for higher education. Anyone who wants to study abroad, as many of my classmates do, **has to prove** their English level. That said, I think we **put too much emphasis** on grammar at school and not enough on speaking. Plenty of people can write a decent essay but **freeze up** when they have to talk to a foreigner. If schools **focused more on conversation**, that would change quickly.
notes: 'get by' and 'freeze up' are natural phrasal verbs.
'as many of my classmates do' is a short comparative clause, a sign of flexible grammar.
'put too much emphasis on' is a precise collocation.
'If schools focused more on conversation, that would change' is a second conditional that ends the answer with a clear idea.

blocks.x: Your goal on the day is not perfection. Band 7 still allows some mistakes. Keep talking, stay natural and show the examiner the range of English you have.
